The writers did not form a single school or share one style. “Magical realism” is a critical and marketing term with a longer genealogy — including Alejo Carpentier’s lo real maravilloso — and it fits some Boom books better than others. This lesson treats the Boom as novels, prizes, translators, and Cold War cultural circuits, not as a tropical brand. High modernism is an earlier Thursday in this archive; its experiments with time and form are named here only where the narrative method honestly overlaps. Existentialism is the previous literature Thursday; it is not repeated as a Paris café lesson. Literature literature 1949–55 Precursors Carpentier’s prologue on lo real maravilloso (1949). Juan Rulfo’s Pedro Páramo (1955) as a hinge novel of place and the dead. Borges already a master of the short form. 1959–61 Circuits open Cuban Revolution; Casa de las Américas founded in Havana (1959). Borges shares the 1961 Prix Formentor with Beckett — prestige for Spanish-language letters before the Boom label sticks. 1962–63 Early Boom novels Fuentes’s The Death of Artemio Cruz (1962). Vargas Llosa’s La ciudad y los perros wins Seix Barral’s Biblioteca Breve (1962) and appears as a book in 1963. Cortázar’s Rayuela (1963). 1966–67 Translation / Macondo Rabassa’s Hopscotch (1966) wins a U.S. National Book Award for translation. Cien años de soledad published in Buenos Aires by Sudamericana (1967). 1970 English solitude Rabassa’s One Hundred Years of Solitude appears in English. García Márquez later says he prefers the translation to his Spanish — a checkable boast about English as much as about Rabassa. c. 1971–75 The label thins Sales cool; political fights harden; critics begin to speak of a post-Boom. This lesson’s core stops here. 1982 / 1990s After-edges García Márquez’s Nobel (1982) is after the core Boom years. McOndo and the Crack generation later refuse the Boom’s export brand — named only as After, not as a full 1990s lesson. García Márquez waited years for Rabassa — then preferred the English Gregory Rabassa’s first major translation job was Julio Cortázar’s Rayuela, published in English as Hopscotch (1966); it won a U.S. National Book Award for translation. When García Márquez wanted One Hundred Years of Solitude rendered into English, Cortázar urged him to wait until Rabassa was free. García Márquez waited. The English book appeared in 1970. He later said he preferred Rabassa’s English to his own Spanish — a remark Rabassa waved toward the English language rather than toward himself. The Boom’s Anglophone life ran through a translator’s calendar as much as through a novelist’s desk. Latin American Boom Boom the Boom el Boom Critical and marketing name for the mid-1960s to mid-1970s international surge of Latin American novels in Spanish and in translation. A publishing event and a set of books, not a single school. magical realism magic realism realismo mágico realismo magico Critical and marketing label for fiction that treats extraordinary events in a matter-of-fact tone. It fits some Boom novels (especially García Márquez) better than others (Cortázar, Vargas Llosa). Older and wider than the Boom. lo real maravilloso lo real maravilloso americano the marvelous real marvelous realism Alejo Carpentier’s phrase, elaborated in his 1949 prologue to The Kingdom of This World: the marvelous as something encountered in American history and landscape, not only invented as fantasy. A precursor vocabulary for later “magical realism” talk. Seix Barral Barcelona publisher. Under Carlos Barral in the 1960s it promoted Latin American novelists through lists and the Biblioteca Breve prize; a key Spanish hub of the Boom’s European circulation. Biblioteca Breve Literary prize of Seix Barral. Vargas Llosa’s La ciudad y los perros won in 1962 (book 1963). A concrete prize date often used to mark the Boom’s publishing takeoff. Casa de las Américas Casa de las Americas Havana cultural institution founded in 1959 after the Cuban Revolution. Publisher, magazine, prize house, and meeting point on the Cold War cultural map many Boom writers argued over. regionalismo regionalism Earlier twentieth-century Latin American fiction centered on local landscape, custom, and rural or provincial life. The Boom’s international novels are often described against this prior horizon. criollismo Related earlier tendency emphasizing Creole local color and national types. Named here as Before, not as a full lesson. high modernism High modernism Earlier twentieth-century formal experiment treated in this archive’s Thursday lesson of that name. Named here where Boom narrative method — overlapping time, reader choice — honestly invites comparison. existentialism Previous literature Thursday in this archive (c. 1943–1960 Paris). Named only as the prior capsule; not repeated as a café syllabus. Jorge Luis Borges Borges Argentine writer (1899–1986). Master of the short fiction and essay before the Boom’s long-novel fame; shared the 1961 Prix Formentor with Beckett. Juan Rulfo Rulfo Mexican writer (1917–1986). Pedro Páramo (1955) is treated here as a hinge novel between regional place and later Boom experiments with time and the dead. Pedro Páramo Pedro Paramo Rulfo’s 1955 novel. A son enters a town of ghosts; place and the dead share the page. Precursor hinge, not a Boom marketing title. Alejo Carpentier Carpentier Cuban novelist and musicologist (1904–1980). Articulated lo real maravilloso; a precursor often filed beside, not inside, the Boom’s core cohort. The Kingdom of This World El reino de este mundo Carpentier novel, 1949. Its prologue is a usual source for lo real maravilloso. Gabriel García Márquez García Márquez Garcia Marquez Gabo Colombian novelist (1927–2014). One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967); Nobel Prize in Literature 1982 (after the core Boom years). Julio Cortázar Cortázar Cortazar Argentine writer (1914–1984). Rayuela / Hopscotch (1963); short stories including the one behind Antonioni’s Blow-Up. Formal experiment and Paris–Buenos Aires traffic. Mario Vargas Llosa Vargas Llosa Peruvian novelist (1936–2025). La ciudad y los perros / The Time of the Hero (1963); later a major post-Boom career and the 2010 Nobel. Often the Boom’s realist and political-novel pole. Carlos Fuentes Fuentes Mexican novelist (1928–2012). The Death of Artemio Cruz (1962); Aura (1962). History, power, and compact fantastic tales in the same years. José Donoso Donoso Jose Donoso Chilean novelist (1924–1996). Named among the Boom cohort; The Obscene Bird of Night (1970) is a later core exhibit often cited beside the “big four.” Guillermo Cabrera Infante Cabrera Infante Cuban writer (1929–2005). Tres tristes tigres (1967) and a baroque, nightlife Havana prose; Boom-adjacent, not a Macondo twin. Gregory Rabassa Rabassa American translator (1922–2016). Hopscotch (1966); One Hundred Years of Solitude (1970). A central courier of the Boom into English. Carlos Barral Barral Spanish poet and editor at Seix Barral. Promoted Latin American novelists from Barcelona in the 1960s. One Hundred Years of Solitude Cien años de soledad Cien anos de soledad 100 Years of Solitude García Márquez novel, Buenos Aires (Sudamericana), 1967. Seven generations of the Buendía family in Macondo; circular and overlapping time; the Boom’s most famous single book. Macondo Fictional town in One Hundred Years of Solitude. Founded, peopled, and finally erased in the novel’s weather and memory. Buendía Buendia Buendía family Family at the center of One Hundred Years of Solitude. Repeated names across generations are part of how the book makes time feel recursive. Hopscotch Rayuela Cortázar novel, 1963. Chapters can be read in more than one order; Paris and Buenos Aires share the book. English by Rabassa, 1966. The Time of the Hero La ciudad y los perros The City and the Dogs Vargas Llosa novel, 1963 (Biblioteca Breve 1962). Cadets in a Lima military academy; overlapping viewpoints; a crime and a cover-up. The Death of Artemio Cruz La muerte de Artemio Cruz Fuentes novel, 1962. A dying Mexican power broker remembered in shifting persons and tenses; Revolution to business empire. Aura Fuentes novella, 1962. A short, uncanny Mexico City narrative often filed beside the Boom’s longer books. Blow-Up Las babas del diablo Blow-Up stories Cortázar’s story “Las babas del diablo” (1959) was adapted by Michelangelo Antonioni as the film Blow-Up (1966). Named here as Cortázar’s short-form traffic into a wider arts public. Michelangelo Antonioni Antonioni Italian filmmaker. Blow-Up (1966) adapted Cortázar’s story; named because the film is how many non-Spanish readers first met the title. Sudamericana Editorial Sudamericana Buenos Aires publisher. Issued the first edition of Cien años de soledad in 1967. Prix Formentor Formentor Prize International Publishers’ Prize International publishers’ prize. Borges shared it with Beckett in 1961 — a prestige marker for Spanish-language letters just before the Boom label. Samuel Beckett Beckett Named here only as Borges’s 1961 Formentor co-winner, not as a Boom novelist. Cuban Revolution 1959 political rupture. A horizon many Boom writers supported, debated, or later broke over; not a single cause of novelistic style. Cold War Geopolitical frame for magazines, prizes, travel, and cultural funding that helped move Latin American books through Havana, Paris, Barcelona, and New York. McOndo 1990s anthology and slogan (McOndo, 1996) associated with a younger generation refusing the Boom’s export “magical” brand. Named only in After. Crack Crack generation generación del Crack Mexican 1990s writers’ manifesto and cohort reacting against Boom inheritance and magical-realist expectation. Named only in After. Nobel Prize Nobel Nobel Prize in Literature García Márquez received the literature prize in 1982 — after this lesson’s core Boom years. Place it in After. nouveau roman French nouveau roman French “new novel” of the 1950s–60s (Robbe-Grillet and others). By the Boom years its Paris prestige was fading; named as a same-time European comparison. Alain Robbe-Grillet Robbe-Grillet French novelist associated with the nouveau roman. Named as a marker of that fading Paris fashion. Chinua Achebe Achebe Nigerian novelist (1930–2013). Things Fall Apart (1958) was already famous when Boom novels toured; a same-time African comparison, not a Boom twin. Things Fall Apart Achebe’s 1958 novel. Named as an already-canonical African novel during the Boom’s takeoff years. Wole Soyinka Soyinka Nigerian writer (b. 1934). Plays and poetry across the 1960s independence years; named as a contemporaneous African literary public, not as magical realism. postmodernism US postmodern experiment American postmodernism Loose name for 1960s–70s U.S. experimental fiction (Pynchon and others) running in the same decades as the Boom. A parallel market of long, difficult novels — not a source code for Macondo. Thomas Pynchon Pynchon American novelist. Gravity’s Rainbow (1973) sits near the Boom’s later years as a concrete U.S. experimental long novel. Gravity’s Rainbow Gravity's Rainbow Pynchon novel, 1973. Named as a same-time U.S. doorstop of experimental ambition. Paris Translation and exile hub. Cortázar lived there; many Boom careers passed through French and Spanish European circuits. Madrid Spanish capital and publishing city named as a translation and distribution hub beside Barcelona. Barcelona Catalan city; Seix Barral’s base and a center of the Boom’s Spanish publishing story. Buenos Aires Argentine capital. Cortázar’s other city in Rayuela; Sudamericana’s home for the first Cien años edition. Havana La Habana Cuban capital. Site of Casa de las Américas and a political-cultural magnet after 1959. Lima Peruvian capital. Setting of The Time of the Hero’s military academy world. Mexico City Ciudad de México Ciudad de Mexico Setting and workplace associated with Fuentes; a major Spanish-language literary capital of the Boom years. Aracataca Colombian town of García Márquez’s childhood. Often named as a real-world hinge toward Macondo; the train tracks and church are later photographs of place, not of the novel. Cartagena Cartagena de Indias Colombian Caribbean city. Later associated with García Márquez’s life and public image; the walls photograph in this lesson is a city fact, not a Macondo map. National Book Award U.S. prize. Rabassa’s Hopscotch translation won in the translation category (1967 award for 1966 book). Richard Mortel Photographer of the 2016 Barcelona Gothic Quarter image used as this lesson’s hero. Escla Wikimedia photographer of the Casa de las Américas building image. Jose Lara José Lara Photographer of the CC-licensed García Márquez portrait used as this lesson’s thumbnail. The Cosmonaut Photographer of the Plaza de Mayo panorama used in this lesson. Ralf Treinen Ralf.treinen Photographer of the rue de Seine, Paris, image. Óscar Badillo Pérez Oscar Badillo Perez Photographer of the Aracataca train-tracks image. Manuel González Olaechea Manuel González Olaechea y Franco Manuel Gonzalez Olaechea Photographer of the Vargas Llosa portrait used here. Bernard Gotfryd Gotfryd Photographer of the 1987 Carlos Fuentes portrait (Library of Congress collection; treated as public domain on Commons). ProtoplasmaKid Photographer of the aerial Zócalo image of Mexico City. Joe Ross Photographer of the Cartagena city walls image. Plaza de Mayo Central square in Buenos Aires. The panorama in this lesson stands for Cortázar’s Argentine city, not for a single novel scene. Zócalo Zocalo Plaza de la Constitución Mexico City’s main square. The aerial photograph stands for Fuentes’s capital, not for a page of Artemio Cruz. rue de Seine Rue de Seine Street in Paris’s 6th arrondissement. Used here as a concrete Paris address for Cortázar’s European half of Rayuela. Vedado Havana neighborhood where the Casa de las Américas building stands. Leaf Storm La hojarasca García Márquez novella, 1955. Named as an earlier book before One Hundred Years of Solitude. The Autumn of the Patriarch El otoño del patriarca El otono del patriarca García Márquez novel, 1975. A dictator novel at the edge of this lesson’s Boom center. The Obscene Bird of Night El obsceno pájaro de la noche El obsceno pajaro de la noche Donoso novel, 1970. Often cited beside the Boom’s core shelf; named as a Donoso exhibit. Tres tristes tigres Three Trapped Tigers Cabrera Infante novel, 1967. Havana nightlife prose; Boom-adjacent. Virginia Woolf Woolf Novelist named here only as high modernism’s prior Thursday — a comparison of narrative method, not a Boom character. James Joyce Joyce Novelist named here only as high modernism’s prior Thursday — Dublin as a formal precedent for experimenting with time, not as Macondo’s twin. Dublin City of Joyce’s Ulysses. Named only in a negative comparison: Macondo is not Dublin. Before Regional novels, master short forms, and translation hubs Before the Boom became a press word, much Spanish-American fiction was still read primarily inside national or regional markets. Regionalismo and criollismo had taught readers to expect landscape, custom, and local types as the novel’s job. That older horizon matters because the Boom’s international fame was partly a contrast effect: long, ambitious novels that claimed world attention rather than only a provincial mirror. The contrast was never absolute. Earlier masters were already on the table. Jorge Luis Borges had remade the short story and the essay as philosophical machines; his 1961 Prix Formentor, shared with Samuel Beckett, was a prestige signal for Spanish-language letters before “Boom” stuck as a label. Juan Rulfo’s Pedro Páramo (1955) sits as a hinge: a Mexican novel of a town dense with the dead, where place is not scenery but the structure of the book. It is not a Boom marketing title. It is a prior technique of haunting that later readers cannot unread when they open Macondo. Train tracks in Aracataca, Colombia, photographed in the 2010s. García Márquez grew up in this town; later publicity often treated it as a real-world hinge toward Macondo. The rails and weeds are a place photograph. They are not a page from Cien años de soledad. Single railroad track running through green brush toward a low horizon under a pale sky in Aracataca, Colombia. The other Before is institutional geography. Paris and Madrid had long been translation and exile hubs for Spanish-language writers. Barcelona’s publishing houses — especially Seix Barral under Carlos Barral — would become decisive in the 1960s. After 1959, Havana’s Casa de las Américas offered prizes, a magazine, and a revolutionary cultural address on the Cold War map. Those circuits did not invent novelistic talent. They changed who could find a book, in which language, and with which prize sticker on the cover. The era Prizes, translations, and a political horizon The trigger is not a single manifesto. It is a pile-up of publication and translation dates. Carlos Fuentes’s The Death of Artemio Cruz appeared in 1962; his compact Aura belongs to the same year. Mario Vargas Llosa’s La ciudad y los perros won Seix Barral’s Biblioteca Breve in 1962 and was published as a book in 1963 — a Spanish prize launching a Peruvian novel into a wider Hispanic market. Julio Cortázar’s Rayuela appeared in 1963. Gabriel García Márquez’s Cien años de soledad was issued in Buenos Aires by Sudamericana in 1967; Gregory Rabassa’s English One Hundred Years of Solitude followed in 1970. Around them: José Donoso, Guillermo Cabrera Infante, and others who shared the traveling shelf without sharing one style. Spanish publishing in Barcelona, Argentine publishing in Buenos Aires, French and English translation desks, university reading lists in the United States — those are the Boom’s machinery. Casa de las Américas, Vedado, Havana. Founded in 1959, the institution was a prize house, publisher, and meeting point. Boom writers argued for, against, and about the Cuban Revolution as a political horizon. The building is that horizon made of concrete and a map relief — not a claim that Havana caused magical realism. Grey Art Deco Casa de las Américas building in Havana with a tall clock tower and a relief map of the Americas on the facade; pedestrians cross the street. The Cuban Revolution belongs in the Trigger section as politics, not as a style gene. Many writers initially saw Havana as a hope; Casa de las Américas institutionalized a hemispheric conversation; later breaks and disillusionments were just as public. Treat the Revolution as an argument the novels and the interviews kept having — censorship, commitment, travel bans, prizes — rather than as the secret cause of overlapping time or of Remedio’s ascent with the laundry. Cold War cultural circuits (magazines, congresses, funding, suspicion) moved manuscripts and reputations. The Boom is what happened when those circuits and a set of extraordinary novels met. How it showed up Long novels, several methods — and three to read slowly Name the shelf without flattening it. García Márquez: Leaf Storm earlier, then One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967), later The Autumn of the Patriarch (1975) at the edge of this lesson’s center. Cortázar: Rayuela (1963), short stories that include “Las babas del diablo,” the seed of Antonioni’s film Blow-Up (1966). Vargas Llosa: The Time of the Hero (1963), then expanding social canvases that stay closer to historical and institutional realism than to Macondo’s weather. Fuentes: The Death of Artemio Cruz and Aura (both 1962). Donoso and Cabrera Infante complicate any postcard of “the Boom equals magical realism.” Editors and translators matter: Carlos Barral in Barcelona; Gregory Rabassa in English, who reached García Márquez after Cortázar’s Hopscotch had already proved what a translation could do. High modernism’s earlier Thursday — Woolf, Joyce, broken ordinary time — is useful here only as a comparison of narrative method: Boom novels often make chronology itself the experiment, and Rayuela makes the reader’s path through chapters part of the form. That is kinship with modernist experiment, not a claim that Macondo is Dublin. Gabriel García Márquez 1927–2014 Colombian novelist and journalist. One Hundred Years of Solitude made Macondo a world address. The 1982 Nobel comes after this lesson’s core dates; place the prize in After. Portrait by Jose Lara (CC BY-SA 2.0). A later public face than 1967 — the man the Nobel photograph memory kept. Julio Cortázar 1914–1984 Argentine novelist and short-story writer, long based in Paris. Rayuela asks the reader to choose a path through chapters. A free Boom-era studio portrait is hard to license cleanly for this capsule; the Paris and Buenos Aires city photographs carry his geography instead. Mario Vargas Llosa 1936–2025 Peruvian novelist. The Time of the Hero is a military-academy novel of overlapping voices, not a magical-realist exhibit. He is essential to the Boom and a reminder that the Boom was never one style. Portrait by Manuel González Olaechea (CC BY 3.0). A later public image of the novelist whose 1963 debut helped mark the Boom’s prize years. Carlos Fuentes 1928–2012 Mexican novelist and essayist. The Death of Artemio Cruz rebuilds a life and a nation in shifting grammatical persons; Aura shows how compact uncanny fiction sat beside the doorstop novels. Bernard Gotfryd photograph, 1987 (Library of Congress collection; public domain on Commons). Later than Artemio Cruz, still the face of the Mexican Boom novelist. Plaza de Mayo, Buenos Aires. Cortázar’s Rayuela splits its life between Paris and Buenos Aires; this square is the Argentine capital as a public fact. The panorama is a city, not a chapter number. Wide panorama of Buenos Aires’s Plaza de Mayo with the pink Cabildo and Cathedral flanks, trees, and open paved square. Rue de Seine, Paris 6th arrondissement. Cortázar’s European decades make Paris half of Rayuela’s geography. The street photograph is an address for exile and translation culture, not a claim that the Boom was a French movement. Looking up the rue de Seine in Paris toward a cross street, pale stone buildings, parked cars, and a café banner. Deepen three objects. First, One Hundred Years of Solitude. The Buendía family repeats names across generations until chronology feels like a loop rather than a ladder. Macondo is founded, thrives, suffers war and foreign companies, and is finally wiped as if memory itself could be stormed away. Extraordinary events — a flying carpet, a girl rising with the laundry — are narrated in the same deadpan register as marriages and murders. That register is why the book became the classroom exhibit for “magical realism.” Honesty still requires a limit: the label’s genealogy runs through Carpentier’s lo real maravilloso and through earlier fantastic writing; and Vargas Llosa’s academy novel or Cortázar’s hopscotch structure are Boom books that do not live or die by that label. Second, Rayuela / Hopscotch. Cortázar prints a table of instructions: one path reads the chapters in order; another hops through a different sequence. Paris and Buenos Aires are not only settings; they are reading climates. The novel’s experiment is the reader’s agency inside a long form — closer, as narrative method, to high modernism’s formal risks than to a tropical brand. Rabassa’s 1966 English version won a National Book Award for translation and became the reason García Márquez was willing to wait for the same translator. Aerial view of the Zócalo (Plaza de la Constitución), Mexico City. Fuentes’s Boom years are inseparable from this capital’s history and power. The photograph is the square and its monuments — not a still from Artemio Cruz. Aerial view of Mexico City’s Zócalo: the wide paved square, the Metropolitan Cathedral, and the National Palace under a blue sky. Third, the Boom as a market and translation event. Seix Barral’s prizes and lists, Sudamericana’s 1967 first edition, Rabassa’s English, French and other European translations, U.S. university courses — these made “Latin American literature” a traveling category. The books are real achievements. The category was also sold. Holding both facts at once is the point of this Thursday. Same time elsewhere Other long novels, other publics While Boom novels were crossing the Atlantic, other literatures were not waiting for a Barcelona cue card. In the United States, postmodern experiment produced its own difficult doorstops; Thomas Pynchon’s Gravity’s Rainbow (1973) is a concrete same-decade comparison of scale and formal excess, not a source for Macondo. In Africa, Chinua Achebe’s Things Fall Apart (1958) was already famous when the Boom took off, and Wole Soyinka’s plays and public voice marked Nigerian letters through independence and after. From Latin America looking out, those books were contemporaneous world-literary facts: other languages, other empires ending or mutating, other claims on the long novel and the public stage. In Paris, the French nouveau roman associated with Alain Robbe-Grillet was losing the prestige slot it had held in the 1950s; the Boom’s Spanish-language energy was not a sequel to that fashion. City walls of Cartagena, Colombia. A Caribbean port later tied to García Márquez’s public life. Placed here as a Colombian city fact beside the “elsewhere” reminder that Boom fame was international — and that Colombia is not only Macondo. Stone fortification walls of Cartagena, Colombia, with a small white lighthouse tower and people walking along the rampart under a blue sky. After Post-Boom, Nobel edge, later refusals By the early 1970s the Boom label was already thinning under slower sales, aesthetic fatigue, and political fracture. What followed is usually called the post-Boom: writers who inherited an international audience without wanting to repeat Macondo on demand. García Márquez’s 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature belongs in this After paragraph — a global coronation slightly after the core Boom years this lesson maps. Still later, in the 1990s, the McOndo anthology and Mexico’s Crack generation made short, explicit refusals of the export brand of magical realism. Those refusals are a coda, not a second full lesson. The useful after is this: the novels remain; the postcard was always smaller than the shelf. A question A question to keep asking If a novel’s international life depends on a prize list and a translator’s calendar, what exactly are we praising when we praise “the Boom” — the sentences, or the shipping? Gabriel García Márquez — One Hundred Years of Solitude (Penguin UK catalogue) Legal edition listing for the Rabassa translation. Buy or borrow; this capsule does not paste the novel. Julio Cortázar — Hopscotch (Penguin Random House catalogue) Catalogue record for Rayuela in Rabassa’s English (National Book Award for Translation, 1967). Library copies exist; this is not a pirated PDF. Mario Vargas Llosa — La ciudad y los perros / The Time of the Hero (Penguin Random House catalogue) Legal trade listing for the 1963 novel (Biblioteca Breve 1962). Not a full-text dump. One Hundred Years of Solitude — Britannica Short reference entry on the 1967 novel. Check dates and outline here; read the book elsewhere legally. Latin American literature — Britannica Encyclopedia map of periods and names, including Boom context. Useful orientation; not a substitute for the novels. Gabriel García Márquez — Nobel Prize in Literature 1982 (Nobel Foundation) Official Nobel facts page. The 1982 prize is an After-edge for this lesson’s core Boom years.

subject: film
title: Taiwan New Cinema (c. 1982–1990s): local lives after martial-era studio habits
dek: Under martial law the Central Motion Picture Corporation had taught audiences healthy-realism and commercial genres. In the 1980s a younger generation, still often CMPC-backed, turned the camera onto Taipei streets, coming-of-age, and histories that had been hard to name — then learned to travel through festivals.
text: Taiwan New Cinema (c. 1982–1990s): local lives after martial-era studio habits Under martial law the Central Motion Picture Corporation had taught audiences healthy-realism and commercial genres. In the 1980s a younger generation, still often CMPC-backed, turned the camera onto Taipei streets, coming-of-age, and histories that had been hard to name — then learned to travel through festivals. c. 1982–1990s “Taiwan New Cinema” (台灣新電影) is a historians’ and critics’ name for a cluster of films and people from about 1982 into the early 1990s, not a union card and not a single manifesto that started the cameras. Many of the early features were still financed or released through the Central Motion Picture Corporation. Martial law ended on 15 July 1987; the films did not flip overnight with that date. The 1987 “Taiwan Cinema Manifesto” (also called the “Another Cinema” manifesto) was a public fight over policy, media, and criticism as much as a style sheet — and many writers treat it as a hinge toward the end of the first wave, not its birth certificate. French New Wave is a name that traveled; New Hollywood was the American industrial mode ending into blockbusters in the same calendar years. Neither is a template this lesson copies shot for shot. Film stills are usually still in copyright, so the pictures here are festival portraits, later memorials, and free exteriors, captioned as what they actually show. No AI people. Film film 1960s–70s Studio habits CMPC’s healthy-realism line and commercial genres (including Qiong Yao melodramas) under martial law. Hong Kong and Hollywood imports take much of the box office. “National cinema” often means Mandarin, party-aligned, and exportable to overseas Chinese markets. 1982 In Our Time CMPC omnibus In Our Time (光陰的故事): segments by Tao Te-chen, Edward Yang, Ko I-chen, and Chang Yi. Widely treated as the opening date for Taiwan New Cinema. 1983 Early CMPC turns Growing Up (小畢的故事) and the omnibus The Sandwich Man (兒子的大玩偶). Hou Hsiao-hsien, Wan Jen, and others move from script and segment work into features that look and sound unlike healthy-realism. 1985–87 Taipei films / manifesto / martial law Yang’s Taipei Story (1985) and The Terrorizers (1986). Hou’s Dust in the Wind (1986). The Taiwan Cinema Manifesto is drafted around late 1986 and published January 1987. Martial law is lifted 15 July 1987. 1989 Venice Hou’s A City of Sadness wins the Golden Lion at Venice — the first Taiwanese film to take the prize. 2/28 reaches a wide screen. 1991–93 Late first wave / Second New Wave edge Yang’s A Brighter Summer Day (1991). Hou’s The Puppetmaster (1993). Tsai Ming-liang’s early features begin to define a Second New Wave aftershock in the early 1990s. A City of Sadness was the first Taiwanese Golden Lion At the 46th Venice Film Festival in September 1989, Hou Hsiao-hsien’s A City of Sadness won the Golden Lion — Venice’s top prize. It was the first Taiwanese film to take that award. The film had already made a different kind of history at home: it was the first Taiwanese feature to put the February 28 Incident of 1947 openly on screen for a wide audience, two years after martial law ended. Festival travel and domestic argument arrived in the same season. Taiwan New Cinema New Taiwan Cinema Taiwanese New Wave 台灣新電影 New Taiwanese Cinema Critics’ and historians’ name for a cluster of Taiwanese films and filmmakers from about 1982 into the early 1990s: location shooting, understated acting, coming-of-age and urban Taipei, and nativist-literature adaptations, often still linked to CMPC money at the start. CMPC Central Motion Picture Corporation Central Motion Picture Company 中影 中央電影公司 Central Motion Picture Corporation, the major state-linked studio under the Kuomintang. It produced healthy-realism and commercial genres for decades, then financed early New Cinema omnibuses and features such as In Our Time. healthy-realism healthy realism 健康寫實 CMPC production line from the 1960s associated with studio head Kung Hung: films that looked “realistic” in texture while avoiding dark social exposure and promoting positive, humanitarian values. A studio habit, not a free press. martial law Martial Law 戒嚴 In Taiwan, the period of Kuomintang emergency rule lasting from 1949 until 15 July 1987. Film scripts, speech, and public history were constrained; New Cinema’s early years sit partly inside that frame and partly after it. White Terror white terror 白色恐怖 Common name for political repression under martial-law Taiwan: arrests, imprisonment, and executions of real or suspected dissidents. The term is wider than any single incident; 2/28 is an earlier hinge often linked to it in public memory. 2/28 228 February 28 Incident 228 Incident 二二八 二二八事件 The February 28 Incident of 1947: protests after a Tobacco Monopoly crackdown, then violent suppression by Nationalist forces newly administering Taiwan. Thousands were killed. A City of Sadness (1989) was the first Taiwanese feature to put it openly on a wide screen. nativist literature nativist xiangtu literature 鄉土文學 nativist literary Taiwanese literary current of the 1970s emphasizing local language, class, and place against purely mainland-centered or high-Mandarin culture. New Cinema adapted several of these stories; The Sandwich Man draws on Huang Chun-ming. long take long takes 長鏡頭 A shot that runs without a cut for an unusually long time. In Taiwan New Cinema criticism, long takes are often read as a way to watch social time pass — waiting, walking, a family meal — instead of chopping action into Hollywood continuity beats. Hollywood continuity continuity editing classical continuity The dominant classical editing style that matches eyelines, keeps geography clear, and moves the story beat by beat. New Cinema critics and filmmakers often worked against that tempo: longer shots, fewer explanatory cuts, more time left on the table. location shooting location 實景拍攝 Filming in real streets, houses, and landscapes rather than rebuilding everything on a soundstage. Taipei apartments, Jiufen hills, and ordinary rooms are part of how New Cinema looked “local.” Golden Lion Leone d’Oro 金獅獎 The top prize of the Venice Film Festival. A City of Sadness won it in 1989 — the first Taiwanese film to do so. Venice Film Festival Venice Mostra 威尼斯影展 Major European film festival on the Lido. For Taiwan New Cinema it was a path out: festival prizes made films travel when the domestic market was thinning. Taiwan Cinema Manifesto Another Cinema manifesto Another Cinema 台灣電影宣言 Public statement drafted around late 1986 and published in January 1987. Roughly fifty signatories asked for space for “another cinema” against unclear policy, entertainment-first media, and hostile criticism. Many historians treat it as a hinge near the end of the first wave. In Our Time 光陰的故事 1982 CMPC omnibus with segments by Tao Te-chen, Edward Yang, Ko I-chen, and Chang Yi. Conventional starting date for Taiwan New Cinema. Growing Up 小畢的故事 1983 CMPC-backed feature (Chen Kun-hou directing; Hou Hsiao-hsien among the writers). An early turn toward everyday coming-of-age rather than healthy-realism uplift. The Sandwich Man 兒子的大玩偶 1983 CMPC omnibus adapting Huang Chun-ming stories; segments by Hou Hsiao-hsien, Tseng Chuang-hsiang, and Wan Jen. A City of Sadness City of Sadness 悲情城市 1989 Hou Hsiao-hsien feature about a Taiwanese family across the mid-1940s, including 2/28. Golden Lion at Venice 1989. Taipei Story 青梅竹馬 1985 Edward Yang feature. Hou Hsiao-hsien acts opposite Tsai Chin. A mournful account of a couple and a city caught between property, baseball nostalgia, and a changing Taipei. The Terrorizers 恐怖分子 1986 Edward Yang feature. Interlocking Taipei lives, photography, and chance; urban form as the subject, not only the backdrop. A Brighter Summer Day 牯嶺街少年殺人事件 1991 Edward Yang epic about four hours set in early-1960s Taipei, centered on youth, gangs, rock and roll, and a real murder case. Late first-wave monument. Dust in the Wind 戀戀風塵 1986 Hou feature: young people leave Jiufen for work in Taipei. Yi Yi 一一 2000 Edward Yang family film, often a late summation rather than a New Cinema starter. The Puppetmaster 戲夢人生 1993 Hou film about Li Tian-lu and glove-theatre life under Japanese rule. Long takes and staged testimony; Jury Prize at Cannes. Vive L’Amour 愛情萬歲 1994 Tsai Ming-liang feature about empty apartments and lonely orbits in Taipei. Golden Lion at Venice 1994. Second New Wave aftershock, not the 1982 opening. That Day, on the Beach 海灘的一天 That Day on the Beach 1983 Edward Yang first feature. Sylvia Chang among the leads; friendship, marriage, and class in a modernizing Taiwan. Daughter of the Nile 尼羅河女兒 1987 Hou feature set in contemporary Taipei: night work, family strain, neon. Hou Hsiao-hsien Hou 侯孝賢 Taiwanese director, central New Cinema figure. From Sandwich Man and Dust in the Wind through A City of Sadness and later features. Also acted in Yang’s Taipei Story. Edward Yang Yang Yang Dechang 楊德昌 Taiwanese director. Segment in In Our Time; features including That Day on the Beach, Taipei Story, The Terrorizers, A Brighter Summer Day, and later Yi Yi. Tsai Ming-liang Tsai 蔡明亮 Malaysian-born Taiwanese director. Emerges in the early 1990s as Second New Wave aftershock: even longer takes, empty rooms, Lee Kang-sheng as recurring presence. Wang Tung Wang Toon 王童 Director associated with New Cinema-era CMPC and literary adaptations. Part of the wider field, not only the Hou-Yang duo. Wan Jen Wan 萬仁 Director; segment of The Sandwich Man (1983) and later features. One of the early omnibus names that made New Cinema look like a collective turn. Wu Nien-jen Wu Nien-chen Wu 吳念真 Writer, later director. CMPC script department; co-wrote key Hou films including Dust in the Wind and A City of Sadness. Sylvia Chang Chang 張艾嘉 Actor, producer, and later director. Appears in Yang’s That Day on the Beach and other 1980s work; a star-producer presence in the New Cinema years. Chu T’ien-wen Chu Tien-wen Zhu Tianwen 朱天文 Writer; long-time Hou collaborator, including A City of Sadness and Daughter of the Nile. Hsiao Yeh Xiao Ye 小野 Writer and CMPC figure who helped push early 1980s projects such as In Our Time when the domestic industry was losing audiences. Ming Ji Ming Chi 明驥 CMPC general manager in the period when the studio backed early New Cinema omnibuses. Kung Hung Gong Hong Kung Hong 龔弘 CMPC president associated with launching the healthy-realism production line in the 1960s. Chen Kun-hou Chen Kunhou 陳坤厚 Cinematographer-director; directed Growing Up (1983). Tao Te-chen Jim Tao 陶德辰 Director; one of four In Our Time segment directors (1982). Ko I-chen Ke Yizheng 柯一正 Director; In Our Time segment; later New Cinema-era features. Chang Yi Zhang Yi Yi Chang 張毅 Director; In Our Time segment director. Tseng Chuang-hsiang Zeng Zhuangxiang 曾壯祥 Director; segment of The Sandwich Man (1983). Huang Chun-ming Huang Chunming 黃春明 Nativist writer. Stories adapted in The Sandwich Man omnibus. Li Tian-lu Li Tien-lu 李天祿 Glove-theatre performer and actor. Subject and on-screen presence in Hou 1993 film 戲夢人生; also appears in other Hou films. Tony Leung Chiu-wai Tony Leung 梁朝偉 Hong Kong actor; plays the mute photographer Wen-ching in A City of Sadness. Tsai Chin 蔡琴 Singer-actor; leads Taipei Story opposite Hou Hsiao-hsien. Lee Kang-sheng Lee Kangsheng 李康生 Actor closely tied to Tsai Ming-liang films from the early 1990s onward. Second New Wave Taiwan Second New Wave 第二波新電影 Loose label for early-1990s filmmakers after the first New Cinema cluster — especially Tsai Ming-liang — working as domestic commercial cinema dried up and festival circuits mattered more. Fifth Generation Fifth Generation cinema 第五代 PRC film generation that emerged in the early 1980s from the Beijing Film Academy after the Cultural Revolution (Chen Kaige, Zhang Yimou, and others). Yellow Earth (1984) is a usual first international marker. Yellow Earth 黃土地 1984 Chen Kaige film, cinematography by Zhang Yimou. A Fifth Generation landmark that traveled festivals in the same decade as Taiwan New Cinema. Chen Kaige Kaige PRC Fifth Generation director. Yellow Earth (1984); later Farewell My Concubine (1993). Hong Kong New Wave Hong Kong Second Wave Hong Kong directors moving from 1970s television into features around 1979 (Ann Hui, Tsui Hark, and others), with a Second Wave into the 1980s-90s. Ann Hui Hui Hong Kong New Wave director (The Secret, 1979, and later Boat People). Contemporaneous regional peer, not a Taiwan studio product. New Hollywood American New Wave American studio period roughly 1967-1980 when conglomerates financed younger directors and antiheroes. By the mid-1980s that bet had tipped toward blockbusters — the Hollywood mode Taiwan New Cinema was not copying. French New Wave Nouvelle Vague French late-1950s/early-1960s cluster. The phrase new cinema/new wave traveled; Taiwan 1980s turn had its own studio (CMPC), martial-law context, and literary sources. Qiong Yao Chiung Yao 瓊瑤 Romance novelist whose adaptations were a CMPC and commercial staple before and beside New Cinema. Kuomintang KMT Nationalist Party 國民黨 Ruling party of the Republic of China on Taiwan through the martial-law decades. CMPC sat inside that political economy. Republic of China ROC 中華民國 The state governing Taiwan in this lesson’s years. National cinema before the 1980s often meant cinema for that state’s cultural policy and overseas Chinese markets. Government Information Office GIO 新聞局 Government office that oversaw film policy and guidance in the martial-law and early post-martial-law years. A target of the 1987 manifesto complaint about unclear aims. Jiufen Chiu-fen 九份 Hill town in northern Taiwan. Setting and location for Dust in the Wind and later heavily associated with A City of Sadness tourism. Taipei 臺北 台北 Capital and New Cinema main urban set: apartments, offices, night streets, and the middle-class lives Yang filmed. history from below Critical phrase for stories that follow families, workers, and local time instead of leaders’ speeches. Used here for how City of Sadness and related films let political violence arrive through a household. Before CMPC habits, martial law, and what “national cinema” meant Before the phrase Taiwan New Cinema stuck, the Republic of China film business had a clear center of gravity. The Central Motion Picture Corporation — CMPC (中影) — was the major state-linked studio. From the 1960s it promoted healthy-realism: films that borrowed the look of everyday life while keeping the social picture clean enough for a martial-law culture industry. Beside that line sat commercial genres audiences already knew how to buy, including Qiong Yao melodramas, comedies, and patriotic pictures. Hong Kong action and comedy imports, and Hollywood bookings, took a large share of the box office. A domestic Mandarin film was often asked to be national in a narrow sense: speak the language of official culture, travel to overseas Chinese markets, and not open subjects the Government Information Office and the censors preferred closed. Martial law, in force from 1949 until 15 July 1987, is the political frame for that studio habit. It does not mean every film was a propaganda reel. It does mean scripts moved through guidance, and that public history — especially 2/28 in 1947 and the long White Terror — was not ordinary commercial subject matter. National cinema in those decades was less a critics’ aesthetic category than a policy mood: cinema as cultural work for the ROC, produced inside institutions the Kuomintang could see. When audiences drifted toward Hong Kong and Hollywood, the problem for CMPC was industrial as well as ideological. By the late 1970s and early 1980s the studio’s own managers and writers were looking for cheaper, younger, more local films that might bring people back without simply copying a Hong Kong gag reel. Memorial to the Victims of the White Terror, at the northwest corner of Taipei Jieshou Park area, photographed in 2014. The sculptures and plaza are later public memory, not a 1980s film set. They stand here because martial-law repression is the political weather New Cinema inherited — including the histories early features could not yet name openly. Stone memorial sculptures of bound figures in an outdoor plaza in Taipei, with high-rises beyond the trees. That inheritance matters for how to read the “before.” Healthy-realism had already claimed the word realism. New Cinema would claim a different realism: location sound and rooms that were not moral examples, speech in Taiwanese as well as Mandarin where the story needed it, and — later — histories the studio system had kept off the marquee. The break was not a sudden private indie scene. It began, awkwardly, inside CMPC’s own attempt to renew product. The era 1982 as a door, 1987 as weather, festivals as a path The conventional opening date is 1982: In Our Time, a CMPC omnibus with four segments by Tao Te-chen, Edward Yang, Ko I-chen, and Chang Yi. The Chinese title means a story that unfolds with time; the English title nods at Hemingway. The industrial fact is simpler. CMPC, under managers such as Ming Ji and with writers including Hsiao Yeh and Wu Nien-jen in the pipeline, backed young directors to shoot everyday lives across decades of postwar Taiwan. The film’s success — limited booking windows and all — showed that a quieter, more observational domestic picture could still move tickets. It also gave critics a cluster they could name. 1983 widened the door. Growing Up, directed by Chen Kun-hou with Hou Hsiao-hsien among the writers, treated coming-of-age as something you could watch without a healthy-realism sermon. The Sandwich Man packaged three Huang Chun-ming adaptations directed by Hou, Tseng Chuang-hsiang, and Wan Jen — nativist literature moved onto film with CMPC still on the letterhead. These are not underground tapes. They are studio-backed turns that changed what a local film was allowed to look like: non-professional or understated acting, location shooting, long takes that let a street or a kitchen run longer than continuity editing would usually permit. Hou Hsiao-hsien, Tseng Chuang-hsiang, and Wan Jen at an open forum on The Sandwich Man during the International Film Festival of India in Goa, 29 November 2010. The suits and banner are 2010. The three names are the 1983 omnibus fact: early New Cinema as a shared CMPC package, not a lone genius myth. Hou Hsiao-hsien, Tseng Chuang-hsiang, and Wan Jen seated at a long table with microphones at a festival forum. Through the mid-1980s the look hardened into a critical vocabulary. Hou’s Dust in the Wind (1986) followed young people from Jiufen into Taipei work. Yang’s Taipei Story (1985) and The Terrorizers (1986) treated the capital’s apartments, offices, and chance meetings as form, not postcard. Critics talked about the long take as a concrete choice: stay with a corridor, a meal, a mute photographer’s waiting, instead of cutting every glance into Hollywood continuity. History from below is a useful phrase for the same habit when the subject turns political — let a family absorb the news, rather than stage a leader’s speech. None of this required a single switch on 15 July 1987, when martial law ended. The lift mattered as context: more room to speak, more risk that films would test what could be shown. It was weather, not a clapperboard. The cultural fight that does have a date on paper is the Taiwan Cinema Manifesto of early 1987 — sometimes called the “Another Cinema” manifesto — drafted around a late-1986 gathering associated with Edward Yang and published in January 1987. Roughly fifty filmmakers and cultural workers argued that policy swung unclearly among propaganda, industry, and culture; that mass media preferred star gossip to film as art; and that much local criticism pushed Hong Kong and Hollywood models. They asked for space for another cinema. Many historians read the document less as a birth certificate than as a hinge: the first wave already existed, domestic returns were softening, and the argument was about whether that cinema would be allowed to survive as culture rather than only as a failed commercial genre. Festival paths — especially European competitions — became one practical answer when Taipei bookings thinned. 228 Peace Memorial Park in Taipei Zhongzheng District, photographed in 2005 from the Shin Kong Life Tower observation deck. The park was New Park under martial law; it was renamed after democratization. The monument at center is later memory architecture. A City of Sadness (1989) put 2/28 on screen before this skyline view became a tourist caption. Aerial view of 228 Peace Memorial Park in Taipei with the central monument and tree canopy, city towers beyond. The field Many names, and three films to look at closely The field is wider than two auteurs. Hou Hsiao-hsien and Edward Yang are the names international festivals repeated first. Beside them: Wan Jen and Tseng Chuang-hsiang on The Sandwich Man; Wang Tung in CMPC literary and historical films; Wu Nien-jen in the script department and as Hou’s collaborator; Chu T’ien-wen as Hou’s other constant writer; Chen Kun-hou on Growing Up; Sylvia Chang as actor and producer in Yang’s That Day, on the Beach and across the industry’s star-producer lane. Tsai Ming-liang belongs at the edge of this lesson — early 1990s Second New Wave aftershock, not the 1982 omnibus door. The point of listing is industrial: New Cinema was a cohort overlapping CMPC, literature, and later independent production, not a club with one address. A City of Sadness (1989) is the film to deepen first. Hou, with Wu Nien-jen and Chu T’ien-wen writing, follows the Lin family across the mid-1940s: Japanese surrender, Nationalist arrival, 2/28, and the first cold years of repression. Tony Leung Chiu-wai plays Wen-ching, a deaf-mute photographer; much of what politics does to the household arrives as letters, absences, and rooms that hold still. The long take here is not decoration. It is how you watch people wait for news they cannot control. Venice gave the film the Golden Lion in September 1989 — the first Taiwanese Golden Lion — which meant the island’s forbidden history traveled as festival prestige at the same moment domestic audiences argued over it. Jiufen locations later became tourism; the film’s fact is older and colder than the souvenir shops. Hou Hsiao-hsien in 1989, the year of A City of Sadness and the Venice Golden Lion. A journalist’s outdoor portrait, not a still from the Lin family story. Close portrait of Hou Hsiao-hsien in 1989, jacket collar up, facing left of frame. Yang’s Taipei films are the second deepening. Taipei Story (1985) pairs Tsai Chin with Hou as a former baseball player drifting through property deals and old loyalties while the city rebuilds around them. The Terrorizers (1986) crosses a novelist, a doctor, a photographer, and a young woman whose phone calls puncture other lives; Taipei is mapped as simultaneous rooms rather than a single hero’s route. A Brighter Summer Day (1991) then widens the canvas to early-1960s youth — school uniforms, street gangs, American rock — and a murder case that becomes national allegory without ceasing to be a long, concrete adolescence. Against Hollywood continuity, Yang’s camera often holds a hallway or a night street until social geometry becomes visible. Urban form is the subject: who owns the apartment, who still talks about baseball, who gets left in the frame after the cut that never comes. Edward Yang with the Best Original Screenplay Golden Horse for A Confucian Confusion, 10 December 1994. The tuxedo and trophy are an awards-night document from after Taipei Story and The Terrorizers. The face is the director who had already made Taipei a formal problem for cinema. Edward Yang in a tuxedo holding a Golden Horse trophy in 1994. The third deepening is the CMPC-to-festival path itself. Early New Cinema needed the state studio’s schedules and money. International recognition — Venice for City of Sadness, later Cannes attention for Hou, Criterion and archive restorations decades on — is how the films kept circulating when Taiwan’s commercial screens preferred other product. Dust in the Wind and The Puppetmaster show Hou’s other mode: rural and colonial memory, Li Tian-lu’s testimony, trains and glove-theatre stages, still built from long looking. Sylvia Chang’s presence in Yang’s first feature reminds you that stars and producers shared the same years; Wan Jen’s career reminds you the omnibus was a group door. Theory talk that stays honest stays concrete: a long take is a decision about time; history from below is a decision about whose kitchen the news enters; both are arguments with continuity cinema’s habit of explaining too fast. Wan Jen at the Festival international des cinémas d’Asie in Vesoul, France, 2010. A later festival portrait of one of The Sandwich Man’s three 1983 directors. Wan Jen outdoors in a dark jacket, facing the camera, at a film festival in 2010. Sylvia Chang at the Hong Kong International Film Festival, 2011. Actor-producer in Yang’s That Day, on the Beach (1983) and a durable industry presence across the New Cinema years. The microphone and backdrop are 2011; the career overlap is 1980s fact. Sylvia Chang at a microphone in 2011, dark blazer, short hair. Elsewhere Same years: Fifth Generation, Hong Kong waves, Hollywood after New Hollywood Look out from Taipei, not from a worksheet that assigns one peer per continent. In the People’s Republic, the Fifth Generation was leaving the Beijing Film Academy into features: Chen Kaige’s Yellow Earth (1984), with Zhang Yimou photographing northern landscape and folk form, became an international marker the same decade Hou and Yang were redefining Taiwanese screens. The state, the censorship map, and the market were different. The shared fact is calendar and festival: both cinemas learned that European competitions could carry films their home booking systems undervalued. Chen Kaige speaking after a screening of Yellow Earth (1984) at the 50th Hong Kong International Film Festival (photograph dated 2026). The panel furniture is contemporary. The film named in the program is the 1984 Fifth Generation landmark — a PRC contemporaneous argument, not a Taiwanese sequel. Chen Kaige speaking into a microphone at a film festival panel, glasses and dark jacket. Hong Kong New Wave had already moved from television (especially TVB) into features around 1979 — Ann Hui, Tsui Hark, and others — with a Second Wave carrying into the 1980s. Those films shared a language market and a ferry distance with Taipei; they did not share CMPC’s martial-law brief. For Taiwanese producers the practical pressure was often Hong Kong’s commercial pull on local screens. That is a regional industrial fact, not a claim that Hui equals Hou. In the United States, New Hollywood was already ending. The director-driven studio bets of the 1970s had tipped, after Jaws and Star Wars, toward wide-release blockbusters; Heaven’s Gate (1980) is the usual tombstone in that American story. By the mid-1980s Hollywood’s loud export mode was the blockbuster and the high-concept booking, not Easy Rider. Taiwan New Cinema did not grow as a franchise of that American decade. It grew as a local answer to CMPC habits, Hong Kong imports, and a political thaw — while French New Wave remained a circulating name for young cinema, useful as analogy and misleading as origin myth. This lesson’s related links are for those honest comparisons: Nouvelle Vague as a traveling label; New Hollywood as the Hollywood mode that had already turned toward blockbusters when Taipei’s new films were finding their feet. After Second New Wave, commercial drought, festival auteurs By the early 1990s the first-wave energy had scattered. Domestic commercial cinema entered a long drought; Hong Kong and Hollywood continued to dominate bookings. Tsai Ming-liang’s early features — Rebels of the Neon God, then Vive L’Amour (1994), which itself took a Golden Lion — are usually filed as Second New Wave: even emptier Taipei rooms, bodies that wait, Lee Kang-sheng as a recurring presence. Hou and Yang became festival auteurs whose films might matter more in Paris or New York than in a Saturday Taipei multiplex. Yang’s Yi Yi (2000) arrived as a late summation. Later Taiwanese festival careers grew from this split: local screens thin, international prestige thick. The New Cinema years remain the hinge when local lives and difficult history got a camera style equal to them. Tsai Ming-liang at Tokyo Filmex, 2013. A Second New Wave aftershock portrait — years after In Our Time — of the director of Vive L’Amour. The coat and backdrop are 2013; the empty-room cinema is the 1990s fact. Tsai Ming-liang in a dark coat at Tokyo Filmex in 2013, looking toward the camera. A question A question to keep asking If a film holds a Taipei hallway or a family meal longer than continuity editing would usually allow, what history is it asking you to notice that a faster cut would skip? A City of Sadness — Criterion film page Hou Hsiao-hsien, 1989. Licensed home-video edition. This capsule does not link a pirated full film. Taipei Story — Criterion film page Edward Yang, 1985. Hou Hsiao-hsien acts opposite Tsai Chin. Licensed edition. The Terrorizers — Criterion film page Yang, 1986. Urban Taipei as crossed paths, not a tourist postcard. A Brighter Summer Day — Criterion film page Yang, 1991. Long coming-of-age epic set in early-1960s Taipei. Licensed edition. Dust in the Wind — Criterion film page Hou, 1986. Jiufen to Taipei; Wu Nien-jen among the writers. The Puppetmaster — Criterion film page Hou, 1993. Li Tian-lu’s life under Japanese rule; long takes and staged testimony. Vive L’Amour — Criterion film page Tsai Ming-liang, 1994. Second New Wave edge / aftershock, not the 1982 opening. Licensed edition.

subject: music
title: Punk (c. 1974–1978): short songs, small rooms, a fight with the 1970s
dek: After the long songs and large rooms of the early 1970s, New York and London — overlapping years, different class politics — brought the track back to two minutes. Independent labels, fanzines, and a few small clubs did the work. The press called it punk.
text: Punk (c. 1974–1978): short songs, small rooms, a fight with the 1970s After the long songs and large rooms of the early 1970s, New York and London — overlapping years, different class politics — brought the track back to two minutes. Independent labels, fanzines, and a few small clubs did the work. The press called it punk. c. 1974–1978 “Punk” is a press and fan word, not a union card. New York and London made short, loud records in overlapping years. They were not copies of each other, and they did not share a committee. Cleveland, Akron, Brisbane, Sydney, and late-1970s Tokyo were contemporaneous rooms, not a required pairing. MC5, the Stooges, and the New York Dolls are precursors — loud, short, ugly records before the word stuck. This lesson stops at the first wave. Post-punk and hardcore are named as the next rooms, not taught. 1970s band photographs are usually still in copyright, so the pictures here are venue exteriors and one museum object, all later than 1978 and captioned as such. Where a free picture could not be found, the lesson does without. No AI people. Music music 1973–74 Rooms and precursors Hilly Kristal opens CBGB at 315 Bowery, 10 December 1973. The New York Dolls have already issued a debut (1973). In London, Malcolm McLaren and Vivienne Westwood restyle 430 King’s Road as SEX in 1974. Pub rock is filling British pubs with short R&B. These are feeders and precursors, not yet the word “punk.” 1975 Horses / first Pistols gig Patti Smith’s Horses (Arista, 10 November). The Ramones are a CBGB regular. The Sex Pistols play their first gig at Saint Martin’s School of Art, 6 November. New York’s fiscal crisis is a fact of the streets around the Bowery; Britain is in recession. 1976 Records, fanzines, Grundy Ramones (Sire, 23 April). The Saints issue “(I’m) Stranded” on Fatal Records in Brisbane (September). Mark Perry starts Sniffin’ Glue (July). The 100 Club Punk Special, Oxford Street, 20–21 September. The Damned’s “New Rose” (Stiff, 22 October). “Anarchy in the U.K.” (EMI, 26 November). Bill Grundy’s Today interview, Thames Television, 1 December. 1977 Majors, bans, Bollocks EMI drops the Sex Pistols in January; A&M signs and drops them in one week in March; Virgin signs in May. “God Save the Queen” (27 May). The Clash (CBS, 8 April). Television’s Marquee Moon (February). X-Ray Spex, “Oh Bondage Up Yours!” (September). Never Mind the Bollocks, Here’s the Sex Pistols (Virgin, 28 October) enters the UK Albums Chart at number one. Wire’s Pink Flag (December). 1978–79 The first wave burns out Sex Pistols’ last gig of the original run: Winterland, San Francisco, 14 January 1978. The group splits. Nancy Spungen dies in October 1978; Sid Vicious dies in February 1979. Tokyo Rockers gigs at S-KEN in Roppongi from July 1978. Post-punk and hardcore are already opening other rooms. The album went to number one while a shop was in court for the sleeve Virgin released Never Mind the Bollocks, Here’s the Sex Pistols in the United Kingdom on 28 October 1977. The Clash are the political argument inside punk, not the only politics and not a pure one. Joe Strummer came from the 101ers. Mick Jones and Paul Simonon had been around the early London groups that never quite existed. They signed to CBS, a major, and spent a lot of “Complete Control” complaining about it. The debut album, The Clash, appeared in the United Kingdom on 8 April 1977. “White Riot,” the first single, was written after the 1976 Notting Hill Carnival clashes: white British punks watching Black Londoners fight the police and wanting a riot of their own. That is an awkward sentence on purpose. The band were more interested in reggae, in the dole, and in the idea that a three-minute song could name an enemy, than the Pistols were. They were also a rock group with a CBS catalogue number. Treat the politics as a real quarrel inside the scene — Strummer’s slogans against Rotten’s refusal — and not as a halo. Rough Trade on Talbot Road, 30 April 2009. Geoff Travis opened the first Rough Trade shop in Notting Hill in 1976 and the label in 1978. This is a later West London storefront, not a 1976 photograph. The stencil on the fascia is the independent-label fact made into a sign. A Notting Hill shopfront with a white sign reading ROUGH TRADE in black stencil letters, records in the window, a passer-by with a stroller on the pavement. The rest of the field is not a supporting cast. The Damned got the first UK punk 45 out: “New Rose,” Stiff Records, 22 October 1976, a week before “Anarchy.” Buzzcocks, from Manchester, treated the short song as pop — Pete Shelley and, at the start, Howard Devoto — and by September 1978 were on Top of the Pops. Television’s Marquee Moon (February 1977) is a CBGB record that allows a guitar to run, which is why it sits awkwardly in any list that thinks punk only means two chords. Wire, from London, made Pink Flag at the end of 1977: twenty-one tracks, most of them brief, already looking at the next room. Poly Styrene of X-Ray Spex shouted “Oh Bondage Up Yours!” in 1977 as a refusal of the same 1970s, from a different mouth. The Slits formed in 1976; their first album is 1979, which is why this lesson names the band and not the LP. Poison Ivy, with the Cramps, took rockabilly and a New York stage and did not ask permission. Patti Smith’s Horses remains the New York document that is a book as well as a record. Name them because they were there, not because a syllabus needed a balance. Elsewhere The same years, not a ranking of cities In Brisbane, the Saints recorded “(I’m) Stranded” in 1976 and issued it themselves on Fatal Records in September, with Ed Kuepper and Chris Bailey, because no Australian major wanted it. Copies went to British music papers. Sounds called it single of the week. EMI in London signed them. The 45 is earlier than “New Rose” and “Anarchy.” That is a date, not a trophy. Brisbane under Joh Bjelke-Petersen was a police town; the Saints were not a King’s Road boutique band, and they did not take kindly to being told to look like one when they reached England in 1977. In Sydney, Radio Birdman were playing a related short, loud set, closer to the Stooges than to McLaren, and issued Radios Appear in 1977. Australia was not waiting to be notified. In Cleveland and Akron, a Midwestern circuit had been making difficult records before the British tabloids discovered the word. Rocket from the Tombs lasted long enough in 1974–75 to split into Pere Ubu and the Dead Boys. The Dead Boys went to CBGB. Pere Ubu stayed stranger. Devo, from Akron, were art-school Ohio in the same years; Q: Are We Not Men? A: We Are Devo! is 1978. None of this is London exported to the lakes. It is a set of American rooms that used some of the same older records — Stooges, Velvets — and did not need a Grundy interview to exist. In Japan, the calendar runs a little later, which is why it belongs here as contemporaneous and not as a twin. SS formed in Kyoto in 1977 with the stated aim of playing faster than the Ramones; their records came out after the fact. In Tokyo, from July 1978, the musician and promoter S-KEN ran Sunday gigs at his Roppongi studio under the name Tokyo Rockers — Friction, Lizard, Mirrors among them — and Shinjuku Loft, which had opened in October 1976, was one of the live rooms. A live compilation followed in 1979. That is the end-edge of this lesson’s years, a local circuit hearing imported 45s and answering in Japanese rooms. It is not an assigned Asian verse to make the map look fair. After 1978–79: the first wave ends, other rooms open The Sex Pistols’ last concert of the original run was at the Winterland Ballroom in San Francisco on 14 January 1978, a Bill Graham room, far larger than CBGB or the 100 Club. Sid Vicious was barely playing. Lydon ended the night with a question — “Ever get the feeling you’ve been cheated?” — and left. The group split. Nancy Spungen died in New York in October 1978. Vicious died in February 1979. Those dates are the burnout of one band and one press story, not a moral. By then the first-wave rooms were already emptying or turning over. What opened next were other rooms with other names: post-punk, which kept the shortness and changed the harmony and the rhythm; and hardcore, which kept the shortness and raised the speed. Wire were already on that hinge. This lesson does not teach those eras. It only notes that 1974–78 was a fight with the 1970s, and that the fight did not end when the Pistols did. It moved. A question A question to keep asking If a two-minute song in a small room is a refusal of stadiums and solos, who still owns that refusal once the tabloids, the majors, and the uniform arrive? Ramones — Blitzkrieg Bop (1976) YouTube Topic upload provided by Rhino/Warner from the 1976 Sire album Ramones, 2016 remaster. Studio recording, about two minutes. Official audio, not a later concert film. If the file moves, search the title plus Sire or Rhino. Patti Smith — Gloria: In Excelsis Deo (1975) YouTube Topic upload provided by Arista/Legacy from Horses (1975), produced by John Cale. The Horses album version, not the later RCA demo issued for the 50th-anniversary edition. Official audio. Sex Pistols — Anarchy in the U.K. (1976/77) YouTube Topic upload provided by Rhino/Warner from Never Mind the Bollocks, Here’s the Sex Pistols. The original UK 45 was EMI, 26 November 1976; this is the album master issued on Virgin in 1977 and later by Warner in the United States. Official audio of the studio recording, not the 1978 Dallas live tape. The Clash — White Riot (1977) Official video on theclashVEVO. UK 45, CBS, 18 March 1977; also on The Clash. This upload is the promotional film, not a 1977 television clip. If it moves, search the title on the Clash’s official channel. X-Ray Spex — Oh Bondage Up Yours! (1977) YouTube Topic upload provided by Universal/Castle from the 1977 Virgin single, Poly Styrene on vocals. Official audio. About two and a half minutes. Buzzcocks — Ever Fallen in Love (With Someone You Shouldn’t’ve?) (1978) Official upload on the Domino Recording Co. channel: the Top of the Pops performance recorded for BBC 1 and first broadcast 21 September 1978, licensed courtesy of BBC Studios. This is a television date at the end of the first wave, not the studio 45. Labeled as what it is.

subject: feminism
title: Third Wave (c. 1991–2010s): after the backlash, many feminisms
dek: A televised harassment hearing, a 1992 essay in Ms., riot-grrrl zines, and a legal name for compounded harm made feminism look like several projects at once. The number was later. The fights were not one movement with a single face.
text: Third Wave (c. 1991–2010s): after the backlash, many feminisms A televised harassment hearing, a 1992 essay in Ms., riot-grrrl zines, and a legal name for compounded harm made feminism look like several projects at once. The number was later. The fights were not one movement with a single face. c. 1991–early 2010s “Third wave” is a later Anglo-American classroom and magazine name, not what most of the people in this lesson called themselves in 1991. The dates are a convenience: Anita Hill’s testimony and Rebecca Walker’s Ms. essay at one end, the early 2010s at the other, before hashtag feminism became a different media ecology. The United States is the spine because the numbering is. Riot grrrl is a scene, not a synonym for the whole span. Intersectionality is a legal concept that escaped the academy; it is not a personality. Other countries’ 1990s feminisms are contemporaneous — not copies of an American original. 1990s press portraits are often still in copyright. The photographs here are a congressional collection image with no known restrictions, a Creative Commons concert picture, a later Creative Commons portrait (captioned as later), and a U.S. government photograph from Beijing. Where a free picture could not be found, the lesson does without. Feminism feminism 1989 Intersection Kimberlé Crenshaw, “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex,” University of Chicago Legal Forum. A legal paper about how employment-discrimination doctrine missed Black women. The word intersectionality is here. The who-counts problem is older. 1991 Backlash / Hill / zines Susan Faludi, Backlash. Anita Hill testifies, 11 October; Clarence Thomas confirmed 15 October, 52–48. Riot grrrl meetings, shows, and zines in Olympia and Washington, D.C. Crenshaw, “Mapping the Margins.” 1992 The name Rebecca Walker, “Becoming the Third Wave,” Ms., January/February. Third Wave Direct Action Corporation founded. U.S. elections later nicknamed the Year of the Woman: four new women enter the Senate, including Carol Moseley Braun. 1995 Beijing Fourth World Conference on Women, Beijing, 4–15 September. Governments adopt the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action. A parallel NGO Forum meets in Huairou. Not an American meeting with foreign guests. 1996–98 Taiwan statutes After the murder of Peng Wan-ru in 1996, Taiwan passes a Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act (1997) and a Domestic Violence Prevention Act (1998). The Awakening Foundation had already been lobbying Civil Code family law. 1999–2000 Parité / Manifesta France revises the Constitution for equal access of women and men to elective office (1999) and passes a parité law (2000). Jennifer Baumgardner and Amy Richards publish Manifesta in the United States. early 2010s A later ecology The numbered “third wave” is already a classroom label. Hashtag campaigns and #MeToo belong to a later media system. They are the after, not a fourth-wave lesson in disguise. The committee that questioned her had no women on it When Anita Hill testified on 11 October 1991, every member of the Senate Judiciary Committee was a man. There were two women in the whole Senate that year: Nancy Kassebaum of Kansas and Barbara Mikulski of Maryland. Neither sat on the committee. In 1992 the press named the elections the Year of the Woman. Four new women arrived in the Senate in January 1993 — Barbara Boxer and Dianne Feinstein of California, Patty Murray of Washington, and Carol Moseley Braun of Illinois, the first Black woman elected to that body. The nickname is journalism. The arithmetic is the record: an all-male panel on television, then a small change in who held the seats. third wave Third Wave third-wave third-wave feminism A later Anglo-American label for feminist work roughly from 1991 through the early 2010s. Rebecca Walker’s 1992 Ms. essay is the usual christening. Most people in the work did not carry membership cards. Rebecca Walker American writer, born 1969. “Becoming the Third Wave,” Ms., January/February 1992. Co-founder, with Shannon Liss, of the Third Wave Direct Action Corporation. Alice Walker is her mother; that fact is biography, not a job description. Becoming the Third Wave Rebecca Walker’s essay in Ms., January/February 1992, written after the Hill–Thomas hearings. It ends: she is not a postfeminism feminist; she is the Third Wave. Ms. Ms. magazine Ms magazine U.S. feminist magazine, first standalone issue 1972. Walker’s essay ran in the January/February 1992 issue of the relaunched, ad-free Ms. The magazine is a second-wave institution publishing a younger writer. Anita Hill American lawyer and professor, born 1956. In October 1991 she testified that Clarence Thomas had sexually harassed her when she worked for him at the Department of Education and the EEOC. She was then on the faculty at the University of Oklahoma. Anita Hill hearings Hill hearings Hill–Thomas hearings Clarence Thomas hearings Senate Judiciary Committee hearings, 11–13 October 1991, on Hill’s sexual-harassment allegations against Supreme Court nominee Clarence Thomas. Televised. Thomas was confirmed 15 October, 52–48. Clarence Thomas U.S. jurist, born 1948. Nominated to the Supreme Court in 1991 to succeed Thurgood Marshall. Denied Hill’s allegations; described the process as a “high-tech lynching.” Confirmed 52–48 on 15 October 1991. Senate Judiciary Committee Judiciary Committee U.S. Senate committee that handles judicial nominations. In October 1991 every member was a man. Joseph Biden of Delaware chaired it. Joseph Biden Joe Biden Biden U.S. senator from Delaware in 1991; chair of the Judiciary Committee during the Hill hearings. Later U.S. president. The chairmanship is the fact this lesson needs. Thurgood Marshall Supreme Court justice, 1967–1991, the first Black justice. Thomas was nominated to the seat he left. George H. W. Bush George Bush President Bush U.S. president who nominated Clarence Thomas in 1991. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission EEOC U.S. federal agency that enforces workplace civil-rights statutes. Hill and Thomas both worked there. Sexual harassment was already within its mandate. Department of Education U.S. Department of Education U.S. federal department. Hill worked in its Office for Civil Rights when she first worked for Thomas. University of Oklahoma Public university. Hill was a law professor there in 1991. Title VII Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the U.S. employment-discrimination statute. By 1986 the Supreme Court had read it to cover sexual harassment. The Hill hearings were not the invention of that law. They were a public lesson in whether anyone believed it. sexual harassment Unwelcome sexual conduct that is made a condition of work or that creates a hostile workplace. U.S. law already named it before 1991. The hearings made the phrase ordinary television language. backlash Faludi’s 1991 name for a 1980s cultural and political reaction that treated feminist gains as excess and blamed them for women’s unhappiness. The conservative turn itself is already in the Second Wave lesson’s last years. Susan Faludi American journalist. Backlash: The Undeclared War Against American Women (Crown, 1991). A named diagnosis of the 1980s, published the same year as the Hill hearings. Backlash Backlash: The Undeclared War Against American Women Susan Faludi’s 1991 book. Subtitle: The Undeclared War Against American Women. A later name for a mood already in motion. postfeminism post-feminism postfeminism feminist A 1980s–90s media claim that feminism had succeeded and was no longer needed, or had become the problem. Walker’s essay refuses the word. intersectionality Kimberlé Crenshaw’s name, from 1989, for the way race and sex (and other structures) compound so that a person at the overlap can disappear from laws and movements built on a single axis. In the 1989 paper it is a problem in employment-discrimination doctrine, illustrated with cases in which Black women lost because an employer hired white women and Black men. It is a legal concept, not a mood. Kimberlé Crenshaw Crenshaw Kimberle Crenshaw American legal scholar, born 1959. “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989); “Mapping the Margins” (1991). The usual source for the word intersectionality. Combahee had already described interlocking oppressions without that word. Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex Demarginalizing Crenshaw’s 1989 article in the University of Chicago Legal Forum. Employment discrimination, single-axis doctrine, Black women. The named origin of “intersectionality.” Mapping the Margins Mapping the Margins: Intersectionality, Identity Politics, and Violence against Women of Color Crenshaw’s 1991 Stanford Law Review article. Subtitle: Intersectionality, Identity Politics, and Violence against Women of Color. Battering, rape, and how feminist and antiracist politics each miss women who live in both. DeGraffenreid v. General Motors DeGraffenreid Employment-discrimination case Crenshaw uses in the 1989 paper. Black women alleged they were not hired or were laid off because they were Black and women. The court treated race and sex as separate claims. GM hired women (who were white) and Black people (who were men). The overlap had no place to stand. Combahee River Collective Combahee Black feminist lesbian socialist collective, Boston, 1974–1980. Their April 1977 statement is in the Second Wave capsule. Pointer, not a reprint: interlocking racial, sexual, heterosexual, and class oppression. Crenshaw’s later word names a problem they had already stated. Combahee River Collective Statement Combahee statement April 1977. The who-counts document of the previous Monday lesson. Third-wave writers inherited it even when they did not cite it. riot grrrl Riot Grrrl riot grrl A feminist punk scene, especially Olympia, Washington, and Washington, D.C., from about 1991. Zines, shows, meetings, “girls to the front.” Bikini Kill and Bratmobile are the bands most often named. A scene with a growl in the spelling. Not a synonym for third-wave feminism. zine zines fanzine A small, usually photocopied magazine made by its editors and handed out or mailed. Short for fanzine. Riot grrrl’s method: you did not wait for a New York house to print you. Bikini Kill Punk band formed in Olympia, Washington, 1990: Kathleen Hanna, Kathi Wilcox, Tobi Vail, Billy Karren. A riot-grrrl band. Not the whole scene and not the whole wave. Kathleen Hanna Hanna Musician and zine writer, born 1968. Bikini Kill’s singer. Associated with early riot-grrrl meetings and with the “Riot Grrrl Manifesto” printed in Bikini Kill no. 2 (1991). Kathi Wilcox Bassist of Bikini Kill. Tobi Vail Drummer of Bikini Kill; also a zine writer. The band is a four-person fact, not a solo. Billy Karren Guitarist of Bikini Kill in the early 1990s. Bratmobile Riot-grrrl band, Olympia and D.C., associated with Allison Wolfe, Molly Neuman, and Erin Smith. Named here so Bikini Kill is not the only band in the sentence.
