Riot Grrrl Manifesto riot grrrl manifesto Statement printed in Bikini Kill no. 2, 1991, often titled that later. It starts from records, books, and fanzines that include girls, and from the refusal to wait. A zine page, not an office platform. girls to the front girl to the front A riot-grrrl practice at shows: girls asked to come to the front of the room so they could see, be seen, and not be shoved by a male pit. A method, not a metaphor. DIY Do-it-yourself. In this lesson: photocopying zines, booking shows, recording without waiting for a major label. A method borrowed from punk. Jennifer Baumgardner Baumgardner American writer. Co-author, with Amy Richards, of Manifesta (2000). Amy Richards Richards American writer and organizer. Co-author of Manifesta (2000); later work with the Third Wave Foundation. Manifesta Manifesta: Young Women, Feminism, and the Future Jennifer Baumgardner and Amy Richards, Manifesta: Young Women, Feminism, and the Future (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2000). A U.S. attempt to describe the generation after the second wave. A book, not a census. Shannon Liss Shannon Liss-Riordan Organizer. Co-founded the Third Wave Direct Action Corporation with Rebecca Walker in 1992. Later known as Shannon Liss-Riordan. Third Wave Direct Action Corporation Third Wave Foundation Third Wave Fund Organization founded in 1992 by Rebecca Walker and Shannon Liss to get young women into political work. Later the Third Wave Foundation; today’s descendant is the Third Wave Fund. bell hooks hooks Gloria Jean Watkins Writer (Gloria Jean Watkins, 1952–2021). Ain’t I a Woman (1981) is already in the Second Wave window. In the 1990s she published Teaching to Transgress (1994) and, in 2000, Feminism is for Everybody. A through-line, not a third-wave founder. She kept the name lowercase. Teaching to Transgress Teaching to Transgress: Education as the Practice of Freedom bell hooks, Teaching to Transgress: Education as the Practice of Freedom (Routledge, 1994). A 1990s book, read in classrooms that also read third-wave essays. Feminism is for Everybody Feminism Is for Everybody Feminism is for Everybody: Passionate Politics bell hooks, 2000 (South End Press). A short book that tries to explain feminism without requiring a graduate seminar. Dated at the end of this lesson’s window. Judith Butler Butler American philosopher, born 1956. Gender Trouble (1990). Adjacent theory: gender as performed under constraint. Not “the third wave,” and not a substitute for Hill, Walker, or Crenshaw. Gender Trouble Gender Trouble: Feminism and the Subversion of Identity Judith Butler, Gender Trouble: Feminism and the Subversion of Identity (Routledge, 1990). A theory book that circulated on campuses in the same years. Adjacent, not a founding pamphlet. sex-positive feminism sex-positive sex positive feminism A current that treated sexual speech, pornography, and queer practice as sites of freedom as well as harm. It argued with late-second-wave anti-porn campaigns. Third-wave writing is often described as more sex-positive. The description is a tendency, not a vote. Women Against Pornography WAP Organization founded in New York in 1979. Already in the Second Wave lesson. The argument continued into the 1990s; it did not restart as a third-wave invention. Bust Bust magazine Independent feminist magazine, first issue 1993. One of the small print projects that carried girl culture and sex-positive writing outside Ms. Bitch Bitch magazine Independent feminist magazine, first issue 1996, founded by Lisa Jervis, Benjamin Shaykin, and Andi Zeisler. Pop-culture criticism. In copyright; named as a publication, not reproduced. Alice Walker American writer; author of The Color Purple. Rebecca Walker’s mother. Named because Ms. said so and because the younger Walker writes in that fact. Not a third-wave figure. Fourth World Conference on Women Beijing conference Beijing 1995 UN Fourth World Conference on Women United Nations conference, Beijing, 4–15 September 1995. 189 governments. Produced the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action. The official meeting. The NGO Forum was nearby, in Huairou. Beijing Declaration Document adopted by governments at Beijing in September 1995, paired with the Platform for Action. Platform for Action Beijing Platform for Action The 1995 Beijing plan: twelve critical areas of concern, from poverty and education to violence, armed conflict, the economy, power, human rights, media, the environment, and the girl child. A UN document, not a U.S. statute. Huairou NGO Forum NGO Forum on Women District outside Beijing. Site of the 1995 NGO Forum on Women, parallel to the official UN conference. Tens of thousands of non-governmental delegates. Not a footnote to the hall with the flags. Hillary Rodham Clinton Hillary Clinton Clinton U.S. First Lady in 1995. She addressed the Beijing conference on 5 September. The line “human rights are women’s rights, and women’s rights are human rights” is hers in that speech. She did not run the conference. Sharon Farmer White House photographer. She made the 5 September 1995 Beijing photographs used in this capsule. U.S. government work. Awakening Foundation 婦女新知 婦女新知基金會 Awakening Taiwanese feminist organization (婦女新知基金會). Magazine from 1982; foundation after martial law was lifted in 1987. In the 1990s it lobbied family-law reform and trained women for public life. Peng Wan-ru 彭婉如 Taiwanese feminist and Democratic Progressive Party official (彭婉如). Murdered in 1996. The killing became a public catalyst for sexual-assault legislation the next year. Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act Sexual Assault Prevention Act Taiwan statute, 1997, passed after Peng Wan-ru’s murder and years of feminist lobbying. Domestic Violence Prevention Act Taiwan statute, 1998. A 1990s women’s-movement law, not an import of a U.S. wave name. Civil Code Book of Family Taiwan’s civil law. The family chapters treated married women’s residence, property, and children’s surnames as the husband’s default. Awakening and allied groups spent the 1990s trying to rewrite those chapters. Huggy Bear British riot-grrrl band, early 1990s. Evidence that the scene was not only Olympia. Named so the U.S. bands are not the whole map. Loaded Loaded magazine British men’s magazine, launched 1994. A flagship of 1990s “lad” culture. The tabloid counterpart was the “ladette.” ladette ladettes British tabloid word, mid-1990s, for young women who drank, smoked, and were sexually blunt in public. Sometimes claimed as agency, sometimes used as a moral panic. Contemporaneous with third-wave years; not a chapter of Ms. parité parite parité law French campaign in the 1990s for equal numbers of women and men in elective office. Constitutional revision, 8 July 1999; election law, 6 June 2000. Year of the Woman U.S. press name for the 1992 elections, after the Hill hearings. Four new women senators, including Carol Moseley Braun. A headline, not a revolution in the body’s sex ratio. Carol Moseley Braun Carol Moseley-Braun Moseley Braun Illinois Democrat; elected to the U.S. Senate in 1992. First Black woman in that body. Barbara Boxer California Democrat; elected to the U.S. Senate in 1992. Dianne Feinstein California Democrat; elected to the U.S. Senate in 1992. Patty Murray Washington Democrat; elected to the U.S. Senate in 1992. Nancy Kassebaum Republican senator from Kansas in 1991. One of two women in the Senate during the Hill hearings. Not on the Judiciary Committee. Barbara Mikulski Democratic senator from Maryland in 1991. The other woman in the Senate that year. Not on the Judiciary Committee. Tarana Burke Burke American organizer. She used “Me Too” as a phrase for survivors of sexual violence in 2006, in community work, not on Twitter. The 2017 hashtag is later and larger. #MeToo Me Too MeToo hashtag feminism Hashtag that spread globally in 2017 after public accusations against Harvey Weinstein. A later media ecology than zines and C-SPAN. This lesson names it as after, not as a fourth-wave chapter. Harvey Weinstein Film producer. Public accusations against him in 2017 helped ignite the #MeToo cascade. Named only as a date in the after. Roe v. Wade Roe U.S. Supreme Court decision, 1973, already treated in the Second Wave capsule. It still stood during the third-wave years. Dobbs (2022) is later. Equal Rights Amendment ERA The U.S. ERA’s extended deadline expired 30 June 1982. That failure is the Second Wave lesson’s ending, not this one’s opening tour. Title IX Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972. Already in the previous Monday lesson. Campus sex-discrimination fights in the 1990s stood on this statute. Olympia City in Washington state. One of the two early riot-grrrl centers, with Washington, D.C. First Wave Later label for the suffrage-era fights in this archive’s Monday lesson of 16 August 2026. The who-counts problem did not end when the vote arrived. Second Wave Later label for the 1963–1982 span in this archive’s Monday lesson of 17 August 2026. Consciousness-raising, Title IX, Roe, Combahee, the ERA’s failure. This lesson starts after that failure, not inside it. R. Michael Jenkins Jenkins CQ Roll Call staff photographer. He made the 11 October 1991 Anita Hill photograph used as this capsule’s hero. CQ Roll Call Congressional Quarterly U.S. congressional news organization. Staff photographs in the Library of Congress collection used here carry the advisory “no known restrictions on publication.” Jonathan Charles Photographer of the 1991 Bikini Kill outdoor picture used in this lesson. Flickr, CC BY-SA 2.0. Mohamed Badarne Photographer of the 2018 Kimberlé Crenshaw portrait used here. Taken for the Heinrich Böll Foundation. CC BY-SA 2.0. Heinrich Böll Foundation Heinrich-Böll-Stiftung Böll Foundation German political foundation. Source of the 2018 Crenshaw photograph. Tavi Gevinson Tavi American writer, born 1996. Style Rookie blog from 2008; Rookie magazine from 2011. Named in this lesson only to say she is not stretched backward into 1991. She belongs with a later media system. Democratic Progressive Party DPP Taiwanese political party. Peng Wan-ru held a party post in its women’s organization when she was murdered in 1996. Named as her workplace, not as the women’s movement. Comoros Island country in the Indian Ocean. Its country placard is readable in the 5 September 1995 Beijing photograph used in this lesson. Evidence that the hall was a UN meeting of states, not a U.S. rally. Before What the second wave won, and what a 1991 book called the backlash The Second Wave capsule in this archive ends in 1982, when the Equal Rights Amendment’s extended deadline expired three states short. That lesson already covers the ground this one should not tour again: Betty Friedan’s book as a public starting point, consciousness-raising as a method, Title IX, Roe v. Wade, the Combahee River Collective Statement of April 1977, Houston, Phyllis Schlafly, and the conservative turn that put Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher in office. Those last years are the floor this lesson walks onto. They are not a second visit to the same rooms. By the late 1980s a public story said feminism had been tried. Magazines ran features on women who had “had it all” and were exhausted. The word postfeminism circulated as if the remaining task were to relax. In 1991 Susan Faludi, then a reporter, published Backlash: The Undeclared War Against American Women. She argued that the 1980s had produced a cultural and political reaction — in news, in Hollywood, in Washington — that blamed feminism for unhappiness it had not caused. The book is a named source for that diagnosis. It is not a census of every country. It is not a claim that organizing had stopped. Faludi was writing about a mood that treated women’s gains as the problem. The who-counts fight was unfinished. The Combahee River Collective had already written, in 1977, that racial, sexual, heterosexual, and class oppression lock together, and that they would not choose which liberation to stand in line for. That statement is in the Second Wave lesson. It is the parent of much that later gets called intersectionality. The later word is Kimberlé Crenshaw’s. The problem is older. A third-wave story that pretends Black feminists arrived in 1991 is repeating the error the previous lesson tried to correct. The era A hearing on television, a sentence in Ms., a scene with a growl, and a legal word On 11 October 1991 Anita Hill sat at a witness table in Washington and testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee. Hill was a law professor at the University of Oklahoma. She had worked for Clarence Thomas at the U.S. Department of Education and at the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. Thomas, a federal appeals judge, had been nominated to the Supreme Court by President George H. W. Bush to succeed Thurgood Marshall. Hill told the committee that Thomas had sexually harassed her in those workplaces — comments, pressure, a pattern she said she had not made public because she feared for her career. Every member of the committee that questioned her was a man. Joseph Biden of Delaware chaired it. The hearings were televised. Thomas denied the allegations and described the process as a “high-tech lynching for uppity Blacks.” On 15 October the Senate confirmed him, 52 to 48. The hearings were a public school. Millions of people watched a Black woman describe sexual harassment to a panel of white men, and watched a Black man answer in the language of racial persecution. Viewers did not agree about who was telling the truth. They did agree, in large numbers, that the subject was now national. Sexual harassment was already in U.S. law; Title VII of the Civil Rights Act had been read to cover it. What the hearings changed was the audience. A private injury, of the kind second-wave organizers had called political, was now a weekend of C-SPAN. Rebecca Walker, then twenty-two, wrote about that audience in Ms. magazine’s January/February 1992 issue. The essay is titled “Becoming the Third Wave.” Walker is Alice Walker’s daughter; the magazine said so, and the fact is true, and it is not her whole biography. She described the hearings as a test of whether a woman’s account could matter when it cut across race and party. She ended with a refusal: she was not a postfeminism feminist. She was the Third Wave. The sentence named a generation that did not feel finished. It did not, by itself, found an organization. In 1992 Walker and Shannon Liss did found the Third Wave Direct Action Corporation — later the Third Wave Foundation — to put young women into electoral and community work. Bikini Kill playing outdoors in 1991. Kathleen Hanna is at the microphone — that is the identification used on the Wikimedia Commons crop of this photograph — with a red bass in her hands. Another member plays guitar. Amplifiers sit on the floor of a park gazebo. This is a show in daylight, not a press conference, and not a picture of “the third wave.” It is a picture of one method: you booked a room, you played, you handed people paper. Two musicians performing outdoors under a white park gazebo, 1991: a woman at a microphone holding a red bass guitar, another member playing guitar, amplifiers on the wooden floor, trees behind the railings. The same years, in Olympia, Washington, and in Washington, D.C., young women in punk scenes were photocopying zines, booking shows, and holding meetings they called riot grrrl. Bikini Kill — Kathleen Hanna, Kathi Wilcox, Tobi Vail, Billy Karren — was one band in that scene. Bratmobile was another. The method was DIY. You did not wait for a New York house to print you. You ran off a stack of copies, handed them out at a show, and told girls to come to the front of the room so they could see and be seen. A manifesto printed in Bikini Kill no. 2 in 1991 started from records, books, and fanzines that included girls, and from the refusal to be a polite guest in someone else’s pit. Riot grrrl was a scene with chapters and a growl in the spelling. It was not a synonym for third-wave feminism. Treating Kathleen Hanna as the face of a decade is the flattening this lesson is trying not to do. In 1989 Kimberlé Crenshaw, a legal scholar, published “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” in the University of Chicago Legal Forum. In 1991 she published “Mapping the Margins” in the Stanford Law Review. The first paper is about employment-discrimination doctrine. The second is about violence against women of color. Together they gave a name, intersectionality, to a problem courts and movements kept missing. Third-wave writing used the word. The word is a tool. It is not a slogan, and it is not a personality. How it showed, if you want a list instead of a face: zines and other independent media, including Bust (1993) and Bitch (1996); leftover fights from the late-1970s sex wars, with sex-positive writers arguing against the anti-porn campaigns already named in the previous lesson; girl culture as a market, a joke, and a serious claim; campus feminism standing on Title IX, women’s studies, and arguments about date rape and consent. The critique, from Black feminists and from people outside the United States, was that “third wave” was a U.S. magazine label. It grouped very different work under a number. It made some young white women in media the face of a decade that was not only theirs. The field A crowded field, then three things to look at closely A gallery of three portraits is the wrong picture. Name them, then stop treating the names as the era. Anita Hill at a microphone. Rebecca Walker in Ms. Kimberlé Crenshaw on the law review. Kathleen Hanna in a gazebo. Jennifer Baumgardner and Amy Richards at the end of the decade, trying to write the generation down in Manifesta. Shannon Liss at the new organization. Susan Faludi on the 1980s, published in 1991. bell hooks in the 1990s classroom with Teaching to Transgress, and in 2000 with Feminism is for Everybody — a through-line from the previous lesson, not a mascot invented in 1992. Judith Butler’s Gender Trouble, 1990, as adjacent theory: gender as something done under constraint, not a third-wave membership card. Hillary Rodham Clinton at a United Nations lectern in Beijing, which is not the same thing as American feminism going abroad. Peng Wan-ru in Taipei, whose death is a Taiwanese political fact. Tavi Gevinson’s later blog and magazine sit at the far edge of this window and belong with a later media system; they are not stretched backward to make a 1991 story look complete. Slow down for three, as examples inside the field, not as the field. The Hill hearings as a public school. Riot grrrl as a method — zines, shows, a room rearranged. Intersectionality as a legal concept that escaped the academy. A story A weekend of C-SPAN, a photocopier, and a traffic accident in the law The school: for one long weekend the country sat in on a sexual-harassment seminar it had not enrolled in. Hill had to be believed as a lawyer and disbelieved as a woman; believed as a Black witness to workplace harm and suspected as a traitor to a Black nominee. Thomas’s “lynching” sentence named a real American crime and used it to close the subject of sex. The committee had no women on it, which was not a metaphor. People who had never read a feminist pamphlet learned the phrase “sexual harassment” from a split screen. That is what a public school looks like. It is also why the hearings cannot be filed only under “feminism” or only under “race.” The overlap was the lesson, whether or not the senators wanted one. The method: riot grrrl treated culture as a workplace. If the pit at a show shoved girls back, you put them in front. If music magazines did not write about you, you wrote the magazine. A zine is a political fact because it is cheap, local, and under your own name. Chapters met in living rooms. Some of the meetings were about rape and incest; some were about guitar chords. When commercial media discovered the scene around 1992 and 1993, some participants stopped talking to reporters. That retreat is part of the method too. A scene that can be summarized as “girl power” on a magazine cover has already lost the photocopier. Bikini Kill is the band in the photograph. The method is the stack of paper. Kimberlé Crenshaw photographed in Berlin in 2018, not in 1989. The legal papers this lesson is about are thirty years older than this picture. The portrait is here because a free, clearly licensed photograph of her exists, and because 1990s press pictures often do not. It is a later photograph of the same person. It is not a picture of the University of Chicago Legal Forum. Later color portrait of Kimberlé Crenshaw, 2018, looking to the side, black sleeveless top, silver hoop earrings and chain necklaces, dark background. The legal concept: Crenshaw asked what happens when a rule against race discrimination and a rule against sex discrimination are written as if those were two separate lines. In DeGraffenreid v. General Motors, Black women said they were left out of jobs and then first in line for layoffs. The court looked at GM’s record and saw that the company hired women (who were white) and hired Black people (who were men). Each single-axis claim failed. The harm was at the overlap, so the law had no plaintiff. Crenshaw’s image was a traffic intersection: injury can come from more than one direction, and a person standing in the crossing is not “half” of each street. In the 1991 paper she took the same tool to shelters, rape law, and movement politics — to rooms that said “women” and meant a white woman, or said “Black community” and treated talking about gender violence as disloyalty. Third-wave essays borrowed the word. The word does not belong to a wave. It belongs to a doctrinal problem that was already true when Combahee wrote in 1977, and that Crenshaw specified for lawyers in 1989. Elsewhere Beijing was a world conference; Taipei, London, and Paris were not waiting for a U.S. name The Fourth World Conference on Women, Beijing, 5 September 1995. Hillary Rodham Clinton is at the United Nations lectern in a pink jacket. The banner behind the stage names the meeting: United Nations, Fourth World Conference on Women, Beijing, 4–15 September 1995. Red flowers run along the stage. Country placards sit on the tables in the hall; one that can be read in this frame is Comoros. This is a government conference with 189 delegations. It is not an American rally held abroad, and it is not a portrait of “global feminism” reduced to one speaker. Hillary Rodham Clinton in a pink jacket at a United Nations lectern, 5 September 1995, with a banner behind her reading United Nations Fourth World Conference on Women, Beijing, 4–15 September 1995, red flowers along the stage, country placards in the audience. From 4 to 15 September 1995 the United Nations held the Fourth World Conference on Women in Beijing. One hundred and eighty-nine governments adopted a Beijing Declaration and a Platform for Action: twelve “critical areas of concern,” from poverty and education to violence, the economy, power, and the girl child. A parallel NGO Forum met in Huairou, with tens of thousands of people who were not sitting behind country flags. Hillary Rodham Clinton addressed the official conference on 5 September and said that human rights are women’s rights, and women’s rights are human rights. The sentence travelled. The document is longer than the sentence. Taiwanese feminist groups, including the Awakening Foundation, were not treated as a national delegation; some Taiwan organizations were denied accreditation, which is part of the 1995 record, not a detail to skip so the map looks tidy. In Taipei the 1990s women’s movement was a legislative movement, not a reprint of Ms. The Awakening Foundation, which had begun as a magazine in 1982 and become a foundation after martial law ended in 1987, spent the decade on the Civil Code’s family chapters — residence, property, children’s names — and on getting women into public life. In 1995 it delivered a family-law draft to the legislature with a large petition behind it. In November 1996 Peng Wan-ru, a feminist official in the Democratic Progressive Party, was murdered. The next years produced a Sexual Assault Crime Prevention Act (1997) and a Domestic Violence Prevention Act (1998). Those statutes are Taiwanese political facts. They do not need a U.S. wave number to be real. In Britain the same years held more than one current. Huggy Bear played riot-grrrl shows. Loaded magazine, launched in 1994, sold a “lad” culture of drinking and sex as comedy. Tabloids answered with the “ladette”: a young woman who drank, smoked, and was blunt in public. Some of the women so named treated it as freedom. Some of the coverage treated it as a joke at feminism’s expense. Either way it is contemporaneous. It is not a British branch office of Olympia. In France the 1990s argument that can be dated without stretching is parité: a campaign for equal numbers of women and men on electoral lists. The Constitution was revised on 8 July 1999. A law followed on 6 June 2000. That is a 1990s feminism about who sits in the assembly. It is not a translation of “riot grrrl.” After Hashtag campaigns used a different machine By the early 2010s “third wave” was already a heading in a syllabus. The media ecology had changed. Tarana Burke used the phrase “Me Too” in 2006 in community work with survivors. In 2017 the hashtag #MeToo travelled across platforms after public accusations against Harvey Weinstein, and millions of people used it to name assaults that had not had a Senate hearing. That cascade is real. It is also a different machine from a photocopied zine, a C-SPAN weekend, or a UN platform. It does not make Burke a fourth-wave mascot in this paragraph, and it does not rewind the 1990s as a rehearsal. The unfinished business is obvious: who is believed, whose harm counts as public, what the law can see when two structures hit at once. The next lesson, if there is one, will need its own sources. This one stops before it pretends to be that lesson. A question A question to keep asking When a movement is numbered a third time, whose work has to fit the number in order to be remembered, and whose work is treated as a local exception? Anita Hill — opening statement, 11 October 1991 (C-SPAN) Official C-SPAN upload of Hill’s opening statement to the Senate Judiciary Committee. About twenty minutes. The full hearing is in C-SPAN’s library; this is the statement, not a documentary about it. Hillary Rodham Clinton — remarks, Fourth World Conference on Women, Beijing, 5 September 1995 (Clinton Presidential Library) U.S. government video of the speech, held on Wikimedia Commons as a public-domain federal work. The line later quoted everywhere is in this recording. The conference was larger than the speech. Kimberlé Crenshaw — “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989) University of Chicago Legal Forum, open on Chicago Unbound. The employment-discrimination paper that names intersectionality. Read this before treating the word as a slogan. Kimberlé Crenshaw — “Mapping the Margins” (Stanford Law Review, 1991) JSTOR record for the 1991 article on violence against women of color. Library access; this capsule does not paste the PDF from a random host. Rebecca Walker — “Becoming the Third Wave,” educational excerpt (TeachRock) A licensed classroom excerpt of the January/February 1992 Ms. essay, with a lesson around it. The essay itself is still in copyright; this is not a pirate scan of the magazine. Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (UN Women text) The official conference documents, 4–15 September 1995. Twelve “critical areas of concern,” not a press release. Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action — PDF The same text as a single file from UN Women / WomenWatch. Hillary Rodham Clinton — remarks, Beijing, 5 September 1995 (White House archives) The White House transcript of the speech. “Human rights are women’s rights” is in this text. It is one address at a conference of 189 governments. Susan Faludi — Backlash: The Undeclared War Against American Women (Crown, 1991) WorldCat record for the first edition, ISBN 0-517-57698-8. Still in copyright; buy or borrow. This is the catalog, not a scan. Jennifer Baumgardner and Amy Richards — Manifesta (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2000) Publisher page for the book that tried to describe young U.S. feminism at the turn of the century. In copyright. Judith Butler — Gender Trouble (Routledge, 1990) Publisher page. Adjacent theory, not a third-wave founding text. In copyright. Fourth World Conference on Women, Beijing 1995 — UN WomenWatch UN institutional page for the conference, the NGO Forum, and follow-up. Awakening Foundation — about (婦女新知基金會) The foundation’s own English account of its work from the martial-law magazine through 1990s lobbying. Institutional memory, not a secondary textbook.

subject: history
title: The 1911 Revolution: ending the Qing without a finished republic
dek: A New Army mutiny in Wuchang ended the Qing. A bargain with Yuan Shikai named a republic. A constitution that could bind the man with the army did not follow.
text: The 1911 Revolution: ending the Qing without a finished republic A New Army mutiny in Wuchang ended the Qing. A bargain with Yuan Shikai named a republic. A constitution that could bind the man with the army did not follow. 1911–1912 Xinhai is a calendar name for 1911 in the sixty-year cycle. The soldiers who mutinied in Wuchang did not need that name. This lesson looks out from late Qing China. Sun Yat-sen did not command the Wuchang mutiny; he was in the United States raising money. The dynasty ended because Yuan Shikai, who held the Beiyang Army, cut a deal. A republic was proclaimed. A constitution that could bind the man with the army was not secured. Casualty figures that cannot be sourced here are omitted. Qiu Jin’s execution in 1907 is named as earlier anti-Qing work, not retold. History history 1895 Shimonoseki Qing defeat in the First Sino-Japanese War. The Treaty of Shimonoseki ceded Taiwan and forced a large indemnity. The reform-or-revolution argument that follows starts from this shock. 1898–1901 Reform / Boxer The Hundred Days Reform of 1898, then Empress Dowager Cixi’s coup. The Boxer crisis and the Boxer Protocol of 1901 left the court paying indemnities and launching New Policies to save itself. 1905 Exams / Tongmenghui The civil-service examinations were abolished. In Tokyo, Sun Yat-sen, Huang Xing, Song Jiaoren and others formed the Tongmenghui. Minbao became its paper. 1908–09 Puyi Guangxu and Cixi died in November 1908. The child Puyi became the Xuantong Emperor. Prince Chun ruled as regent. Yuan Shikai was retired from high office. May–Sept 1911 Railways The court nationalized locally financed railway projects and took a four-power loan for the Hukuang lines. Sichuan’s railway protection movement followed. Troops were pulled from Hubei toward Sichuan. 10 Oct 1911 Wuchang After an accidental bomb in Hankou the day before, New Army units in Wuchang mutinied, seized the arsenal, and forced Li Yuanhong to front a Hubei military government. 1 Jan 1912 Nanjing Sun Yat-sen, back from overseas, was inaugurated provisional president of the Republic of China in Nanjing. Li Yuanhong became provisional vice-president. 12 Feb 1912 Abdication Empress Dowager Longyu issued the abdication edict for the six-year-old Xuantong Emperor. Yuan Shikai was already the court’s last general and the revolutionaries’ necessary partner. 10 Mar 1912 Beijing Yuan was sworn in as provisional president in Beijing. The capital stayed where his army was. The Provisional Constitution was promulgated the next day. 1913–16 Song / Hongxian Song Jiaoren was shot at Shanghai railway station on 20 March 1913 and died two days later. Yuan’s monarchy attempt of 1915–16 collapsed. He died in June 1916. Warlord years followed. The man later called the father of the Republic read about Wuchang in a newspaper On 10 October 1911 Sun Yat-sen was in the United States raising money among overseas Chinese. He was in Denver, Colorado. A coded telegram from Huang Xing reached him, but he learned that Wuchang had actually risen from an English-language newspaper. He did not sail straight home to take command of a battle he had not directed. He went first to London and Paris to press the powers not to loan new money to the Qing. By the time he reached Shanghai, in late December, the mutiny was already a string of provincial declarations. The later cult of a founding father has to live with that itinerary. Xinhai Revolution Xinhai 1911 Revolution Chinese Revolution of 1911 辛亥革命 Revolution of 1911 The 1911–12 collapse of the Qing dynasty and proclamation of the Republic of China, conventionally dated from the Wuchang Uprising of 10 October 1911 to the abdication of 12 February 1912. Xinhai is the year-name in the sixty-year cycle for 1911. Qing Qing dynasty Manchu dynasty Qing court Last imperial dynasty of China, 1644–1912, a Manchu ruling house over a mostly Han empire. Ended by the abdication edict of 12 February 1912. Republic of China ROC the Republic State proclaimed in Nanjing on 1 January 1912. In this lesson it is the 1912 republic, not later governments in Nanjing or Taipei. Wuchang Uprising Wuchang Wuchang mutiny Double Ten Double Ten Day 雙十 武昌起義 New Army mutiny in Wuchang (one of the Wuhan cities) on 10 October 1911. The date is still marked as the Republic of China’s national day. It was not commanded by Sun Yat-sen. Hankou Hankow Han-Keou Treaty-port city across the Yangtze from Wuchang. The accidental bomb of 9 October 1911 went off in the Russian concession here. Now part of Wuhan. Hanyang The third of the Wuhan cities, with Wuchang and Hankou. It fell to the revolutionaries after Wuchang. Wuhan Wuhan cities The triple city of Wuchang, Hankou, and Hanyang on the Yangtze in Hubei. The 1911 rising is a Wuhan event with Wuchang as the first mutiny. Sun Yat-sen Sun Yat sen Sun Zhongshan 孫中山 孫文 Sun Wen Sun Yatsen Revolutionary organizer (1866–1925), head of the Tongmenghui, provisional president of the Republic of China from 1 January 1912 until he resigned in Yuan’s favour. In Denver during the Wuchang mutiny. Huang Xing Huang Hsing Huang Keqiang 黃興 Keqiang Hunanese revolutionary (1874–1916), co-founder of the Huaxinghui and a principal military organizer of the Tongmenghui. Fought at Wuhan after Wuchang; minister in the Nanjing provisional cabinet. Song Jiaoren Sung Chiao-jen 宋教仁 Revolutionary and parliamentary politician (1882–1913). Helped found the Tongmenghui and later the Kuomintang. Shot at Shanghai railway station on 20 March 1913; died 22 March. Yuan Shikai Yuan Shih-kai Yuan Shi-kai 袁世凱 Yuan Qing official and Beiyang Army commander (1859–1916). Recalled in 1911, brokered the abdication, became provisional president in Beijing on 10 March 1912, and tried to become emperor in 1915–16. Li Yuanhong Li Yuan-hung 黎元洪 New Army officer (1864–1928), not a Tongmenghui plotter, pressed into serving as military governor of Hubei after Wuchang. Provisional vice-president in 1912; later president of the Republic. Puyi Pu Yi Xuantong Xuantong Emperor 宣統 溥儀 Last Qing emperor (1906–1967). Enthroned as a child after 1908. Abdicated, in Longyu’s edict, on 12 February 1912, aged six. Empress Dowager Longyu Longyu Empress Longyu 隆裕 Qing empress dowager (1868–1913) who issued the abdication edict of 12 February 1912 in the child emperor’s name. Empress Dowager Cixi Cixi Tz’u-hsi 慈禧 De facto ruler of the late Qing (1835–1908). Crushed the Hundred Days Reform in 1898, survived the Boxer crisis, and died the day after Guangxu in November 1908. Guangxu Emperor Guangxu Kuang-hsu 光緒 Qing emperor (1871–1908) who backed the Hundred Days Reform of 1898, was confined by Cixi, and died in November 1908. Prince Chun Zaifeng Regent 醇親王 Father of Puyi and prince regent from 1908. Retired Yuan Shikai from high office in 1909; had to recall him in 1911. Kang Youwei Kang Yu-wei 康有為 Scholar-reformer (1858–1927). A leader of the 1898 Hundred Days. In exile he argued for a constitutional monarchy, not a republic. Liang Qichao Liang Ch’i-ch’ao 梁啟超 Writer and reformer (1873–1929), Kang’s most famous student. After 1898 he published from exile for constitutional monarchy and a new citizen, against Sun’s republican program. Qiu Jin Ch’iu Chin 秋瑾 Revolutionary (1875–1907). Studied in Japan, edited a women’s journal in Shanghai, executed in Shaoxing after Xu Xilin’s 1907 Anqing rising. Named here as 1907 anti-Qing work, not retold as a suffrage life. Xu Xilin Hsü Hsi-lin 徐錫麟 Revolutionary (1873–1907) who assassinated the Anhui governor Enming in Anqing in July 1907. The failed rising led to Qiu Jin’s arrest. Sheng Xuanhuai Sheng Hsuan-huai 盛宣懷 Minister of Posts and Communications in 1911. Ordered railway nationalization and signed the Hukuang loan. A chief civilian target of the railway protection movement. Zhao Erfeng Chao Erh-feng 趙爾豐 Qing official who suppressed the Sichuan railway protection movement in Chengdu in September 1911. The crackdown pulled Hubei troops westward. Rui Cheng Jui Cheng 瑞澂 Viceroy of Huguang in October 1911. Fled Wuchang when the New Army mutinied. Xiong Bingkun Hsiung Ping-k’un 熊秉坤 Junior leader in the 8th Engineering Battalion of the Hubei New Army. Among those who started the 10 October mutiny and moved on the Chuwangtai arsenal. Wu Zhaolin Wu Chao-lin 吳兆麟 New Army company officer in Wuchang. Not the original plot’s commander; given field command on 10 October because the mutiny wanted a more senior officer in charge. Peng Chufan 彭楚藩 Hubei revolutionary executed on the morning of 10 October 1911 after the Hankou bomb exposed membership lists. Liu Fuji Liu Fu-chi 劉復基 Hubei revolutionary executed 10 October 1911 after the Hankou lists were seized. Yang Hongsheng Yang Hung-sheng 楊宏勝 Hubei revolutionary executed 10 October 1911 after the Hankou lists were seized. With Peng and Liu, one of the three names the mutiny moved to avenge. Jiang Yiwu Chiang I-wu 蔣翊武 Literary Society leader in the Hubei New Army, designated commander of the planned rising. He escaped the 9–10 October round-up. Sun Wu 孫武 Gongjinhui organizer in Wuhan, injured in the 9 October Hankou explosion while explosives were being prepared. Cai Yuanpei Ts’ai Yuan-p’ei 蔡元培 Scholar and Tongmenghui member (1868–1940). Minister of education in the Nanjing provisional cabinet of January 1912. Wang Chonghui Wang Ch’ung-hui 王寵惠 Jurist (1881–1958). Foreign minister in the first Nanjing cabinet, seated near Sun in the 5 January 1912 photograph. Chen Tianhua Ch’en T’ien-hua 陳天華 Revolutionary writer (1875–1905), in the 1905 Tokyo Minbao group photograph. Died in Japan that year; named here as a Tongmenghui-generation publicist. Zhang Shizhao Chang Shih-chao 章士釗 Writer (1881–1973), in the 1905 Tokyo Minbao photograph with Huang Xing. Wu Tingfang Wu T’ing-fang 伍廷芳 Diplomat and jurist (1842–1922). Represented the revolutionaries in the north–south peace talks that produced Yuan’s presidency and the Qing abdication. Porfirio Díaz Diaz Porfirio Diaz Mexican president and long-time strongman, resigned May 1911. Named as a contemporaneous old regime that fell the same year as Wuchang. Francisco I. Madero Madero Francisco Madero Mexican civilian politician who became president in November 1911 and was killed in February 1913. The unfinished-civilian-republic problem in the same years. Tongmenghui Revolutionary Alliance United League Chinese United League 同盟會 中國同盟會 Secret revolutionary alliance founded in Tokyo on 20 August 1905 by Sun Yat-sen, Huang Xing, Song Jiaoren and others, merging earlier groups including the Xingzhonghui and Huaxinghui. Core of the later Kuomintang. Xingzhonghui Revive China Society 興中會 Anti-Qing society Sun founded in Honolulu in 1894. Later folded into the Tongmenghui. Huaxinghui China Revival Society 華興會 Revolutionary society Huang Xing, Song Jiaoren and others organized in Hunan, 1903–04. Merged into the Tongmenghui in Tokyo in 1905. Guangfuhui Restoration Society 光復會 Anti-Qing revolutionary society based among Zhejiang and Anhui activists. Qiu Jin and Xu Xilin worked in this stream. Parts of it cooperated with, and sometimes quarrelled with, the Tongmenghui. Minbao Min Bao People’s Journal 民報 Tokyo newspaper of the Tongmenghui, launched 1905. The 1905 studio photograph in this lesson is of Huang Xing with Minbao colleagues. Literary Society Wenxueshe 文學社 Revolutionary group recruiting inside the Hubei New Army. Together with the Gongjinhui it organized the Wuchang rising. Jiang Yiwu was a leading name. Gongjinhui Progressive Association Co-Progress Society 共進會 Revolutionary society with a Yangtze and secret-society base, allied with the Literary Society inside the Hubei New Army. Sun Wu was a Wuhan organizer. New Army Xinjun 新軍 Late-Qing Western-style forces trained under the New Policies. The Hubei units mutinied at Wuchang. Yuan’s Beiyang divisions were the strongest New Army cluster in the north. Beiyang Army Beiyang Peiyang Army 北洋軍 Yuan Shikai’s New Army in north China, the force that could decide 1911–12. After Yuan’s death in 1916 its factions became warlord armies. New Policies Xinzheng late Qing reforms 新政 Qing reform program after 1901: new schools, abolition of the examinations in 1905, New Army, provincial assemblies, a promised constitution. Intended to save the dynasty. It trained the people who could bury it. civil-service examinations examination system keju 科舉 The old path from classical learning to Qing office. Abolished in 1905. After that date, schools, armies, and overseas study became the new ladders. provincial assemblies provincial assembly Consultative bodies seated from 1909 as part of the New Policies. In 1911 assemblymen in many provinces were the civilians who declared against the Qing alongside New Army officers. Railway Protection Movement railway protection Baolu 保路 保路運動 Railway Rights Protection 1911 protest, strongest in Sichuan, against Qing nationalization of locally financed railways and the transfer of rights toward a foreign loan. The Chengdu crackdown pulled Hubei troops west and thinned the Wuchang garrison. Hukuang loan Hukuang Railway Huguang Railway Hukuang four-power loan 1911 foreign loan from British, French, German, and American banks for the Guangdong–Hankou and Sichuan–Hankou railways. The financial instrument behind railway nationalization. Hubei Military Government Hubei military government 鄂軍都督府 The revolutionary regime declared in Wuchang after 10 October 1911, with Li Yuanhong as military governor, using the old provincial assembly building. The 18-star flag photograph in this lesson is taken in front of it. Nanjing Provisional Government provisional government Nanjing government Nanking Provisional Government Revolutionary national government seated in Nanjing from January 1912, with Sun as provisional president, until Yuan took the presidency in Beijing. Provisional Senate Nanjing Senate provisional senate 臨時參議院 Legislature of the Nanjing republic in early 1912. The 1 April photograph shows Sun resigning to it. provisional president Provisional President Title Sun held from 1 January 1912 and Yuan from 10 March 1912. Provisional meant the office was supposed to wait on a full constitution and a proper election. It became the prize. abdication edict Imperial Edict of Abdication abdication 退位詔書 Edict issued by Empress Dowager Longyu on 12 February 1912, announcing the Xuantong Emperor’s abdication and authorizing Yuan to organize a republic. The legal end of the Qing. Articles of Favorable Treatment Favorable Treatment 優待條件 Terms attached to the 1912 abdication: a stipend for the court, continued residence in the Forbidden City for a time, and the rituals of a retired emperor. Abdication as a contract, not a trial. Provisional Constitution Provisional Constitution of the Republic of China 臨時約法 Promulgated 11 March 1912. It sketched a cabinet responsible to a legislature. It did not control Yuan’s army or keep the capital in Nanjing. Kuomintang KMT Nationalist Party Guomindang 國民黨 Party formed in 1912 when Song Jiaoren merged the Tongmenghui with smaller groups for parliamentary elections. Largest bloc in the 1912–13 National Assembly. Not yet the later Leninist party of the 1920s. National Assembly parliament the assembly The elected legislature of 1912–13 in which the Kuomintang won the largest bloc. Song was on his way to it when he was shot. Three People’s Principles Sanmin zhuyi 三民主義 Sun’s public program: nationalism, democracy, and people’s livelihood. A vocabulary for the Tongmenghui, not a drafted constitution in 1912. queue bianzi Manchu queue pigtail 辮子 The braided hairstyle Qing law required of men as a sign of submission to the Manchu dynasty. Cutting it in 1911 was a public way of leaving the old regime. The 7 November photograph in this lesson shows that act. Iron Blood 18-star flag 18-star flag Iron Blood flag eighteen-star flag 鐵血十八星旗 Banner of the Wuchang rising: a ring of eighteen stars for the provinces of China proper. Crossed in front of the Hubei Military Government in the photograph used as this lesson’s thumbnail. Not the later five-color flag of the Republic. Chuwangtai Chuwan Terrace 楚望台 Arsenal in Wuchang seized on the night of 10 October 1911. Taking it gave the mutineers rifles and a chance. Battle of Yangxia Yangxia October–November 1911 fighting around Hankou and Hanyang between revolutionary forces (Huang Xing among the commanders) and Beiyang units. The revolution did not win Wuhan on the battlefield; it won because provinces kept declaring and Yuan bargained. First Sino-Japanese War Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95 1894–95 war War of 1894–95 in which Qing forces lost to Meiji Japan. The Treaty of Shimonoseki followed. The before of the 1911 argument. Treaty of Shimonoseki Shimonoseki 1895 treaty ending the First Sino-Japanese War. Taiwan ceded; a large indemnity; Qing influence in Korea broken. The shock that made reform and revolution both thinkable. Hundred Days Reform Hundred Days Wuxu Reform 戊戌變法 June–September 1898 reform edicts under Guangxu, associated with Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao. Ended by Cixi’s coup. Boxer Protocol Boxer crisis Boxer Rebellion Boxer indemnity 辛丑條約 1901 settlement after the Boxer crisis: a huge indemnity to the foreign powers and occupation of access routes to Beijing. The New Policies follow from this humiliation. Baohuanghui Protect the Emperor Society 保皇會 Overseas organization of Kang Youwei’s constitutional monarchists after 1898, in argument with Sun’s republicans for the money and loyalty of Chinese abroad. Second Revolution second revolution of 1913 Failed 1913 armed rising by Sun, Huang Xing and others against Yuan after Song’s assassination. Its failure left Yuan free to crush the KMT in parliament. Twenty-One Demands Twenty-One Demands of 1915 Japanese demands on Yuan’s government in 1915. The shortened acceptance still showed how little the new republic could refuse a foreign power. Hongxian Hongxian Emperor Hongxian era Empire of China (1915–16) 洪憲 Era name of Yuan’s attempted monarchy, announced December 1915, cancelled March 1916. The republic’s president tried on a crown and could not make it hold. warlord years warlords warlord era Period after Yuan’s death in 1916 when Beiyang factions and regional armies governed by force. The after of an unfinished republic, not a full later lesson. Agadir Crisis Agadir Panther’s leap July 1911 Franco-German confrontation over Morocco, opened when Germany sent the gunboat Panther to Agadir. The European imperial summer in which the Qing was still taking foreign railway loans. Mexican Revolution Mexican Revolution of 1910 Uprising against Díaz from 1910. Díaz resigned in May 1911; Madero became president that November and was killed in 1913. Named here as a contemporaneous unfinished civilian republic. Forbidden City palace Imperial palace compound in Beijing. Under the Articles of Favorable Treatment the abdicated court was allowed to remain there for a time. Nanjing Nanking Former Ming capital on the Yangtze. Taken by revolutionaries in December 1911; seat of Sun’s provisional government. The failed attempt to keep the national capital here is part of the Yuan bargain. Beijing Peking Beiping Qing capital, and Yuan’s. After 10 March 1912 the republic’s president sat here because the Beiyang Army did. Shanghai railway station Shanghai Railway Station Where Song Jiaoren was shot on 20 March 1913 while boarding a train for Beijing and the new parliament. Denver Denver, Colorado Colorado city where Sun was fundraising in October 1911. He learned of Wuchang from a newspaper there, not from a field headquarters. Russian concession Russian concession of Hankou Foreign-administered zone in Hankou. The 9 October 1911 bomb went off in a revolutionary hideout here, which is why Russian police, then Qing authorities, got the membership lists. four-power consortium China Consortium four-power group British, French, German, and American banks behind the 1911 Hukuang railway loan. The foreign money in the railway crisis. military governor dudu 都督 Title Li Yuanhong took in Hubei after Wuchang: a provincial military head of a declared republic. Other provinces copied the form. Ministry of Posts and Communications minister of Posts and Communications Late-Qing central ministry. Sheng Xuanhuai headed it in 1911 when railway nationalization and the Hukuang loan were pushed through. Ministry of Foreign Affairs Beijing Ministry of Foreign Affairs The Beijing ministry in whose rooms Yuan was photographed with his officers on 10 March 1912 after taking the oath as provisional president. 8th Engineering Battalion Engineering Battalion eighth engineering battalion Hubei New Army unit that opened the Wuchang mutiny on the evening of 10 October 1911 and moved on the Chuwangtai arsenal. Enming En Ming Manchu governor of Anhui, killed by Xu Xilin in Anqing in July 1907. The failed rising led to Qiu Jin’s arrest and execution. Panther SMS Panther German gunboat sent to Agadir in July 1911. The ship that made the Agadir Crisis visible. Fu Sheng Fulong Photography Studio Fu Sheng, Photographer Tianjin studio that made the circa-1900 cabinet card of Yuan Shikai used in this lesson. The printed English line on the mount reads ‘Fu Sheng, Photographer, City North East Wall Street Tientsin.’ Agence Rol French press-photography agency. The 1911 Hankou street photograph in this lesson is an Agence Rol print now in the Bibliothèque nationale de France. Bibliothèque nationale de France BnF Gallica French national library. Holds the Agence Rol 1911 Hankou photograph (EST EI-13). University of Washington Libraries Chandless Photographs Robert Henry Chandless Photographs Holds the Fu Sheng cabinet card of Yuan Shikai (PH Coll 214.61) used in this lesson. Anqing Anhui city. Site of Xu Xilin’s 1907 rising. Qiu Jin was arrested after it failed. Chengdu Sichuan capital. Center of the 1911 railway protection movement and of Zhao Erfeng’s September crackdown. Hubei Province on the middle Yangtze. Wuchang was its capital. The New Army mutiny of 10 October 1911 began here. Sichuan Szechwan Province whose railway shareholders led the 1911 Railway Protection Movement. The Qing transfer of Hubei troops toward Sichuan thinned the Wuchang garrison. Guangdong–Hankou Canton–Hankou Hankou-Guangdong Railway One of the two Hukuang railway routes whose rights the 1911 foreign loan pledged. Locally backed in Hubei, Hunan, and Guangdong. Sichuan–Hankou Sichuan-Hankou Railway The other Hukuang route. Barely begun, and the line Sichuan shareholders thought they still owned when the court nationalized it. Spaarnestad Photo Dutch picture archive (now with the Nationaal Archief’s collections) that holds the 7 November 1911 queue-cutting photograph. The Dutch caption anachronistically says ‘Guomindong army’; the print is dated 1911, before the Kuomintang existed under that name. Before After 1895 the court tried to save itself; students in Japan learned how to bury it The First Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95 ended with the Treaty of Shimonoseki. Taiwan was ceded. A large indemnity was due. Korea slipped from Qing suzerainty. The defeat was not only a lost campaign. It showed that a neighboring state which had rewritten its army and schools could beat the empire that still recruited officials by the civil-service examinations. From that shock two programs were argued in public, often by people who had known one another and then split. Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao wanted a constitutional monarchy under the Guangxu Emperor. In 1898 they had a hundred days of edicts — the Hundred Days Reform — before Empress Dowager Cixi staged a coup, confined Guangxu, and drove the reformers overseas. In exile they organized to protect the emperor, not to kill the dynasty. Sun Yat-sen had already chosen the other door. A commoner schooled in Hawai‘i and Hong Kong, trained as a physician, he had founded the Xingzhonghui in Honolulu in 1894 after the Qing would not hear his reform petition. Failed risings followed. After 1900 the Boxer crisis and the Boxer Protocol left the court paying another indemnity to the foreign powers and trying, late, to modernize itself in order to survive. Huang Xing (seated, center, hat on his lap) with colleagues of Minbao in Tokyo, 1905. The Commons identification puts Chen Tianhua and Zhang Shizhao in the front row and Song Jiaoren standing at back left. This is the overseas student world in which the Tongmenghui was formed that August: a paper, a studio carpet, and a program to replace the Qing with a republic. Studio group of eight Chinese men in Tokyo, 1905: some in Western suits, some in high-collared tunics; Huang Xing seated at center holding a bowler hat. The New Policies of the 1900s were the court’s answer. The examinations were abolished in 1905, which cut the old path from classical study to office. New schools and military academies were opened. Provincial assemblies were promised and, from 1909, seated. A New Army was trained on foreign drill, with Yuan Shikai’s Beiyang divisions as the strongest cluster in the north. None of this was intended to produce a republic. It produced the people who could staff one. Students went to Japan in large numbers. In Tokyo on 20 August 1905, Sun, Huang Xing, Song Jiaoren and others merged older groups — including the Xingzhonghui and Huang’s Huaxinghui — into the Tongmenghui, the Revolutionary Alliance. Minbao carried the arguments. The Three People’s Principles — nationalism, democracy, and a livelihood plank Sun never made into a finished economic program — were the public vocabulary. The work on the ground was also older: secret societies, failed putsches, and women as well as men. Qiu Jin, who had studied in Japan, edited a women’s journal in Shanghai and was executed in 1907 after Xu Xilin’s rising at Anqing. That death belongs in this decade of anti-Qing organizing. It is not a suffrage sequel, and it is not retold here. Guangxu and Cixi died on successive days in November 1908. The child Puyi became the Xuantong Emperor. Prince Chun, his father, served as regent and pushed Yuan Shikai into retirement. The court still talked of a constitution, on a timetable it kept shortening. What it could not do was finish a railway map without foreign money, or keep the New Army’s junior officers from reading the same Tokyo papers as the students. The Xuantong Emperor Puyi as a small child, in a 1910 court photograph. The woman with the Manchu headdress, partly behind the table, is identified as Empress Dowager Longyu. In February 1912 it would be her name, not his, on the abdication edict. The picture is a household still. It is not a government. A small child in Qing court dress sitting on a large chair; to the left, a woman in an elaborate Manchu headdress partly hidden by a table with a vase. The era A railway crisis, an accidental bomb, and a New Army that mutinied without a single hero In the spring of 1911 the Ministry of Posts and Communications, under Sheng Xuanhuai, moved to nationalize locally financed railway projects. A four-power consortium — British, French, German, and American banks — supplied a large loan for the Hukuang lines, the Guangdong–Hankou and Sichuan–Hankou routes that were supposed to tie the interior to the Yangtze. On 9 May the nationalization order went out. Shareholders in Sichuan, who had put provincial money and gentry savings into a railway company that had barely begun to lay track, were offered terms they rejected. The Railway Protection Movement that followed was not a Tongmenghui plot. It was merchants, students, and the provincial assembly against a court that looked as if it were selling the road to foreigners in order to pay old debts. In September the Sichuan authorities, with Zhao Erfeng as the hard edge, broke up the movement in Chengdu. New Army units were ordered in from neighboring Hubei. That transfer thinned the garrison around Wuchang. Hankou, 1911, photographed for the French agency Rol: a street crowd, queues still worn, a porter with tubs, shop signs, and foreign hats in the same frame. Hankou, Hanyang, and Wuchang made up the Wuhan cities on the Yangtze. The uprising began next door in Wuchang. This is the treaty-port street the mutiny did not have to invent. A crowded Hankou street in 1911: a porter with shoulder pole and wooden tubs, men with queues, shop signs in Chinese, and Westerners in pith helmets among the crowd. The men who actually took Wuchang were not Sun’s travelling staff. They were New Army soldiers in Hubei, organized in two overlapping groups, the Literary Society and the Gongjinhui, who had been recruiting inside the ranks. Huang Xing and Song Jiaoren were not in the city. Sun was in the United States. A rising had been discussed for early October, then delayed. On 9 October, in a hideout in the Russian concession of Hankou, someone preparing explosives set off a bomb by accident. The blast brought police. Membership lists were found. Arrests followed. On the morning of 10 October three men — Peng Chufan, Liu Fuji, and Yang Hongsheng — were executed. The remaining plotters inside the barracks could wait to be named from the lists, or they could move. They moved. That evening the 8th Engineering Battalion, with Xiong Bingkun among the junior leaders, mutinied and made for the Chuwangtai arsenal, where other comrades were already posted. Artillery and transport units came over. Wu Zhaolin, a company officer with more rank than the first mutineers, was pushed into field command because a mutiny still wanted a chain of command. The Viceroy, Rui Cheng, fled. By the next day Wuchang was in rebel hands; Hankou and Hanyang followed. There is no single hero in that sequence. There is an accident, a list, three executions, and a garrison that decided not to wait its turn. Revolutionary troops at the Wuchang uprising, 1911. Several men wear a white cloth armband on the left sleeve — the field sign used so mutineers could tell one another from loyal units in the same uniform. The photograph is a group of soldiers, not a painting of a named general winning a battle. Soldiers in dark New Army uniforms and peaked caps, some with white cloth armbands on the left sleeve, holding rifles with bayonets; a wooden structure behind them. Posing in front of the Hubei Military Government in Wuchang after the uprising, with the 18-star Iron Blood flags of the rising crossed at the door. The building had been the provincial assembly. The flags are not yet the five-color flag of the Republic. They are the banner of a mutiny that had to look like a government by the next morning. A line of soldiers in light uniforms standing before a two-storey Western-style brick building; two large dark flags with rings of stars are crossed in front of the entrance. A government needed a name the provincial assembly and the city’s merchants would recognize. Li Yuanhong was a New Army brigade commander, popular enough with soldiers, not a Tongmenghui member, and not a plotter of the bomb. He was pressed into serving as military governor of Hubei. The later stories about how reluctantly he accepted are less important than the political fact: the mutineers borrowed a non-revolutionary officer because a republic, even a local one, still had to look like command. Telegrams went out asking other provinces to follow. Through October and November, assemblymen, New Army officers, and gentry in province after province declared against the Qing. The map did not wait for Sun. Li Yuanhong in a republican military uniform, photographed around 1915 — later than the mutiny. In October 1911 he was a New Army officer without a revolutionary party card. The mutineers needed his name on the Hubei government. The later portrait is the career that name made possible. Studio portrait of Li Yuanhong in a dark high-collared military tunic and peaked cap with a star badge, an aiguillette on his right shoulder. Huang Xing reached the Wuhan cities and took a field command in the fighting that followed, the Battle of Yangxia against Beiyang units Yuan was sending south. The revolution did not win that fight on points. It won because other provinces had already peeled away, and because Yuan did not use the Beiyang Army only to restore the court. Nanjing was taken in early December. Delegates from the independent provinces gathered there. Sun, having gone from Denver to London and Paris to argue against new foreign loans to the Qing, reached Shanghai in late December. On 29 December the delegates elected him provisional president. On 1 January 1912, in Nanjing, he was inaugurated and the Republic of China was proclaimed. The calendar of the Republic would number 1912 as Year One. Li Yuanhong was named provisional vice-president. A cabinet sat. Cai Yuanpei took education; Huang Xing was at the center of the military side. The photograph of that first state council is a table, not a constitution. Sun Yat-sen chairs the first cabinet meeting of the Nanjing Provisional Government, 5 January 1912. Huang Xing is among the ministers at the table; so are Cai Yuanpei and Wang Chonghui. The republic at this point is a room in Nanjing and a list of offices. Yuan Shikai’s army is still in the north. Sun Yat-sen seated at the center of a cloth-covered table with other men in dark suits; papers on the table; a lamp hanging above. A revolutionary soldier cutting a man’s queue, 7 November 1911. The Dutch archive that holds the print dates it that day and describes the braid as the Manchu-mandated sign of the old regime. The location is not named beyond China. The act is the point: leaving the Qing could be done with scissors in a street, in the same weeks that provinces were declaring. A man in a dark uniform and peaked cap holding a long braid cut from the head of a younger man in light padded clothing; two older men in robes and skullcaps watch. How it showed up The Yuan bargain, and why a republic was not yet a constitution The court, in panic, recalled Yuan Shikai and put the Beiyang Army in his hands. He fought enough to show he could take Wuhan back, and not enough to restore a child emperor. He negotiated with the revolutionaries through Wu Tingfang and others while squeezing the palace. Sun offered the presidency if Yuan would deliver a republic. Yuan offered the palace survival if it would abdicate. On 12 February 1912 Empress Dowager Longyu issued the abdication edict in the name of the Xuantong Emperor. The Articles of Favorable Treatment promised the court a stipend, the right to remain in the Forbidden City for a time, and the rituals of a retired monarchy. The Qing ended as a contract. Puyi was six. Sun resigned. The photograph on the steps of the Provisional Senate records that resignation, not the January inauguration. On 10 March Yuan was sworn in as provisional president in Beijing, among his officers, at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The next day the Provisional Constitution of the Republic of China was promulgated. It described a cabinet responsible to a legislature and a president who was not supposed to be a new emperor. The capital remained Beijing because that was where Yuan’s army lived. Nanjing had been a revolutionary choice. It was not a military fact. “Republic” in 1912 meant: no emperor, a flag, a calendar, a senate, and a general who had not been elected in any popular sense. It did not yet mean a rule that could stop that general. Yuan Shikai after being sworn in as provisional president, 10 March 1912, photographed with staff at the Beijing Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The uniforms and swords are the argument. The republic’s second provisional president is still a Beiyang commander standing in a northern ministry, not a Nanjing legislator. Yuan Shikai standing at the center of a group of officers in high-collared uniforms and boots, some with swords, in a curtained interior; he holds a peaked cap in his right hand. Sun Yat-sen 孫中山 1866–1925 Physician, overseas organizer, head of the Tongmenghui. He spent 1911 on a fundraising circuit in the United States and learned of Wuchang from a newspaper in Denver. Elected provisional president in Nanjing, inaugurated 1 January 1912, he held the office for weeks and then resigned so Yuan would take the Qing down with him. The later cult treats him as founder. The 1911 file treats him as the name a scattered alliance already had, and as the man who could talk to foreign capitals about loans. Sun as provisional president, 1912, in a high-collared tunic. The portrait is an office image, taken after Wuchang, not a field photograph from 10 October. Yuan Shikai 袁世凱 1859–1916 Builder of the Beiyang Army, retired by the regent, recalled to save the dynasty. He saved himself. The abdication is his leverage made into an edict. The presidency in Beijing is his army made into a title. In 1915–16 he tried to become emperor under the era name Hongxian and failed. He died in 1916. The warlord years are what his army became once there was no longer one Yuan to hold it. Yuan Shikai as a Qing official, photographed in Tianjin by Fu Sheng, about 1900. The verso of the University of Washington print calls him viceroy of Zhili, afterwards first president of the Republic. The robe is the career the court recalled in 1911. Song Jiaoren 宋教仁 1882–1913 Tongmenghui organizer, then the man who tried to turn the alliance into a parliamentary party. In 1912 he helped merge the Tongmenghui into the Kuomintang and campaigned for a cabinet that would check the president. The 1912–13 elections gave his party the largest bloc in the new National Assembly. On 20 March 1913 he was shot at Shanghai railway station on his way to Beijing. He died on 22 March, not yet thirty-one. Without him the republic lost the person who had treated the Provisional Constitution as a job, not a decoration. Song Jiaoren, studio portrait from before his death in 1913. The suit is the parliamentary career he was building, not a battlefield costume. Huang Xing had been the military organizer of the Tongmenghui, the man who stood in the Tokyo photographs and later in the Wuhan fighting. He is in the Nanjing cabinet picture. He is not a fourth founder-statue in this lesson because the unfinished republic is clearer in Song’s murder than in another portrait of a general. Li Yuanhong’s career after Wuchang — vice-president, later president — is what happens when a mutiny’s borrowed name stays in politics. Empress Dowager Longyu’s one state act that still matters is the edict. The child on the throne did not write it. Same time elsewhere Mexico’s civilian was not safe either; Europe was still sending gunboats In Mexico the old regime of Porfirio Díaz had already begun to crack in 1910. In May 1911 Díaz resigned. Francisco I. Madero, a civilian who had called for elections, became president that November — the same autumn as Wuchang. In February 1913 he was overthrown and killed. The Mexican Revolution did not end with a finished constitution in 1911 any more than China’s did. The comparison is not a formula about continents. It is the same problem in the same years: removing a long personal regime is not the same work as binding the next man who has troops. Europe, that summer, was still in the gunboat business. In July 1911 Germany sent the Panther to Agadir in a quarrel with France over Morocco — the Agadir Crisis. The Qing court was, at the same moment, borrowing from a four-power banking group to pay for railways it had just seized from its own provinces. The foreign loan and the foreign gunboat were the world in which a Chinese republic had to open. They are contemporaneous facts, not assigned peers. After Song was killed, Yuan tried on a crown, and the army divided The Kuomintang’s showing in the 1912–13 elections made Song Jiaoren the obvious premier of a cabinet that would have narrowed Yuan’s room. The shooting at Shanghai railway station on 20 March 1913 ended that path. Evidence ran toward people around Yuan’s government; Yuan was never put on trial for it. Sun and Huang tried an armed Second Revolution in the summer of 1913 and lost. Yuan banned the party, hollowed out the assembly, and in 1915 accepted Japan’s Twenty-One Demands in a shortened form that still marked how weak the new state was abroad. In December 1915 he announced a monarchy, with 1916 as the Hongxian era. Provinces rebelled. He cancelled the empire in March 1916 and died on 6 June. What remained was the Beiyang Army without Beiyang’s one manager, and a south that had already learned to declare independence. The warlord years are that split made routine. The Republic of China kept its name, its calendar, and, on paper, its offices. It did not keep a monopoly of force. The student movement of 1919 and the later reorganized Nationalist Party would work in that wreckage. They are the next problems, not this lesson. 1911 ended an empire. It did not finish a republic. That unfinished ground is the fact later politics had to stand on. A question A question to keep asking If a mutiny still needed a non-revolutionary officer’s name, and a republic still needed Yuan’s army, what did the word republic actually bind in 1912? Chinese Revolution (1911–12) — Encyclopaedia Britannica Named encyclopedia entry on the mutiny, the railway crisis, Sun’s return, and Yuan’s bargain. A reference article, not a substitute for a monograph. The Chinese Revolution of 1911 — U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian U.S. government historical sketch of the Tongmenghui, Wuchang, and recognition of the Republic. Written from Washington’s file. Retired ‘Milestones’ series; still a named public text. Sun Yat-sen — Encyclopaedia Britannica Biography of the Tongmenghui leader and provisional president. Use it for the overseas career; it will not narrate Wuchang as his field command, because it was not. Yuan Shikai — Encyclopaedia Britannica Biography of the Beiyang commander who took the presidency and later tried to become emperor. Marie-Claire Bergère — Sun Yat-sen (Stanford University Press, 1998) Publisher page for the English translation by Janet Lloyd. A standard critical biography: the myth, the overseas networks, and the man who was in Denver in October 1911. Buy or borrow; this capsule does not paste the book. Joseph W. Esherick — Reform and Revolution in China: The 1911 Revolution in Hunan and Hubei (University of Michigan Press) Publisher page for the study that locates 1911 in late-Qing New Policies, provincial elites, and the New Army, rather than in Sun’s itinerary abroad. First issued by University of California Press in 1976. Gordon H. Chang — “American Influences on Sun Yatsen” (Education About Asia / Association for Asian Studies) Open essay. Useful on Sun’s 1911 U.S. fundraising tour and on learning of Wuchang from a newspaper rather than from a headquarters he commanded. Agence Rol — crowd in a Hankou street, 1911 (BnF / Gallica) French press photograph in the Bibliothèque nationale de France. The street, not a battle painting. Catalogue notice: http://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb40475660b

subject: literature
title: Existentialism (c. 1943–1960): literature after the occupation
dek: After high modernism’s broken sentence came war, occupation, and Liberation. In Paris a press word — existentialism — stuck to novels and plays of situation, to Les Temps modernes, and to a public break between Camus and Sartre.
text: Existentialism (c. 1943–1960): literature after the occupation After high modernism’s broken sentence came war, occupation, and Liberation. In Paris a press word — existentialism — stuck to novels and plays of situation, to Les Temps modernes, and to a public break between Camus and Sartre. c. 1943–1960 “Existentialism” is a later press and classroom label. Sartre and Beauvoir used it; Camus did not accept it as a school name for himself. Gabriel Marcel had already used related language in 1943. This lesson looks out from occupied and post-Liberation Paris — cafés, a magazine, novels and plays of situation — then notices other 1950s literatures that were running at the same time. They are contemporaneous events, not a West-plus-Asia formula. High modernism is the previous Thursday in this archive; it is not repeated here. Literature literature 1938 La Nausée Sartre’s novel appears. A forerunner written before the war that later readers folded into the postwar label. 1942–43 L’Étranger / L’Être et le Néant Camus’s novel (1942). Sartre’s Being and Nothingness (1943). Occupation Paris is the room, not only the theory. 1944 Huis clos / Liberation No Exit premieres at the Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier, 27 May. Paris is liberated in August. 1945 Les Temps modernes First issue, October. Named after Chaplin’s Modern Times. A magazine becomes an institution. 1947–49 La Peste / Le Deuxième Sexe Camus’s The Plague (1947). Beauvoir’s The Second Sex (1949), first serialized in Les Temps modernes. 1951–52 The break Camus’s The Rebel (1951). Francis Jeanson’s review in Les Temps modernes (May 1952); Camus and Sartre exchange open letters (August). Friendship ends in public. 1952–53 Elsewhere / Paris Ellison’s Invisible Man (1952). Fanon’s Black Skin, White Masks (1952). Wright’s The Outsider (1953), written in Paris. c. 1960 The label thins Structuralism and other Paris fashions take the prestige slot. The press word goes stale. This lesson stops before a full postmodernism chapter. Les Temps modernes took its name from a Chaplin film When Sartre’s circle settled on a title for their new review in late 1944, they chose Les Temps modernes — Modern Times — after Charlie Chaplin’s 1936 film. The first issue appeared in October 1945, after paper shortages delayed it. The board included Sartre, Beauvoir, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Raymond Aron, Michel Leiris, Albert Ollivier, and Jean Paulhan. A comedy about factory life became the letterhead of a magazine that argued for littérature engagée. The film is still the easier object to name than the paper ration. existentialism Existentialism Press and classroom name for a mid-twentieth-century cluster of novels, plays, and philosophy that treated freedom, situation, and bad faith as public problems. Sartre and Beauvoir used the word; Camus did not accept it as a school label for himself. high modernism Earlier twentieth-century formal experiment — Woolf, Joyce, Eliot, and others — treated in this archive’s Thursday lesson of that name. The immediate literary past before the 1930s political novel and the war. situation Sartre’s theatre and novel term: a concrete set of constraints and choices, not an abstract theme. A play of situation puts characters into a closed room of consequences. theatre of situation theater of situation Sartre’s name for drama built around a concrete dilemma rather than psychological portrait alone. Huis clos is the usual exhibit. engagement littérature engagée litterature engagee committed literature French for commitment: the claim that writing is not neutral. Sartre’s Qu’est-ce que la littérature? and Les Temps modernes made engagement a magazine program. mauvaise foi bad faith mauvaise foi / bad faith Sartre’s bad faith: lying to oneself about freedom or facticity — pretending one has no choice, or pretending one has no past. The café waiter who overplays being a waiter is the classroom example. the absurd absurd absurdity Camus’s word for the clash between the human demand for meaning and a world that does not answer it. Not a synonym for nihilism in his essays. occupation Occupation the Occupation occupied Paris German occupation of France, 1940–44. The political weather for Huis clos, Combat, and the cafés that still had heat. Liberation Libération liberation of Paris The freeing of Paris in August 1944 and the wider end of occupation. The public after against which Les Temps modernes launched. Les Temps modernes Temps modernes Les Temps Modernes Literary-political review founded by Sartre’s circle; first issue October 1945; titled after Chaplin’s Modern Times. Serialized parts of The Second Sex; published the 1952 Camus–Sartre break. Café de Flore Cafe de Flore the Flore Café on Boulevard Saint-Germain. During the Occupation, Sartre and Beauvoir worked there because the upstairs rooms stayed heated when many hotels did not. Les Deux Magots Deux Magots Café opposite the Flore on the Place Saint-Germain-des-Prés side of the boulevard. The other famous terrace; later a tourist address. Saint-Germain-des-Prés Saint-Germain-des-Pres Saint Germain Left-Bank neighborhood around the old abbey church. The cafés, hotels, and Gallimard offices that made the press story of existentialism a place name. Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier Vieux-Colombier Theatre du Vieux-Colombier Theater du Vieux-Colombier Theatre at 21 rue du Vieux-Colombier. Huis clos premiered there on 27 May 1944. Jean-Paul Sartre Sartre Jean Paul Sartre Philosopher and writer (1905–1980). La Nausée (1938), Being and Nothingness (1943), Huis clos (1944), Les Temps modernes. Public face of the label he partly accepted. Simone de Beauvoir Beauvoir de Beauvoir Simone de Beauvoir Writer and philosopher (1908–1986). The Second Sex (1949); novels and memoirs; co-founder of Les Temps modernes. Not only “Sartre’s partner.” Albert Camus Camus Writer (1913–1960). L’Étranger (1942), The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), The Plague (1947), The Rebel (1951). Editor at Combat; broke with Sartre in 1952. Refused the school label “existentialist.” Maurice Merleau-Ponty Merleau-Ponty Philosopher (1908–1961). Phenomenology of Perception (1945); early Temps modernes editor. Adjacent to the literary circle, not a novelist of situation. Jean Genet Genet Writer and playwright (1910–1986). Thief, prisoner, then Gallimard author. Sartre’s long Saint Genet (1952) made him a philosophical exhibit as well as a literary one. Samuel Beckett Beckett Writer (1906–1989). Waiting for Godot (1953 Paris premiere). Adjacent absurdist theatre, not the Sartre school; named because the same years put both on Paris stages. Frantz Fanon Fanon Psychiatrist and writer (1925–1961). Black Skin, White Masks (1952); The Wretched of the Earth (1961) at the edge of this lesson’s dates. Richard Wright Wright American novelist (1908–1960). Native Son (1940); settled in Paris after the war; The Outsider (1953). Named in the 1930s political past and in the Paris years. Ralph Ellison Ellison American novelist (1914–1994). Invisible Man (1952). Jim Crow and Harlem, not Saint-Germain. Francis Jeanson Jeanson Critic and Temps modernes editor. His May 1952 review of The Rebel triggered Camus’s letter to “Monsieur le Directeur.” Raymond Aron Aron Philosopher and journalist (1905–1983).
