On the first Temps modernes board; later broke with Sartre’s politics. Named as board fact, not as a deep dive. Jean Paulhan Paulhan Editor (1884–1968). Gallimard / NRF figure on the first Temps modernes board. Michel Leiris Leiris Writer and ethnographer (1901–1990). On the first Temps modernes board. Charlie Chaplin Chaplin Filmmaker. Modern Times (1936) gave Les Temps modernes its title. Modern Times Les Temps modernes namesake Chaplin film, 1936. The magazine’s namesake. Gallimard Paris publisher. Issued many of the books in this lesson and housed early Temps modernes offices. Combat Resistance and postwar newspaper. Camus was a leading editorial voice there during and after the Liberation. La Nausée Nausea Sartre novel, 1938. Prewar forerunner; Roquentin’s nausea at contingency. Place it before 1943, not as a Liberation product. L’Être et le Néant Being and Nothingness L'Etre et le Neant Sartre’s Being and Nothingness, 1943. Philosophical treatise written under occupation; bad faith and freedom as technical terms. L’Étranger The Stranger L'Etranger The Outsider (Camus) Camus novel, 1942 (English: The Stranger / The Outsider). Meursault in Algiers; flat prose; a killing on a beach; a trial that moralizes sunlight and manners. Huis clos No Exit Huis Clos Sartre play, premiered 27 May 1944 at the Vieux-Colombier. Three people locked in a room; “Hell is other people.” Le Mythe de Sisyphe The Myth of Sisyphus Myth of Sisyphus Camus essay, 1942 (The Myth of Sisyphus). The absurd as a starting problem, not a slogan on a beret. La Peste The Plague Camus novel, 1947 (The Plague). Oran under epidemic; read then and later as occupation allegory and as plague narrative. Le Deuxième Sexe The Second Sex Le Deuxieme Sexe Beauvoir’s The Second Sex, 1949. Two volumes: history and myth, then lived experience. Method from philosophy and reportage, not only a feminist label. L’Homme révolté The Rebel L'Homme revolte Camus’s The Rebel, 1951. Essay on revolt and limits; attacked Stalinist apologetics; the book Jeanson reviewed. Peau noire, masques blancs Black Skin, White Masks Fanon’s Black Skin, White Masks, 1952. Colonial racism as lived psychic situation. Les Damnés de la terre The Wretched of the Earth Les Damnes de la terre Fanon’s The Wretched of the Earth, 1961. At the far edge of this lesson’s dates; named only as later edge. The Outsider The Outsider (Wright) Richard Wright novel, 1953, written in Paris. American existential thriller; not Camus’s L’Étranger under another title. Invisible Man Ralph Ellison novel, 1952. Narrator’s invisibility under American racism. Same year as Fanon’s first book; different city. Native Son Wright novel, 1940. Named as 1930s–40s political-novel past, not as the Paris chapter. Homage to Catalonia Orwell’s 1938 account of the Spanish Civil War. Named as 1930s political writing in the Before section. The Grapes of Wrath Steinbeck novel, 1939. Named briefly as 1930s political fiction. George Orwell Orwell British writer (1903–1950). Named for the 1930s political novel/reportage past. John Steinbeck Steinbeck American novelist (1902–1968). Named for The Grapes of Wrath as 1930s political fiction. Angry Young Men angry young men British press label for mid-1950s writers and playwrights — Osborne’s Look Back in Anger (1956) as the usual stage marker. Class anger in London, not Paris cafés. John Osborne Osborne Playwright (1929–1994). Look Back in Anger, Royal Court Theatre, 1956. Look Back in Anger Osborne play, 1956. The Angry Young Men stage date. Royal Court Theatre Royal Court London theatre in Sloane Square. Look Back in Anger premiered there. Abe Kōbō Kobo Abe Abe Kobo Kōbō Abe Japanese writer (1924–1993). The Woman in the Dunes (1962) is just after this lesson’s center; named as a contemporaneous writer working related problems of confinement and absurdity, not as a Sartre disciple. Ōe Kenzaburō Oe Kenzaburo Kenzaburo Oe Ōe Japanese novelist (1935–2023). Early work from the late 1950s; read Sartre as a French literature student. Contemporaneous, not a twin. The Woman in the Dunes Suna no onna Abe novel, 1962. Sand pit as situation. Named at the edge of the dates. structuralism 1960s Paris intellectual fashion — Lévi-Strauss and others — that took prestige as the existentialist label went stale. Named only as After, not as a full lesson. Qu’est-ce que la littérature? What Is Literature? Qu'est-ce que la litterature? Sartre’s What Is Literature?, 1948 (parts earlier in Temps modernes). Engagement as a theory of prose. Saint Genet Saint Genet, Actor and Martyr Sartre’s long 1952 study of Jean Genet. A philosophical biography that made Genet a case. Waiting for Godot En attendant Godot Beckett play; Paris premiere 1953. Absurd theatre adjacent to this lesson. Jim Crow Legal and customary racial segregation in the United States. The American situation behind Invisible Man. Algiers City where L’Étranger is set. French Algeria, not Paris. Oran Algerian city setting of The Plague. Gabriel Marcel Marcel French philosopher (1889–1973). Used “existentialism” as a label in 1943; later distanced himself from Sartre’s atheist version. Existentialism Is a Humanism L’existentialisme est un humanisme Existentialism is a Humanism L'existentialisme est un humanisme Sartre’s public lecture of 29 October 1945, later a short book. The event that made the press word hard to unsay. Virginia Woolf Woolf Novelist named here only as high modernism’s prior Thursday, not as a character in 1945 Paris. James Joyce Joyce Novelist named here only as high modernism’s prior Thursday. T. S. Eliot Eliot T.S. Eliot Poet named here only as high modernism’s prior Thursday. Meursault Narrator of L’Étranger. His sentences refuse the remorse the court wants. Roquentin Narrator of La Nausée. Named because the 1938 novel is the forerunner. Hell is other people L’enfer, c’est les autres L'enfer, c'est les autres English for Sartre’s line in Huis clos: “L’enfer, c’est les autres.” A claim about the gaze, not a slogan against having friends. Phenomenology of Perception Phénoménologie de la perception Phenomenologie de la perception Merleau-Ponty’s 1945 treatise. Named as his main book in these years, not as a novel. Albert Ollivier Ollivier Journalist on the first Temps modernes board. Named because the masthead is the institution. Lévi-Strauss Claude Lévi-Strauss Levi-Strauss Claude Levi-Strauss Anthropologist (1908–2009). Named only as a marker of 1960s structuralism taking the Paris prestige slot. Gordon Parks Parks American photographer (1912–2006). The Harlem newsboy picture in this lesson is his OWI work, May 1943. Adam Clayton Powell Jr. Adam Powell Adam Clayton Powell Harlem congressman and pastor. His People’s Voice tour poster is in the 1943 newsboy photograph. People’s Voice People's Voice Harlem newspaper associated with Adam Clayton Powell Jr. Visible on the newsstand in the Parks photograph. Pittsburgh Courier Major African American newspaper. A clipping is visible behind the 1943 newsboy. Carl Van Vechten Van Vechten Photographer of the 1939 Wright portrait used in this lesson. 28th Infantry Division 28th Division U.S. Army division marching on the Champs-Élysées in the 29 August 1944 photograph. Champs-Élysées Champs-Elysees Champs Elysees Paris avenue in the Liberation parade photograph. Arc de Triomphe Monument at the head of the Champs-Élysées, visible in the 1944 parade photograph. Lucrèce Borgia Lucrece Borgia Victor Hugo play advertised on a 2018 poster at the Vieux-Colombier in this lesson’s theatre photograph. Named because it is in the picture, not because it is existentialist. Victor Hugo Hugo Playwright of Lucrèce Borgia, visible on the 2018 theatre poster. Named because the caption uses the title. Office of War Information OWI U.S. Office of War Information U.S. wartime information agency. Parks’s Harlem photograph is an OWI assignment. Harlem New York neighborhood. Setting for much of Invisible Man and for Parks’s 1943 newsboy photograph. Second Wave second-wave second wave Later Anglo-American feminism, treated in this archive’s Monday lesson of that name. Named only as a later use of The Second Sex, not as this Thursday’s subject. Nobel Prize Nobel Camus received the literature prize in 1957. Sartre refused it in 1964. Named as after-dates, not as the center of 1945. Poinsett U.S. Army Signal Corps photographer credited on the 29 August 1944 Champs-Élysées parade picture. Signal Corps U.S. Army Signal Corps Army Signal Corps U.S. Army photographic unit. Source of the Liberation parade picture. T1980 Wikimedia username of the photographer who took the August 1967 Venice portrait of Sartre used in this lesson. Diego Delso Delso Photographer of the 2022 Saint-Germain-des-Prés church picture. Tom Hilton Photographer of the 2015 Café de Flore window picture. Britchi Mirela Photographer of the 2011 Les Deux Magots terrace picture. Celette Wikimedia photographer of the 2018 Vieux-Colombier entrance picture. Studio Harcourt Paris portrait studio. Its 1945 Camus photograph is often treated as a French collective work; this capsule does not reproduce it. Constance Borde Borde Co-translator, with Sheila Malovany-Chevallier, of the complete English The Second Sex used in current catalogues. Sheila Malovany-Chevallier Malovany-Chevallier Co-translator of the complete English The Second Sex. Matthew Ward Translator of the American English The Stranger listed in this lesson’s read section. BnF Bibliothèque nationale de France Bibliotheque nationale de France Bibliothèque nationale de France. Hosts the Sartre exhibition notes linked under Read. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy SEP Open reference encyclopedia. The existentialism entry is linked under Read. Penguin Random House Publisher catalogue used for legal edition links to The Stranger and Invisible Man. Before A broken sentence, then a political decade, then a war High modernism had already broken the ordinary novel sentence. Woolf, Joyce, and Eliot made time and attention into structure; vernacular Chinese modernism was running in the same years. That work is another Thursday in this archive. What stands between those experiments and the books in this lesson is not a clean handover. The 1930s put politics back into the foreground of fiction and reportage: George Orwell’s Homage to Catalonia (1938), Richard Wright’s Native Son (1940), John Steinbeck’s The Grapes of Wrath (1939). Those titles are named here as the immediate literary past, not as a second lesson. Then came defeat, occupation, collaboration, deportation, and camps. By 1944 the question for many French writers was not how to fragment a day on the page. It was what a person was free to do inside a situation that had already chosen them. The abbey church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, photographed in November 2022. The cafés that sold the postwar story sit on the boulevard beside this tower. The cars and the news kiosk are later. The address is the fact. The Romanesque tower and dark spire of the church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés above lower stone buildings and a green Paris news kiosk, photographed in 2022. Sartre’s novel La Nausée had already appeared in 1938. It belongs in this lesson as a forerunner, not as a Liberation product. The occupation years then forced the argument into public rooms: heated cafés when hotels were cold, a theatre still open in May 1944, a Resistance paper, and, after August, a city that had to invent what “after” meant. The era Occupied Paris, Liberation, and a press word The trigger is concrete. Under occupation, Sartre and Beauvoir wrote at the Café de Flore because the upper floor stayed warm when charcoal and hotel heating failed. Huis clos — No Exit — opened at the Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier on 27 May 1944, still under German control of the city. Three characters locked in a Second Empire drawing room discover that they are one another’s torture. The line everyone remembers, “Hell is other people,” is a situation joke with philosophical teeth, not a poster about hating company. In August the city was liberated. The photographs of soldiers on the Champs-Élysées are the public fact. The literary fact is what a circle of writers did with the next fifteen years. Café de Flore, photographed through the window on 4 June 2015. Red banquettes, waiters in long aprons, a pastry case, a no-smoking sticker on the glass. This is the later tourist interior. During the Occupation the same address was a heated workplace for Sartre and Beauvoir. The caption has to say both things. Looking through a café window at red banquettes, arched mirrors, waiters in long white aprons, and a pastry case under warm lamps. Les Deux Magots, Boulevard Saint-Germain, 6 September 2011. The green awning and the name in gold are the postcard. Sartre’s circle also used this terrace; after the war the two cafés became interchangeable in the press. The timestamp in the corner is the photographer’s; the building is older. Sidewalk terrace of Les Deux Magots under a green awning with gold lettering, round tables and woven chairs, a waiter near the door. In October 1945 Les Temps modernes published its first issue. The title came from Chaplin’s Modern Times. Sartre directed; the board included Beauvoir, Merleau-Ponty, Aron, Leiris, Ollivier, and Paulhan. Camus was busy with Combat and was not on that masthead. The magazine serialized fiction and argument, printed Sartre’s claims for littérature engagée, and later carried chapters of Beauvoir’s The Second Sex. It was an institution in the plain sense: an office, a paper ration, a telephone number printed for visitors, and a place where a review could end a friendship in public. Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier, 21 rue du Vieux-Colombier, September 2018. The gold letters and the dove emblems mark the house where Huis clos premiered on 27 May 1944. The scooter, the Lucrèce Borgia poster, and the red lobby light are later. The address is the 1944 fact. Street entrance of the Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier with gold lettering, a dark modern canopy, red light inside the glass doors, a parked scooter and pedestrians. The word “existentialism” itself was partly a journalist’s convenience. Gabriel Marcel had used related language in 1943. On 29 October 1945 Sartre gave the lecture later published as Existentialism Is a Humanism; the room was crowded enough that the newspapers treated the word as a brand. Sartre and Beauvoir accepted a version of the name in public; Camus kept saying he was not an existentialist in Sartre’s sense. The useful literary unit is not the beret. It is the novel and the play of situation: a character thrown into a set of constraints — a beach, a plague city, a locked room, a sexed body, a colonized gaze — and forced to choose without a guaranteed script. How it showed up Novels and plays of situation — and three to read slowly Name the shelf without pretending it is one committee. Sartre: La Nausée (1938 forerunner), Being and Nothingness (1943), Huis clos (1944), the Temps modernes editorials, What Is Literature? (1948), Saint Genet (1952). Beauvoir: novels, memoirs, and The Second Sex (1949). Camus: L’Étranger (1942), The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), The Plague (1947), The Rebel (1951). Beside them: Genet’s plays and prose; Beckett’s Waiting for Godot (Paris, 1953), adjacent absurd theatre rather than Sartre’s school; Merleau-Ponty’s philosophy in the same offices; Fanon’s Black Skin, White Masks (1952), with The Wretched of the Earth (1961) at the far edge; Richard Wright in Paris writing The Outsider (1953). In Japan, Ōe Kenzaburō was reading French literature and Sartre as a student in the late 1950s; Abe Kōbō’s The Woman in the Dunes (1962) sits just after this lesson’s center and works a confinement problem that later readers filed beside the absurd. Those Japanese names are contemporaneous writers facing related pressures after defeat and occupation — not an assigned Asian twin for a Paris trio. Jean-Paul Sartre 1905–1980 Novelist, playwright, philosopher, magazine director. He made “situation” and “bad faith” into tools a general reader could argue with. The 1967 photograph is not a 1944 document; it is a free portrait of the public man the earlier decade produced. Venice, August 1967 — later than the Occupation café years. The face the cameras kept. Simone de Beauvoir 1908–1986 Philosopher and novelist; co-founder of Les Temps modernes. The Second Sex (1949) is a book of method — history, myth, lived reports — as much as it is a founding feminist text later waves would claim. A clearly free studio portrait from the 1940s is hard to license cleanly; this lesson does not invent one. Albert Camus 1913–1960 Novelist, playwright, Combat editor. The Stranger and The Plague made the absurd and revolt readable as stories. He rejected the school name “existentialist,” then broke with Sartre in 1952 over The Rebel. Studio Harcourt’s 1945 portrait is treated as public domain in France on collective-work grounds; this capsule skips it rather than lean on a thin cross-border claim. Richard Wright 1908–1960 Native Son (1940) belongs to the political-novel past. After the war he lived in Paris, knew Sartre and Beauvoir, and published The Outsider (1953). An American writer in the same cafés, not a French mascot. Carl Van Vechten’s studio portrait, 23 June 1939 — before Wright’s Paris years. The face that Native Son made public. Deepen three objects. First, The Stranger. Camus’s French is short, declarative, and cool: “Mother died today. Or maybe yesterday, I don’t know.” Meursault narrates heat, swimming, sex, and a funeral as if they were weather reports. The killing on the Algiers beach arrives with the same flatness. The trial then invents a moral personality the prose has refused to supply — he did not cry at his mother’s funeral, therefore he is a monster. The book’s force is technical: a style that will not perform the remorse the court demands. That is how the absurd gets into the sentences, not only into an essay. Second, The Second Sex. Beauvoir’s 1949 book is two volumes: how “woman” was made in biology talk, history, and myth, then how girls and women live that making. The famous line — one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman — is a claim about situation and becoming, written by a philosopher who had already co-run a magazine. Later Second Wave feminism would take the book as an ancestor; that reception is real. The book itself is also literature and method: long readings, case descriptions, a refusal to treat “woman” as a timeless essence. Put it beside Huis clos and L’Étranger as a postwar Paris object, not only as a chapter in a feminism syllabus. Third, the Camus–Sartre break. The Rebel appeared in 1951. In May 1952 Francis Jeanson reviewed it harshly in Les Temps modernes. Camus answered with a letter addressed not to Jeanson but to “Monsieur le Directeur” — Sartre. In the August issue Sartre answered at length and with personal heat. The friendship ended in the magazine that had defined their public. The argument was about revolt, history, and Marxism; it was also about who owned the postwar moral microphone. Treat it as a literary-political fact with dates, not as a celebrity feud with no content. Same time elsewhere Other 1950s rooms, not a formula While Paris argued about engagement, other literatures were not waiting for a French cue card. In the United States, Ralph Ellison’s Invisible Man (1952) sent a nameless narrator through a Southern college, a Harlem movement, and a basement with 1,369 lights. The book’s problem is American racial invisibility under Jim Crow and Northern hypocrisy. It is not a translation of Being and Nothingness. Gordon Parks’s wartime Harlem photographs — a newsboy before posters for Adam Clayton Powell Jr. and the Pittsburgh Courier — are the visual weather of that American situation, taken a decade earlier and still the right street. Harlem newsboy, May 1943, photographed by Gordon Parks for the U.S. Office of War Information. Posters for Adam Clayton Powell Jr.’s People’s Voice tour and a Pittsburgh Courier clipping sit behind him; the OWI serial number is printed at the top of the negative. This is New York under wartime Jim Crow, the American “elsewhere” for Invisible Man — not a Paris café. A young Black newsboy in a wool coat and knit cap stands before a newsstand covered with posters, including one for Adam Powell and People’s Voice; OWI serial number at the top. In Britain, the press found “Angry Young Men” after John Osborne’s Look Back in Anger opened at the Royal Court Theatre in 1956. Class resentment and a kitchen sink are the furniture; Saint-Germain is not. In Japan, writers who had lived defeat and occupation were publishing through the 1950s; Ōe’s early fiction and Abe’s later sand-pit novel are named here as parallel pressures, not as proof that existentialism was universal. Latin American boom novels of the 1960s are later and are not forced into this capsule. After The label thins; the books remain By about 1960 the Paris prestige slot was moving. Structuralism — Lévi-Strauss and the arguments that followed — took the seminar glamour. “Existentialist” became a costume in the newspapers: a jazz cellar, a black sweater, a simplified Sartre. Camus died in a car crash on 4 January 1960. Sartre lived long enough to refuse the Nobel Prize in 1964 and to become a different kind of public monument. The useful after is not yet postmodernism as a full lesson. It is this: the novels and plays still work when the beret joke is gone, and other cities had never needed the beret to write their own situations. If this archive takes another Thursday further on, it will not be to complete a French syllabus. It will be because another year also happened. A question A question to keep asking When a magazine can end a friendship in public, what is literature being asked to do that a private letter cannot? Albert Camus — The Stranger (Penguin Random House catalogue) Legal edition listing for L’Étranger (1942). Buy or borrow a standard translation; this capsule does not paste the novel. Simone de Beauvoir — The Second Sex (Penguin UK catalogue) Catalogue record for the Borde/Malovany-Chevallier translation. Library copies exist; this is not a pirated PDF. Ralph Ellison — Invisible Man (Penguin Random House catalogue) 1952 novel. Same-time American book, not a Paris café scene. Existentialism — Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy Open reference essay (Kevin Aho). Philosophy context for the literary label; not a substitute for the novels. Sartre and Camus: An Historic Confrontation — publisher page Edited translations of the 1952 Temps modernes exchange (Jeanson, Camus, Sartre). A map of the break, not a bootleg of Les Temps modernes. BnF — Huis clos (Sartre exhibition note) French national library note: premiere at the Théâtre du Vieux-Colombier, 27 May 1944. A date and a cast list, not a full play text.

subject: film
title: New Hollywood (c. 1967–1980): the studios lose the plot, then bet on directors
dek: Television took the weekly audience, the Production Code lost its force, and the old moguls sold out to conglomerates. American studios then financed younger directors, antiheroes, and profit participants — until Jaws, Star Wars, and Heaven’s Gate taught them a different lesson.
text: New Hollywood (c. 1967–1980): the studios lose the plot, then bet on directors Television took the weekly audience, the Production Code lost its force, and the old moguls sold out to conglomerates. American studios then financed younger directors, antiheroes, and profit participants — until Jaws, Star Wars, and Heaven’s Gate taught them a different lesson. c. 1967–1980 “New Hollywood” is a historians’ name, not a membership card. The useful facts are industrial. The major studios had lost their theaters after the 1948 Paramount Decree, lost the weekly audience to television, and lost the Production Code’s certainty. Conglomerates bought the logos. They then financed younger directors and profit participants because those films were making money with the people who still bought tickets. French New Wave films were something American directors and critics had actually watched — Bonnie and Clyde’s writers offered the script to Truffaut and Godard — not an Asia footnote and not a shot-for-shot template. New German Cinema, the first Hong Kong New Wave features, and the tail of Brazilian Cinema Novo were running in the same years. They are contemporaneous arguments, not assigned peers. Film film 1948 Theaters United States v. Paramount Pictures: the majors have to sell their theater chains. A flop no longer has a captive circuit. 1966 Code, conglomerate, import Jack Valenti becomes MPAA president (May). Gulf+Western takes Paramount (October). MGM releases Antonioni’s Blow-Up in the U.S. without a Code seal (18 December). 1967 The break Bonnie and Clyde (13 August). The Graduate (December). Warner Bros.-Seven Arts; Transamerica buys United Artists. Pauline Kael’s New Yorker essay on Bonnie and Clyde, 21 October. 1968 Ratings The MPAA rating system takes effect on 1 November: G, M, R, and X, replacing the Production Code. 1969 The road Easy Rider. Kinney National buys Warner. Coppola founds American Zoetrope in San Francisco. 1972–74 The studio hit The Godfather (1972). Panaflex camera (1972). The Godfather Part II and Chinatown (1974). Paramount under Robert Evans. 1975–77 The booking change Nashville and Jaws (1975). Taxi Driver (1976). Star Wars (1977). Television advertising and a wide opening become a method. 1979–80 The edge Apocalypse Now (1979). Ann Hui’s The Secret and Tsui Hark’s The Butterfly Murders (1979). Heaven’s Gate premieres (November 1980). Transamerica sells United Artists the next year. Jaws was first to $100 million in rentals, not in tickets Jaws opened on 20 June 1975. It is often called the first film to “gross $100 million.” That is the wrong unit. Several earlier films, including The Sound of Music and The Godfather, had already taken more than $100 million at the box office — the money paid at the window. Theatrical rentals are the distributor’s share of that money. Jaws was the first film to earn $100 million in U.S. theatrical rentals. The distinction is the point of the booking: a wide opening and a television campaign pulled the studio’s share over that line in a single summer. Star Wars took the rentals record two years later. New Hollywood Historians’ name for American studio filmmaking from about 1967 to 1980, when the old contract system had collapsed and studios financed younger directors, antiheroes, and profit participants. A later label, not a union card. Production Code Hays Code Motion Picture Production Code the Code The Motion Picture Production Code: written rules (1930) enforced from 1934 by the studios’ own Production Code Administration. A film without a seal was hard to book in the major theaters. Abandoned in 1968 in favor of age ratings. Hays Code Common name for the Production Code, after Will Hays, who ran the studios’ trade association when the Code was adopted. The enforcement office, from 1934, was Joseph Breen’s Production Code Administration. Will Hays Former U.S. Postmaster General; first head of the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America. The Production Code carries his name. He did not personally stamp every script in the 1960s. Joseph Breen Breen Head of the Production Code Administration from 1934. The Code’s force in Hollywood was his office, not only Hays’s letterhead. MPAA Motion Picture Association of America Motion Picture Association Motion Picture Association of America, the studios’ trade group. Jack Valenti became its president in 1966. On 1 November 1968 it replaced the Production Code with a voluntary age-rating system. Jack Valenti Valenti Lyndon Johnson aide who left the White House in May 1966 to run the MPAA. He junked the Production Code and, with theater owners, installed ratings that took effect on 1 November 1968. MPAA ratings ratings system G, M, R, and X Voluntary age labels that replaced the Production Code on 1 November 1968. The original four were G, M, R, and X. M was later renamed GP, then PG. PG-13 did not exist until 1984. SMA Suggested for Mature Audiences For Mature Audiences “Suggested for Mature Audiences,” a 1966 warning line used on some studio films, including Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?, while the Code was already leaking. Valenti later called it too little and too late. National Legion of Decency Catholic reviewing body that rated films for parish use and could wound a booking. It condemned Blow-Up. Condemnation was not a legal ban. Paramount Decree United States v. Paramount Pictures Paramount decision The 1948 Supreme Court decision in United States v. Paramount Pictures. The major studios had to sell their theaters. Without a guaranteed circuit, a flop was a flop. roadshow roadshows roadshow epic roadshow epics A prestige booking: reserved seats, higher prices, an overture, often a reserved-seat road tour before a wider release. The Sound of Music (1965) made the format look immortal. Several later roadshow epics did not. auteur As American critics used the word after Andrew Sarris: the director as the author of a film, ranked by a body of work. Sarris translated the Cahiers politique des auteurs into an “auteur theory.” Pauline Kael attacked the ranking. Studios in the 1970s used the word more loosely, as a reason to bet on a name. Notes on the Auteur Theory in 1962 Andrew Sarris’s essay in Film Culture (winter 1962–63). It is how many American readers first met “auteur theory” as a set of premises, not only as a French polemic. Circles and Squares Pauline Kael’s 1963 Film Quarterly attack on Sarris and auteur ranking. She argued that a film is a collaboration and that Sarris’s “circles” of directors were a closed game. Andrew Sarris Sarris American critic (Village Voice, Film Culture). “Notes on the Auteur Theory in 1962” gave U.S. readers a name and a ranking method. New Hollywood directors were raised on that argument even when they ignored it. Pauline Kael Kael American critic. “Circles and Squares” (1963) against Sarris; a long New Yorker essay on Bonnie and Clyde (21 October 1967) that treated the film as a break, not a mess. She joined The New Yorker as a regular in 1968. Film Culture New York film magazine. Sarris’s 1962 auteur essay appeared there. The New Yorker New Yorker Weekly magazine. Kael’s Bonnie and Clyde essay ran in the 21 October 1967 issue. William Shawn then hired her as a film critic. movie brat movie brats The Movie Brats Press and book name (Michael Pye and Lynda Myles, The Movie Brats, 1979) for the film-school generation that reached studio features in the 1970s: Coppola (UCLA), Scorsese (NYU), Lucas (USC), De Palma, and, beside them though not from the same school path, Spielberg. package deal package deals packaging A film sold to a studio as a bundle — typically star, director, and script — assembled by an agent or a producer rather than by a studio with people under long-term contract. MCA had packaged television that way. In 1970s features, agencies and independent producers did the same job once the contract lists were gone. high-concept Industry slang for a film whose premise can be stated in a line and sold on television before opening day. The 1962 Oberhausen Manifesto had already said that the old West German cinema was finished. In the 1970s the films that traveled were paid for in part by television and, from 1971, by the Filmverlag der Autoren, a cooperative of filmmakers. Rainer Werner Fassbinder worked at a speed American package deals did not require: Ali: Fear Eats the Soul in 1974, and a long list beside it. Werner Herzog’s Aguirre, the Wrath of God (1972) and Wim Wenders’s Kings of the Road (1976) are other festival names. Volker Schlöndorff’s The Tin Drum would take Cannes in 1979, the same year as Apocalypse Now. The comparison that matters is money and venue: a television-backed German film on the festival circuit beside an American studio film in a few hundred air-conditioned houses. Same years. Different checks. Rainer Werner Fassbinder, photographed at the Venice Film Festival in 1980 — the year Heaven’s Gate opened in the United States. The table, the hat, and the glass are what the picture contains. New German Cinema was a contemporaneous argument, funded by television and a filmmakers’ cooperative, not a Paramount slate. Rainer Werner Fassbinder in a dark hat and vest over a mesh shirt, holding a glass at a crowded table. In Hong Kong the useful 1970s fact is television, not a sudden 1967 mirror of Bonnie and Clyde. TVB hired young directors who had often studied abroad. Ann Hui, Tsui Hark, and Patrick Tam learned to shoot quickly on 16mm and on tight schedules. The theatrical New Wave is usually dated from 1979: Hui’s The Secret, Tsui’s The Butterfly Murders, and a cluster of other first features. That is the end of this American window, not a subplot inside The Godfather. Brazilian Cinema Novo is older. Glauber Rocha’s Black God, White Devil is 1964. By the 1970s the military dictatorship had scattered the movement; Rocha often worked in exile. It belongs here as a tail running in the same decade, not as a peer assigned to Spielberg. The festival circuit was where those cinemas met. Cannes, Berlin, and the New York Film Festival showed European art films to the same journalists who would, a month later, write about a Paramount opening. Coppola’s Apocalypse Now and Schlöndorff’s The Tin Drum sharing Cannes in 1979 is a date, not a merger. American directors had watched the New Wave. German, Hong Kong, and Brazilian filmmakers had their own studios, censors, and broadcasters to fight. The honest look outward is contemporaneous, not a formula of Western frame plus Asian peer. After Heaven’s Gate, the conglomerates, and a calendar Michael Cimino’s The Deer Hunter (1978) won the prizes that buy a director a larger bet. United Artists gave him Heaven’s Gate. The film premiered in November 1980, was pulled, recut, and still failed in American theaters against a cost reported in the tens of millions. Transamerica, tired of being the company that owned that headline, sold United Artists to MGM in 1981. Director-driven packages did not vanish overnight. The public lesson, for conglomerate boards, was that a director’s cut of the profits could also be a director’s cut of the company. The other lesson was already on the calendar. Jaws had shown that summer, television spots, and a wide opening could pull rentals over a line no roadshow had reached so fast. Star Wars had shown that a sentence and a toy line could do it again. The studios that remained — Paramount inside Gulf+Western, Warner inside a communications company, Fox, Universal — kept the logos and learned to slot a few large films rather than to keep a slate of director bets in the 1972 manner. High-concept is the later word. The 1980 fact is simpler: the window this lesson describes had an end. This is not a 1980s chapter. It is the edge where the 1970s bet stopped looking like the future. Paramount’s water tower, photographed in 2025 from Hollywood Forever Cemetery. The tank still carries the mountain and stars. The line “A Viacom Company” is later paint. In the years of this lesson the owner was Gulf+Western. The lot remained. The kind of bet the lot made in 1972 is what changed. The Paramount water tower seen over a wall and trees, mountain-and-stars logo and the later line A Viacom Company. A question A question to keep asking If a studio can sell a film in one sentence on television before anyone has seen it, what is it still paying the director for? Bonnie and Clyde — Warner Bros. film page Studio catalogue record for the 1967 film. Licensed editions exist; this capsule does not link a pirated full film. The Godfather — Paramount Pictures film page Studio page for Coppola’s 1972 film, with legal places to watch. Not a rip. Nashville — Criterion film page Altman, 1975. Licensed home-video edition in the Criterion catalogue. Heaven’s Gate — Criterion film page Cimino, 1980, director’s cut. The catalogue record for a restored licensed edition, not a bootleg of the 1980 opening cut. Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope — official film page Lucasfilm’s page for the 1977 film. Watch a legal copy; this capsule does not link a rip. BFI — A great New Hollywood film for every year (1967 to 1982) Library essay with a year-by-year list. A map, not a pirated film.

subject: music
title: Psychedelia (c. 1965–1969): studios, scenes, and longer songs
dek: After the British Invasion, studios and ballrooms stretched the pop single. San Francisco, London, and a few other cities made longer songs, light shows, and albums you were meant to sit with.
text: Psychedelia (c. 1965–1969): studios, scenes, and longer songs After the British Invasion, studios and ballrooms stretched the pop single. San Francisco, London, and a few other cities made longer songs, light shows, and albums you were meant to sit with. c. 1965–1969 “Psychedelia” is a press and fan word, not a union card. San Francisco ballrooms, London underground clubs, Los Angeles studios, Austin, New York, and São Paulo were not one scene with a shared committee. LSD is part of the history; it is not the whole of the music. This lesson looks out from those rooms and desks. Group Sounds in Japan and Tropicália in Brazil were running in the same years. They are not decoration, and they are not a required Asia pairing. The Velvet Underground is a same-time New York contrast, not a peer assigned by geography. Music music 1965 Rubber Soul / folk-rock The Beatles’ Rubber Soul (UK, 3 December). The Byrds had already put folk songs on electric twelve-string. Ken Kesey’s Acid Tests were running in California. The useful unit was still often a 45. 1966 Studios and ballrooms Pet Sounds (16 May). Revolver (UK, 5 August). The 13th Floor Elevators’ The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators. Bill Graham at the Fillmore; Chet Helms and the Family Dog at the Avalon. UFO opened in London on 23 December. 1967 Monterey / FM / Piper Monterey Pop, 16–18 June. Tom Donahue’s album-cut shows on KMPX-FM in San Francisco. Pink Floyd’s The Piper at the Gates of Dawn (UK, 4 August). Are You Experienced, Surrealistic Pillow, The Velvet Underground & Nico. 1968 Tropicália / AI-5 Tropicália: ou Panis et Circencis and Os Mutantes’ debut. Fillmore West opened. Institutional Act No. 5 in Brazil (13 December). Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil were arrested on 27 December. 1969 Woodstock / Altamont Woodstock, 15–18 August, on Max Yasgur’s farm in Bethel, New York. Altamont Speedway, 6 December. Japanese Group Sounds was past its 1967–68 peak. Veloso and Gil left for London. The first song recorded for Revolver was already a studio machine On 6 April 1966, at EMI Studios on Abbey Road, the Beatles began Revolver with John Lennon’s “Tomorrow Never Knows.” Engineer Geoff Emerick ran Lennon’s voice through a Leslie rotating speaker cabinet built for Hammond organs. Several tape loops — including a laughing voice and a distorted guitar — were mixed live on the desk because four-track tape did not leave much room to stack them later. The finished track is under three minutes. The “long song” in 1966 was often still a single’s length. What had changed was the method: the studio was no longer only a place to photograph a live group. psychedelia psychedelic Press and fan word, mid-to-late 1960s, for music, light shows, and graphics associated with longer forms, studio experiment, and, in some crowds, LSD. It was never a single committee or sound. acid rock American name for the guitar-heavy, often improvising end of the San Francisco ballroom circuit. Not a synonym for every London studio experiment. ballroom ballrooms In this lesson, the San Francisco dance halls — Fillmore, Avalon, later Fillmore West — that booked rock bills on a floor without seats, with light shows. A room and a format, not a waltz. FM FM radio underground FM free-form radio Frequency-modulation radio. From 1967, stations such as KMPX in San Francisco used FM to play album cuts instead of AM Top 40 singles. The LP became a radio unit. concept album concept albums An LP meant to be heard as a set, sometimes with a linking idea or running order that is not just a stack of singles. Sgt. Pepper is the usual example; Pet Sounds and Revolver already asked for the same attention. Tropicália Tropicalismo tropicalia Brazilian late-1960s arts movement. Hélio Oiticica used the word for a 1967 installation; Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil applied it to music that mixed Brazilian forms with electric studio pop under a military dictatorship. folk-rock Mid-1960s electric setting of folk repertoire and songwriting, associated in the United States with the Byrds. A bridge from clubs to the later 1960s studio and ballroom records. light show light shows liquid light show Projected oils, dyes, and slides on ballroom and club walls, run with the band. Part of the Fillmore/Avalon and UFO nights, not a music video. festival festivals Here, multi-act outdoor bills that scaled a dance to a fairground or farm: Monterey 1967, Woodstock 1969, Altamont 1969. Logistics and a crowd, not only a vibe. album culture The late-1960s market habit of selling rock as long-playing records, FM time, and gatefold objects rather than only as 45 rpm singles. British Invasion American press name, from 1964, for British beat groups on the U.S. charts. The immediate past of this lesson. See the earlier capsule on that chart event. beat groups beat group British early-1960s guitar-bass-drums-vocals groups. The school many of the later studio bands came from. folk clubs folk club Small rooms where singers learned traditional and contemporary folk songs, often acoustic, before folk-rock and the later 1960s electric bands. amphetamines amphetamine Stimulant drugs. In early-1960s Britain, some Mods and working musicians used them — including Drinamyl tablets nicknamed purple hearts — to stay awake through all-nighters. Short, fast sets fitted that use. Drinamyl purple hearts purple heart British amphetamine–barbiturate tablet. “Purple hearts” was a street name. Part of the Mod all-nighter, not of the later ballroom light show. LSD lysergic acid diethylamide Hallucinogenic drug. Present in some California and London scenes by the mid-1960s. Where it was part of the room, longer sets and light shows fitted better than a three-minute riff. Not an explanation for every record in this lesson. Acid Tests Acid Test Ken Kesey’s 1965–66 California events: a house band, lights, and LSD in warehouses and halls. One local before of the San Francisco dance. Family Dog San Francisco commune and promotion group around Chet Helms. Ran dances at the Avalon Ballroom from 1966. Group Sounds グループ・サウンズ GS Japanese mid-1960s electric-guitar pop. Peaked 1967–68; fading by 1969–70 as folk and harder rock took students. Same years as this lesson, not an assigned twin of San Francisco. kayōkyoku Japanese popular song of the postwar decades, the domestic tradition Group Sounds bands heard alongside imported beat records. Exploding Plastic Inevitable EPI Andy Warhol’s 1966–67 multimedia events, with the Velvet Underground. New York’s live context for that group, not a Fillmore dance. anthropophagy Oswald de Andrade’s 1928 idea of Brazil “eating” foreign culture. Tropicália musicians used it as a way to mix Beatles records with Brazilian forms without pretending to be a cover band. Institutional Act No. 5 AI-5 AI5 Brazilian decree, 13 December 1968, that hardened military censorship and repression. The political weather of Tropicália’s last months as a public movement. four-track four-track tape 4-track Tape format used at Abbey Road for Revolver: four discrete tracks. Loops and overdubs had to be planned or mixed live because there was little spare space. Leslie speaker Leslie Leslie cabinet Rotating speaker cabinet built for Hammond organs. Geoff Emerick ran John Lennon’s voice through one on “Tomorrow Never Knows.” A hardware fact. tape loop tape loops A length of recording tape joined end to end so a sound repeats. Several loops were mixed live into “Tomorrow Never Knows.” Wrecking Crew Informal name for the Los Angeles session players Brian Wilson used on Pet Sounds. They were studio professionals, not the touring Beach Boys lineup on those tracks. hard rock Louder, riff-based rock that is one line out of Hendrix, the Who, and the heavier ballroom nights. This lesson names it as an after, not as a syllabus. Haight-Ashbury Haight San Francisco neighborhood at Haight and Ashbury streets, the 1967 press address for the local counterculture. Sidewalks and crash pads; the ballrooms were elsewhere in the city. Fillmore Fillmore Auditorium the Fillmore Ballroom at Fillmore and Geary, San Francisco. Bill Graham began booking rock dances there in 1966. Fillmore West Graham’s larger San Francisco room from 1968, in the former Carousel Ballroom. Not the original Fillmore Auditorium. Avalon Ballroom Avalon Dance hall at Sutter and Van Ness, San Francisco. Family Dog / Chet Helms shows, 1966–69. UFO Club UFO London underground club opened 23 December 1966 by Joe Boyd and John Hopkins at 31 Tottenham Court Road. Pink Floyd and Soft Machine played the first night. Moved to the Roundhouse in 1967 and folded that autumn. Roundhouse the Roundhouse Circular former railway building in Chalk Farm, London. UFO’s second address in 1967. Abbey Road EMI Studios Abbey Road Studios EMI’s London studios on Abbey Road. Revolver and The Piper at the Gates of Dawn were recorded there. Western Recorders Western Hollywood studio where much of Pet Sounds was tracked, with engineer Chuck Britz among the staff. Gold Star Gold Star Studios Hollywood studio associated with Phil Spector and used for some Beach Boys dates around Pet Sounds. KMPX KMPX-FM San Francisco FM station where Tom Donahue began playing album-cut rock in 1967. An origin point for underground FM. KSAN KSAN-FM San Francisco FM station that took Donahue’s staff after the KMPX strike. Broadcast a long call-in after Altamont. Monterey International Pop Festival Monterey Pop Monterey Monterey Pop Festival Non-profit festival at the Monterey County Fairgrounds, 16–18 June 1967. Otis Redding, Ravi Shankar, the Who, Hendrix, Airplane, Joplin, and others. Filmed by D. A. Pennebaker. Woodstock Woodstock Music and Art Fair Woodstock Festival Festival on Max Yasgur’s farm in Bethel, New York, 15–18 August 1969. The end-edge of this lesson’s festival story, not its beginning. Altamont Altamont Speedway Altamont Free Concert Free Rolling Stones concert at Altamont Speedway, California, 6 December 1969. Crowding, fights, and the killing of Meredith Hunter. A logistics failure at highway scale. Summer of Love Press name for San Francisco, especially Haight-Ashbury, in 1967. A crowd and a headline, not a recording technique. Radio 1 BBC Radio 1 BBC pop network launched in 1967 as official radio for a habit pirate ships had already trained. British context for the same years as UFO and Piper. BBC British public broadcaster. Needle-time still shaped how many records it could play in the mid-1960s; Radio 1 was part of the 1967 answer. The Beatles Beatles Liverpool group, then Abbey Road. Rubber Soul, Revolver, and Sgt. Pepper are the studio facts in this lesson, not another invasion-era television date. The Beach Boys Beach Boys California group. Pet Sounds (1966) is Brian Wilson’s studio answer to Rubber Soul, made largely with session players. The Byrds Byrds Los Angeles group. Folk-rock on electric twelve-string; “Eight Miles High” (1966) is their usual bridge into this lesson’s years. Jefferson Airplane Airplane San Francisco group. Surrealistic Pillow (1967) put Grace Slick’s “White Rabbit” on the radio while the band still played the ballrooms. Grateful Dead the Dead San Francisco group. Ballroom improvisation as a method; the long set rather than the three-minute single. Big Brother and the Holding Company Big Brother San Francisco group. Janis Joplin sang with them from 1966 until 1968. Cheap Thrills is the 1968 album; Monterey is the 1967 live introduction for many viewers. Janis Joplin Joplin American singer. With Big Brother at Monterey; later a solo name. A ballroom and festival fact in this lesson, not a studio-tape story. Jimi Hendrix Hendrix American guitarist who became famous in London with the Jimi Hendrix Experience. Are You Experienced (1967); Monterey, 18 June 1967, where he destroyed a Stratocaster. The Jimi Hendrix Experience Jimi Hendrix Experience the Experience Hendrix, Noel Redding, Mitch Mitchell. London-based trio, 1966–69. The records were London studio jobs; Monterey made the American name. Pink Floyd London group. House band at UFO in early 1967; The Piper at the Gates of Dawn recorded at Abbey Road and released 4 August 1967, mostly written by Syd Barrett. Soft Machine Canterbury/London group. Played UFO’s opening night with Pink Floyd. Jazz-leaning, not a San Francisco ballroom band. Traffic British group, formed 1967. Mr. Fantasy (late 1967) is a UK studio and cottage fact, not a Fillmore franchise. 13th Floor Elevators the Elevators Austin group. The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators (1966) put the word on the sleeve early, with Roky Erickson and an amplified jug. Love Los Angeles group around Arthur Lee. Forever Changes (November 1967, Elektra) is orchestral folk-rock from that city, not from Haight-Ashbury. The Velvet Underground Velvet Underground VU New York group. The Velvet Underground & Nico (March 1967) and Warhol’s Exploding Plastic Inevitable. A same-time contrast, not the West Coast’s missing conscience. Os Mutantes São Paulo group (Sérgio Dias, Arnaldo Baptista, Rita Lee). Debut album 1968; “Panis et Circenses” opens it. Tropicália’s electric band, not a Beatles tribute act. The Who Who London group. Smashed instruments at Monterey, the theatre Hendrix then had to outdo. Not a San Francisco band. The Rolling Stones Rolling Stones the Stones London group. Headlined the Altamont free concert, 6 December 1969. In this lesson they are that date, not the 1964 Invasion story. The Tigers Tigers Japanese Group Sounds band, a television name at GS’s 1967–68 peak. Otis Redding American soul singer. Played Monterey, 1967. On the bill to show that the festival was not only the local ballroom bands. Ravi Shankar Indian sitar player. Played Monterey, 1967. A full set of Hindustani classical music on a pop-festival bill, not a studio garnish. Brian Wilson Beach Boys writer and producer. Pet Sounds is his studio project with Tony Asher and Los Angeles session players. Tony Asher Lyricist who worked with Brian Wilson on Pet Sounds. George Martin Parlophone/EMI producer for the Beatles. Revolver is a staff-producer record at a major-label studio, not a bedroom experiment. Geoff Emerick Abbey Road engineer on Revolver. Close-miked drums; Leslie cabinet on Lennon’s voice; tape loops mixed live. John Lennon Beatles writer and singer. “Tomorrow Never Knows” is his Revolver track; the vocal is a Leslie cabinet, not a metaphor. Paul McCartney Beatles writer. On the Monterey festival board; insisted the Jimi Hendrix Experience be booked. Bill Graham San Francisco promoter. Fillmore Auditorium from 1966; Fillmore West from 1968. A lease and a door, not a commune. Chet Helms Family Dog promoter. Avalon Ballroom from 1966. Recruited Janis Joplin to Big Brother. Joe Boyd American producer in London. Co-founded UFO with John Hopkins in 1966. John Hopkins Hoppy Hoppy Hopkins London underground organizer. Co-founded UFO; connected to International Times and the 1960s London press scene. Tom Donahue Disc jockey and promoter. Began album-cut rock on KMPX-FM in San Francisco in 1967; later KSAN. Underground FM as a format. Syd Barrett Pink Floyd’s original writer and guitarist. Most of The Piper at the Gates of Dawn is his. The later Floyd is another lesson. Grace Slick Jefferson Airplane singer from 1966. Brought “White Rabbit” and “Somebody to Love” from her previous group, the Great Society. Great Society the Great Society Grace Slick’s San Francisco group before Jefferson Airplane. Source of “White Rabbit.” Roky Erickson 13th Floor Elevators singer. Austin, not San Francisco. Arthur Lee Love’s singer and writer. Forever Changes is his 1967 Los Angeles record. Andy Warhol New York artist. Produced and packaged The Velvet Underground & Nico; ran the Exploding Plastic Inevitable. Nico German singer on The Velvet Underground & Nico. A voice on that album, not a San Francisco ballroom name. Gilberto Gil Gil Brazilian musician, Tropicália. Co-organized the 1968 manifesto album; arrested 27 December 1968; exiled to London in 1969. Caetano Veloso Veloso Brazilian musician, Tropicália. Took Oiticica’s word for a song; arrested with Gil in December 1968; London exile 1969. Gal Costa Brazilian singer on Tropicália: ou Panis et Circencis (1968). Tom Zé Brazilian musician on the Tropicália manifesto album. Rogério Duprat Brazilian arranger on Tropicália: ou Panis et Circencis and Os Mutantes’ debut. Studio craft, not a light show. Hélio Oiticica Brazilian artist. His 1967 Rio installation Tropicália gave the movement its name: penetrable structures, plants, sand, a television. Oswald de Andrade Brazilian writer. His 1928 idea of cultural anthropophagy was reused by Tropicália musicians in 1967–68. Ken Kesey American writer. Organized the Acid Tests in California, 1965–66. D. A. Pennebaker Pennebaker Filmmaker. Monterey Pop (1968) is the licensed documentary of the 1967 festival. Chas Chandler Former Animals bassist; produced the Jimi Hendrix Experience’s early London records. Noel Redding Bassist in the Jimi Hendrix Experience. Mitch Mitchell Drummer in the Jimi Hendrix Experience. Max Yasgur Dairy farmer in Bethel, New York, whose land hosted Woodstock in August 1969. Meredith Hunter Eighteen-year-old killed at Altamont on 6 December 1969, in front of the stage. A fact of that concert, not a symbol to decorate a paragraph. Arnold Skolnick Designer of the 1969 Woodstock bird-and-guitar advertisement poster. Phil Spector American producer. Wall of Sound method Wilson was expanding, not copying, on Pet Sounds. Bob Dylan Dylan American songwriter. His electric turn is a different chapter; named here only as the folk-to-electric bridge other people were also on. Mods Mod British youth style of the early-to-mid 1960s. All-nighters and, for some, amphetamines. The tempo before the light show. Capitol Capitol Records American label. Issued Pet Sounds and, in the United States, the Beatles. Parlophone EMI label that issued the Beatles in Britain, including Rubber Soul and Revolver. RCA RCA Victor Label that issued Jefferson Airplane’s Surrealistic Pillow. Elektra Elektra Records Label that issued Love’s Forever Changes. Verve Label that issued The Velvet Underground & Nico. International Artists Houston label that issued The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators. Track Records Track UK label that issued Are You Experienced in May 1967. Reprise US label that issued Are You Experienced in August 1967 with a different track list and cover. Warner US label that issued the Grateful Dead’s debut album in 1967. Rubber Soul Beatles album, UK release 3 December 1965. The LP Brian Wilson heard as a whole and answered with Pet Sounds. Revolver Beatles album, UK release 5 August 1966. Four-track Abbey Road, Martin and Emerick. Studio method before Sgt. Pepper’s costumes. Pet Sounds Beach Boys album, Capitol, 16 May 1966. Produced by Brian Wilson with session players in Hollywood. Sgt. Pepper Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band Beatles album, May 1967. The usual concept-album example. This lesson treats the 1966 pair as the clearer method. Tomorrow Never Knows Lennon song on Revolver. First track recorded for the album, 6 April 1966. Leslie vocal, tape loops mixed live. Under three minutes. God Only Knows Beach Boys song on Pet Sounds, 1966. Wilson–Asher. A short song whose arrangement is the studio fact. White Rabbit Jefferson Airplane single and Surrealistic Pillow track, 1967. Written by Grace Slick. Bolero-like build; AM radio length. Somebody to Love Jefferson Airplane single from Surrealistic Pillow, 1967. Also brought by Grace Slick from the Great Society. Are You Experienced Jimi Hendrix Experience debut. UK, Track, May 1967; US, Reprise, August 1967, with a different running order that added the early singles. Purple Haze Hendrix single, 1967. On the US Are You Experienced. Two and a half minutes. Official audio exists; the Monterey fire is a different document. The Piper at the Gates of Dawn Piper at the Gates of Dawn Piper Pink Floyd debut, UK 4 August 1967, Abbey Road, mostly Syd Barrett. The studio record of the UFO band. See Emily Play Pink Floyd UK single, 16 June 1967. Official channel upload. Later on the US Piper. A three-minute underground 45. Arnold Layne Pink Floyd’s first UK single, 1967. UFO-era 45, before Piper. Surrealistic Pillow Jefferson Airplane album, RCA, 1 February 1967. First with Grace Slick and Spencer Dryden in the lineup that became the radio version of the band. Forever Changes Love album, Elektra, November 1967. Arthur Lee, Los Angeles, orchestral arrangements. Not a Haight-Ashbury record. The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators The Psychedelic Sounds 13th Floor Elevators album, International Artists, 1966. The word “psychedelic” as a sleeve fact before the Summer of Love headline. You’re Gonna Miss Me You're Gonna Miss Me 13th Floor Elevators track and single, on the 1966 International Artists album. The Velvet Underground & Nico Debut album, Verve, 12 March 1967. Recorded 1966. Warhol packaging. New York, same calendar as Surrealistic Pillow and Piper. Tropicália: ou Panis et Circencis Tropicália ou Panis et Circencis Panis et Circencis 1968 Brazilian collaborative album organized by Veloso and Gil. Manifesto record of musical Tropicália. Panis et Circenses Panis Et Circenses Panis et circenses Veloso–Gil song. Opens Os Mutantes’ 1968 debut; also on the Tropicália manifesto album. Studio shape-shifting in Portuguese. Eight Miles High Byrds single, 1966. Folk-rock group stretching form and modal guitar in the same year as Pet Sounds and Revolver. Mr. Fantasy Traffic album, UK late 1967. British, not a San Francisco export. Cheap Thrills Big Brother and the Holding Company album, 1968, with Janis Joplin. After Monterey; still a San Francisco group record. Eleanor Rigby Beatles song on Revolver. String octet, no Beatles playing as a beat group. A studio fact on the same LP as the tape loops. Wild Thing Song Hendrix closed with at Monterey, 18 June 1967, before destroying the Stratocaster. The theatre, not the studio method. Monterey Pop D. A. Pennebaker’s 1968 documentary of the Monterey festival. Licensed editions exist; it is a film, not a bootleg tape. International Times IT London underground newspaper. Part of the print culture around UFO. San Francisco Oracle Oracle the Oracle Haight-Ashbury underground paper, 1966–68. Psychedelic lettering as print, not only as posters. San Francisco Mime Troupe Political theatre company. Bill Graham’s benefit shows for them in 1965 led him to the Fillmore. Carousel Ballroom San Francisco room that became Fillmore West when Graham moved there in 1968. Bethel Town in New York State. Woodstock the festival was on Yasgur’s farm here, not in the town of Woodstock. Tottenham Court Road London street. UFO’s first address was the basement at number 31, from December 1966 to July 1967. Bahia Brazilian state. Veloso and Gil came from there before São Paulo and the Tropicália records. São Paulo Brazilian city where Tropicália musicians met Os Mutantes and used television song festivals as a public stage. Austin Texas city. Home of the 13th Floor Elevators. Not a suburb of the Fillmore. Before Beat groups, folk clubs, and a change of tempo The British Invasion of 1964–65 had already sold America a British version of American rhythm and blues and rock and roll. From Britain the same years were still a 45 rpm business: beat groups, package tours, pirate ships around a BBC that limited how many records it could play, and folk and R&B clubs where a singer learned other people’s songs before writing. The Byrds in Los Angeles put folk repertoire on electric twelve-string and called it folk-rock. Bob Dylan’s electric turn is a different chapter. The useful fact here is the bridge: acoustic clubs and beat cellars were the school; the next records asked for more time on the disc and more time in the room. The chemical history is narrower than the posters later claimed. In early-1960s Britain, some Mods and working musicians used amphetamines — Drinamyl tablets nicknamed purple hearts among them — to stay awake through all-nighters. The music that fit that use was short, loud, and built to keep a floor moving. Lysergic acid diethylamide, LSD, was an older laboratory compound that a smaller set of writers and musicians in California and London were taking by the mid-1960s. Ken Kesey’s Acid Tests, from 1965, put a house band, lights, and the drug in the same warehouses. What changed in some scenes was tempo and length, not a sudden moral collapse. A three-minute riff and a thirty-minute jam are different jobs. Amphetamines helped with the first. LSD, where it was part of the room, fitted the second: light shows that did not need a verse-chorus to land, and sets that could wander. Not every group used either. The Grateful Dead’s long improvisations and the Beatles’ tape loops are not the same practice. Treat the drug shift as a real historical change in some crowds, and as a poor explanation for every sitar on a B-side. Rubber Soul, released in the United Kingdom on 3 December 1965, is the album that made that change audible on a major label without yet wearing the later costume. Brian Wilson heard it as a whole LP, not a stack of singles, and went into Western Recorders and Gold Star in Los Angeles to answer it. The Beatles, for their part, were about to stop touring and treat Abbey Road as the instrument. Folk clubs and beat groups got them there. The next two years would be studios, ballrooms, and a press word — psychedelia — that tried to name too many rooms at once. The era Studios, ballrooms, FM, and a weekend in Monterey Two kinds of room did most of the work: the recording studio and the dance hall. In Hollywood, Brian Wilson produced Pet Sounds with lyricist Tony Asher and the session players later nicknamed the Wrecking Crew. Capitol released the album on 16 May 1966. Wilson was not taking the Beach Boys on the road as a self-contained instrumental band for those tracks. He was stacking voices and unusual instruments the way Phil Spector had stacked a wall of sound, then going further into quiet, bass harmonica, and dog barks. In London, from April to June 1966, the Beatles recorded Revolver at EMI Studios on Abbey Road with George Martin and a young engineer, Geoff Emerick. They were still on four-track tape. Automatic double tracking, close-miked drums, tape loops, and a Leslie cabinet on a vocal were hardware solutions, not metaphors. Revolver appeared in the United Kingdom on 5 August 1966. The two albums did not cause each other. They were made in the same months, in different buildings, by people who were listening to one another’s finished records. EMI Studios, Abbey Road, photographed in 2005. Revolver was recorded here in 1966, on four-track tape, with George Martin producing and Geoff Emerick engineering. The zebra crossing on the album sleeve is a later photograph. The building is the 1966 fact. The white Georgian front of Abbey Road Studios in London, with a parked car and the famous zebra crossing out of frame to the left. San Francisco’s contribution was not first a studio method. It was a circuit of ballrooms. Bill Graham, who had managed the San Francisco Mime Troupe, began putting on rock dances at the Fillmore Auditorium at Fillmore and Geary in 1966. Chet Helms and the Family Dog took the Avalon Ballroom at Sutter and Van Ness. For a few weeks they had shared the Fillmore on alternate nights; then Graham leased the room and Helms moved. The format was Friday and Saturday, several bands, two sets each, a floor without seats, and a liquid light show on the walls. Jefferson Airplane, the Grateful Dead, and Big Brother and the Holding Company — Janis Joplin joined Big Brother in 1966 — were local bills before they were national names. The posters on the telephone poles were the weekly newspaper: hard to read on purpose, sold afterward as objects. This lesson does not reproduce those posters. Many are still in copyright. The rooms are the evidence that survives without piracy. 1268 and 1244 Sutter Street, March 2022, the former Avalon Ballroom. Family Dog dances ran here from 1966 to 1969. The light show and the $2.50 at the top of the stairs are gone. The upstairs hall is why the address still matters. A three-story white commercial building on Sutter Street, San Francisco, with two street-level entrances and a faded painted sign high on the wall. San Francisco Oracle, volume 1, number 5, January 1967. The Haight-Ashbury underground paper used the same dense, hard-to-scan lettering as the ballroom posters. This cover announced a gathering in Golden Gate Park. The Oracle is a document of the scene’s print culture, not a concert ticket. January 1967 cover of the San Francisco Oracle: ornate lettering around a photograph of a gathering in Golden Gate Park, with names including Timothy Leary and Allen Ginsberg. London’s version was smaller and shorter. Joe Boyd and John “Hoppy” Hopkins opened the UFO Club on 23 December 1966 in the basement of 31 Tottenham Court Road, under an Irish dance hall. Pink Floyd and Soft Machine played the opening night. The bills mixed bands with light shows, films, and poetry. International Times and the rest of the underground press treated UFO as a weekly address. The landlord ended the Tottenham Court Road residency in July 1967 after a tabloid scare; the club moved to the Roundhouse in Chalk Farm and folded that autumn. Pink Floyd’s The Piper at the Gates of Dawn, with Syd Barrett writing most of it, was recorded at Abbey Road and released in the United Kingdom on 4 August 1967. Arnold Layne and See Emily Play were still singles. The British underground could be a three-minute 45 and a late club in the same month. The Roundhouse, Chalk Farm Road, photographed in 2006. UFO moved here from Tottenham Court Road in the summer of 1967 and did not last the year. The building is a former railway turntable shed. In 1966–67 it was one of the few London rooms that could hold the underground’s light show and a band at once. The circular brick Roundhouse in Camden, London, seen from Chalk Farm Road with traffic in the foreground. Radio had to catch up with the length. AM Top 40 still wanted three minutes. In April 1967, Tom Donahue began playing album cuts on KMPX-FM in San Francisco, a small station that had been filling hours with foreign-language shows. Within months the format — no jingles, album sides, records the singles chart did not know what to do with — had a name, underground FM, and copies in other cities. The LP, not the 45, became a radio unit. Concept albums and FM were a pair: Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band (May 1967) is the usual example, but the habit of sitting through a side was already being trained on Pet Sounds, Revolver, and the San Francisco records that did not fade at 2:30. Monterey, 16–18 June 1967, was the weekend the California scene rented a fairground and invited the rest of the touring world. The Monterey International Pop Festival was organized as a non-profit. Artists played for expenses. The bill was not only San Francisco: Otis Redding, Ravi Shankar, the Who, the Jimi Hendrix Experience, Jefferson Airplane, Big Brother and Janis Joplin. Paul McCartney, on the festival board, had insisted Hendrix be booked. D. A. Pennebaker filmed it. The Summer of Love, that same season in Haight-Ashbury, is the press name for the crowd that followed. The useful Monterey fact is the booking: soul, Indian classical music, London guitar theatre, and the local ballroom bands on one weekend, before Woodstock made the festival itself the product. Cash Box, 29 April 1967, page 20. A trade-paper advertisement for Monterey, weeks before the fairground opened. The type is a booking list, not a psychedelic poster. The names are the evidence: this was sold to the industry as an international pop festival, not as a private San Francisco dance. Black-and-white 1967 Cash Box advertisement for the Monterey International Pop Festival, listing dates and a long roster of acts. The Greenville News, 30 April 1967, reprinting an Associated Press picture from Haight-Ashbury. National papers were already touring the neighborhood that spring. The photograph is a wire-service document of a sidewalk, not a concert. Treat the caption’s language as 1967 press, not as a definition of the music. 1967 newspaper photograph of a crowd of young people sitting and standing on a Haight-Ashbury sidewalk, with a short news caption about hippies. United States and United Kingdom were not interchangeable. American psychedelia had ballrooms, FM album radio, and, by 1967–69, festivals that tried to scale a dance to a field. British psychedelia had a short-lived club, an official pop network (BBC Radio 1, 1967) that arrived as the pirates were squeezed, and a studio culture in which the Beatles and Pink Floyd could treat Abbey Road as a lab while still issuing singles. Traffic, from Birmingham, made Mr. Fantasy at the end of 1967 without being a San Francisco franchise. The word “psychedelia” covered both. The jobs in the room were different: a Fillmore night was a dance with lights; a Revolver session was a desk, a tape machine, and a clock. The field Many names, and three rooms to slow down in A gallery of three faces is the wrong picture. Name the field, then slow down. The Beatles and the Beach Boys in the studio. The Byrds. Jefferson Airplane and the Grateful Dead. Janis Joplin with Big Brother and the Holding Company. Jimi Hendrix. Pink Floyd and Soft Machine. Traffic. The 13th Floor Elevators in Austin. Love in Los Angeles. The Velvet Underground in New York. In Brazil, Gilberto Gil, Caetano Veloso, Os Mutantes. The Who and Otis Redding pass through Monterey. Bill Graham and Chet Helms ran the San Francisco doors. Joe Boyd and Hoppy Hopkins ran UFO. Tom Donahue moved albums onto FM. George Martin and Geoff Emerick sat at the Abbey Road desk; Brian Wilson sat at Western. Syd Barrett, Grace Slick, Roky Erickson, Arthur Lee, Andy Warhol and Nico. Hélio Oiticica’s installation gave Tropicália a name before the records did. That is a crowd on purpose. Pet Sounds and Revolver are the studio method at full size. Wilson, not touring those tracks as a five-piece, used Hollywood session players and Capitol’s budget to make an album whose quiet is as deliberate as its hooks. “God Only Knows” is a two-minute-fifty song with a bass line that does not behave like surf. The Beatles, four-track and restless, made Revolver a catalogue of tricks that other engineers could copy: backwards tape, a string octet on “Eleanor Rigby,” a vocal that sounds as if it is spinning because it is spinning inside a Leslie. Sgt. Pepper, the next year, is the record the syllabuses never let go. The 1966 pair is the better evidence of method, because the costumes had not yet become the story. The San Francisco ballroom circuit is the live method. Fillmore and Avalon, then Fillmore West in 1968 when Graham moved into the former Carousel Ballroom. Light shows, posters, and bills that ran past midnight. Airplane’s Surrealistic Pillow (February 1967) put “White Rabbit” and “Somebody to Love” on AM; the same band could still play a ballroom set that did not sound like a singles revue. The Dead treated the night as improvisation. Big Brother, with Joplin, were louder and shorter. Acid rock is the American press name for the guitar-heavy end of that circuit. It is not a synonym for every London studio experiment. The circuit also had a door price, a lease, and a promoter who could lose the room. Graham’s Fillmore and Helms’s Avalon were businesses in disagreement, not a commune with two addresses. Tropicália is a contemporaneous case, not an exotic footnote. In April 1967, at the Museum of Modern Art in Rio de Janeiro, Hélio Oiticica showed an installation he called Tropicália: penetrable structures, plants, sand, a television. Caetano Veloso took the word for a song. In 1968 Veloso and Gilberto Gil organized the collaborative album Tropicália: ou Panis et Circencis, with Os Mutantes, Gal Costa, Tom Zé, and arrangements by Rogério Duprat. Os Mutantes’ own debut the same year opened with “Panis et Circenses,” a Veloso–Gil song that changes shape the way a Beatles track from 1967 changes shape, in Portuguese, with Brazilian rhythm and studio jokes. This was not San Francisco exported. It was Bahia and São Paulo musicians using electric guitars, tropical kitsch, and Oswald de Andrade’s older idea of anthropophagy — eating foreign forms — under a military dictatorship. Institutional Act No. 5, on 13 December 1968, hardened censorship. Veloso and Gil were arrested on 27 December, detained, then pushed toward exile. They left for London in 1969. The records and the arrests are the same years as Monterey and Abbey Road. The police are the local fact. Hendrix is the transatlantic object lesson. He was an American guitarist who became famous in London with Noel Redding and Mitch Mitchell as the Jimi Hendrix Experience. Are You Experienced was issued in the United Kingdom in May 1967. At Monterey on 18 June he closed with “Wild Thing,” set a Fender Stratocaster on fire, and smashed it. A fragment of that guitar — jack, wiring, painted wood — has been exhibited as an object. The theatre was borrowed from the Who, who had already wrecked instruments that weekend. The career was not only the fire: Chas Chandler produced the records in London; American FM then carried the LP. Purple Haze is a two-and-a-half-minute single. The legend is longer than the track. Fragment of the Stratocaster Jimi Hendrix destroyed at Monterey on 18 June 1967, photographed at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2019 (loan from MoPOP, Seattle). The object is wood, metal, and nail polish. The film of the fire is still under copyright. This piece of the guitar is what a museum can show without pirating the footage. A charred, painted fragment of a Fender Stratocaster body, showing the input jack and part of the control cavity, displayed in a museum case. Elsewhere The same years, not a ranking of scenes In Japan, Group Sounds — the mid-1960s electric-guitar boom that had heard the Beatles and kayōkyoku at once — peaked in 1967–68 with acts such as the Tigers still on television. By 1969 major members were leaving; by about 1970 the boom was over. Folk and a harder “new rock” were already taking the students who had bought GS singles. That is a fade in the same years as Fillmore West, not an Asian psychedelic twin assigned to match San Francisco. Some Japanese musicians were already looking past the beat-group format. This lesson does not invent a Tokyo UFO to keep the map tidy. In New York, the Velvet Underground recorded with Nico in 1966 and released The Velvet Underground & Nico in March 1967, with Andy Warhol’s banana on the sleeve and the Exploding Plastic Inevitable as the live context. The Factory was not Haight-Ashbury. The songs were about a different set of streets and a different set of drugs. Treat the album as contemporaneous, not as the West Coast’s missing conscience. Love’s Forever Changes, from Los Angeles in November 1967, is another local fact: Arthur Lee, orchestral folk-rock, paranoia in the arrangements, Elektra Records. The 13th Floor Elevators, from Austin, had already put the word on a sleeve in 1966 — The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators — with Roky Erickson and an amplified jug. Texas was not a suburb of the Fillmore. Brazil’s Tropicália, already slowed down above, belongs in this list as a same-time industry: television song festivals, a collaborative LP, a dictatorship, and then London exile. It used some of the same Beatles records the rest of the world used. It was not a cover band for Revolver. The honest comparison is the calendar, not a contest over who was more psychedelic. After Woodstock, Altamont, and rock as album culture Woodstock, 15–18 August 1969, on Max Yasgur’s dairy farm in Bethel, New York, is the end-edge of this lesson’s festival story, not a beginning. Hundreds of thousands of people arrived at a site that had not been built for them. Hendrix played on the morning of the 18th. The Arnold Skolnick poster — a bird on a guitar neck, three days of peace and music — is the image that survived. The music business learned that a field, a sound system, and an LP culture could be a market. It also learned that the market could lose control of the gate. Arnold Skolnick’s 1969 advertisement for the Woodstock Music and Art Fair. Published in the United States without a copyright notice, it is in the public domain there. The bird is a graphic, not a photograph of the farm. Bethel, not the town of Woodstock, is where the stages stood. Woodstock 1969 poster: white bird on a guitar against a red field, with the words 3 Days of Peace & Music and the festival dates. The crowd at Woodstock waiting out rain, August 1969. Photograph by Derek Redmond and Paul Campbell. The popular picture of the weekend is mud. Saturday was also sun. Either way the fact is scale: a dance hall idea stretched until the fence failed. A dense crowd at Woodstock sitting on a hillside under grey sky, many wrapped against rain, the stage distant. Altamont Speedway, on 6 December 1969, was a free Rolling Stones concert in northern California that ended in crowding, fights, and the killing of Meredith Hunter in front of the stage. KSAN-FM, the San Francisco underground station that had inherited Tom Donahue’s staff from KMPX, put callers on the air the next day. The useful historical point is not a sermon. It is that the ballroom’s security, lights, and door could not be improvised at highway scale. The 1960s festival was already a logistics problem. What remained in the shops was album culture. Rock, as a market category, sold long-playing records, gatefold sleeves, and FM time. Hard rock — louder, riff-based, less interested in the light show — is one line out of Hendrix, the Who, and the heavier San Francisco nights. That line continues into the next decade. A later reaction would treat the album, the solo, and the festival as the things to refuse. That reaction becomes punk. It is not this lesson. The 1965–69 story ends with a longer song, a larger crowd, and a business that had learned to bill the LP as the work. A question A question to keep asking If the unit of the music changes from a three-minute 45 to a side of an LP, who is being asked to sit still, and who is being paid for the extra time? Monterey Pop (D. A. Pennebaker, 1968) Pennebaker’s documentary of the June 1967 festival. Licensed home-video editions exist; this is the catalogue record, not a bootleg upload of the film. The Beatles — Tomorrow Never Knows (1966) Revolver, recorded at EMI Studios, Abbey Road. Official Beatles/UMG upload of the studio recording. Lennon’s vocal through a Leslie speaker; tape loops in the mix. If the file moves, search the title on the Beatles’ official channel. The Beach Boys — God Only Knows (1966) Pet Sounds, Capitol.
