Official Beach Boys channel. This upload is a later video cut to the 1966 studio recording, not a 1966 television clip. Jefferson Airplane — White Rabbit (1967) Surrealistic Pillow, RCA. Official audio on the Jefferson Airplane channel. Grace Slick brought the song from her previous group, the Great Society. The Jimi Hendrix Experience — Purple Haze (1967) Official audio, Experience Hendrix/VEVO. UK single 1967; on the US edition of Are You Experienced. Not the Monterey film. Pink Floyd — See Emily Play (1967) UK single, 16 June 1967, the weekend of Monterey. Official Pink Floyd channel. Later added to the US edition of The Piper at the Gates of Dawn. A three-minute underground record, not a ballroom jam. Os Mutantes — Panis et Circenses (1968) YouTube Topic upload provided by Universal Music Ltda from the 1968 Polydor/Philips-family master. Written by Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil; arranged with Rogério Duprat. Not a 1968 television clip. 13th Floor Elevators — You’re Gonna Miss Me (1966) YouTube Topic upload of the International Artists recording, provided by The Orchard. From The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators. If it moves, search the title plus International Artists.

subject: feminism
title: Second Wave (c. 1963–1982): the personal is political
dek: After the vote, public feminism turned to housework, sex, pay, and who counted as a woman. A bestseller, small consciousness-raising groups, new laws, and a 1977 Black feminist statement made those private facts into politics.
text: Second Wave (c. 1963–1982): the personal is political After the vote, public feminism turned to housework, sex, pay, and who counted as a woman. A bestseller, small consciousness-raising groups, new laws, and a 1977 Black feminist statement made those private facts into politics. c. 1963–1982 “Second wave” is a later Anglo-American classroom name, not what most of the people in this lesson called themselves. The dates are a convenience: The Feminine Mystique (1963) at one end, the Equal Rights Amendment’s extended ratification deadline (30 June 1982) at the other. The United States is the spine because the numbering is. Other countries’ 1960s–70s feminisms are contemporaneous — not copies of an American original. Feminism feminism 1963 Mystique / pay Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique. The Equal Pay Act the same year. A bestseller and a statute; neither was the whole cause. 1966 NOW National Organization for Women founded in Washington, 30 June, after a conference of status-of-women commissions. Friedan first president; Pauli Murray among the founders. 1968 Atlantic City New York Radical Women protest the Miss America pageant, 7 September. Freedom Trash Can. No fire. 1970 Books / strike / Ruskin Sexual Politics; The Dialectic of Sex; Notes from the Second Year; Our Bodies, Ourselves as newsprint; Women’s Strike for Equality, 26 August; first UK Women’s Liberation conference at Ruskin College. 1972–73 Statute / Roe Title IX in the Education Amendments of 1972 (signed 23 June). ERA sent to the states. Ms. magazine. Roe v. Wade decided 22 January 1973. 1977 Combahee / Houston Combahee River Collective Statement (April). National Women’s Conference in Houston (November), and a conservative Pro-Family rally in the same city. 1982 Deadline ERA ratification deadline expires 30 June, three states short. Reagan already in office; Thatcher since 1979. The later names — third wave, intersectionality — are not yet the ones in use. There was no fire on the boardwalk On 7 September 1968, New York Radical Women put bras, girdles, high heels, curlers, and women’s magazines into a “Freedom Trash Can” outside the Miss America pageant in Atlantic City. They asked the city for a permit to burn the contents. The permit was refused: the boardwalk is wood. Nothing was burned. Newspapers, then Art Buchwald’s column, reported a bra-burning anyway. The trash can is the event. The bonfire is the copy. second wave Second Wave second-wave A later Anglo-American label for a span of feminist organizing roughly from the early 1960s through the early 1980s. Most people in it did not use the phrase at the time. It is a later name, not a membership card. doldrums A later name for organized U.S. feminism between the vote and the 1960s: the coalition that had fought for suffrage thinned. It describes one public current going quiet. It does not mean women stopped working, studying, or arguing. the feminine mystique feminine mystique Friedan’s name for the postwar middle-class story that a woman’s fulfillment was husband, children, and house. She treated it as an ideology with a sales force — magazines, advertising, experts — not as a private mood. the problem that has no name Friedan’s phrase in The Feminine Mystique for the dissatisfaction of college-educated housewives who had done what they were told and still felt empty. It named a specific class of unhappiness. It did not name every woman’s. The Feminine Mystique Betty Friedan’s 1963 book, published by W. W. Norton. A survey of her Smith College classmates and a polemic against the house-as-destiny. A public starting point. Not a census of American women. Betty Friedan Friedan American writer (1921–2006). The Feminine Mystique (1963); first president of NOW (1966). She later used the phrase “lavender menace” about lesbians in the movement — a split, not a footnote. Equal Pay Act U.S. statute signed 10 June 1963. It required equal pay for equal work on the basis of sex, with exceptions. A workplace law in the same year as Friedan’s book. Enforcement was another matter. Presidential Commission on the Status of Women status-of-women commissions status of women A federal commission created by John F. Kennedy in 1961; Eleanor Roosevelt chaired it until her death in 1962. State commissions followed. NOW was founded at their Third National Conference in 1966. Title VII Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. It barred employment discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. The word “sex” is in the statute. Early Equal Employment Opportunity Commission practice did not treat it as equal to race. Civil Rights Act of 1964 Civil Rights Act U.S. civil-rights statute. Title VII is the employment title. The Act is the legal floor many workplace feminists stood on; it is not itself a feminist manifesto. EEOC Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, created to enforce Title VII. NOW’s founding complaint was that the Commission was not treating sex discrimination as a real mandate. NOW National Organization for Women National Organization for Women, founded 30 June 1966 in Washington, D.C. Twenty-eight founders; Betty Friedan first president. A civil-rights-style organization for sex equality: lawsuits, lobbying, later the 1970 strike. Not the same thing as women’s liberation small groups. Pauli Murray Murray American lawyer, writer, and later Episcopal priest (1910–1985). Co-founder of NOW; co-author of its Statement of Purpose. “Jane Crow” was her name for the combined racial and sex caste she had already analyzed. Jane Crow Pauli Murray’s term for the system that constrained Black women by race and sex together — not two separate queues. Statement of Purpose NOW Statement of Purpose NOW’s 1966 founding statement. It begins by defining the organization’s purpose as bringing women into “full participation in the mainstream of American society now.” Pauli Murray helped write it. SNCC Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. A major civil-rights organization of the early 1960s. Several white women who later became women’s-liberation organizers had been trained in its discipline — and in its sex hierarchy. New Left The 1960s student and antiwar left, especially Students for a Democratic Society and related groups. A school for organizing. Also a place many women learned they were expected to type, staple, and wait. Casey Hayden Civil-rights organizer. With Mary King she wrote the 1965 memo “Sex and Caste,” circulated in SNCC, naming sex hierarchy inside the movement. Mary King Civil-rights organizer; co-author, with Casey Hayden, of the 1965 SNCC memo “Sex and Caste.” Sex and Caste Memo by Casey Hayden and Mary King, November 1965, circulated in SNCC. It compared the position of women in the movement to a caste. A document from inside civil rights, before NOW’s founding conference. consciousness-raising consciousness raising CR CR groups A women’s-liberation method: a small group speaks from its own lives, then looks for the pattern. Kathie Sarachild presented “A Program for Feminist Consciousness-Raising” in 1968. The point was analysis, not therapy — a distinction Carol Hanisch had to keep defending. Kathie Sarachild Sarachild New York Radical Women member. She presented “A Program for Feminist Consciousness-Raising” at the first national women’s-liberation conference, Chicago, November 1968. A Program for Feminist Consciousness-Raising Kathie Sarachild’s 1968 outline of consciousness-raising as a political method, later printed in Notes from the Second Year. New York Radical Women Early women’s-liberation group, formed in New York in 1967. Among those involved: Shulamith Firestone, Carol Hanisch, Robin Morgan, Kathie Sarachild. It organized the 1968 Miss America protest. the personal is political The Personal Is Political personal is political Phrase attached to Carol Hanisch’s 1969 memo when Shulamith Firestone and Anne Koedt printed it in Notes from the Second Year (1970) and gave it that title. Hanisch has said she did not name the paper. The claim: what gets called a private problem — housework, sex, abortion, shame — is a power relation. Carol Hanisch Hanisch Women’s-liberation organizer; New York Radical Women. She helped organize the 1968 Miss America protest. Her 1969 memo, titled by others in 1970, is the usual source for “the personal is political.” Notes from the Second Year 1970 women’s-liberation anthology edited by Shulamith Firestone and Anne Koedt. It printed Hanisch’s memo under the title “The Personal Is Political,” and Sarachild’s consciousness-raising program. Anne Koedt Koedt Feminist writer and editor. Co-editor, with Firestone, of Notes from the Second Year. Co-founder of New York Radical Feminists. Shulamith Firestone Firestone Shulie Firestone Writer and organizer (1945–2012). New York Radical Women, Redstockings, New York Radical Feminists. The Dialectic of Sex (1970). Co-editor of Notes from the Second Year. The Dialectic of Sex Shulamith Firestone’s 1970 book (William Morrow). A radical materialist argument: pregnancy and the sex class built on it are the base; cybernetic reproduction is a speculative horizon. Not a NOW pamphlet. Kate Millett Millett Writer and sculptor (1934–2017). Sexual Politics (1970), drawn from her Columbia dissertation: literature and theory as a record of patriarchy. Time put her on a cover; the fame was a trap as much as a platform. Sexual Politics Kate Millett’s 1970 book (Doubleday). Close reading of literary patriarchy — Lawrence, Miller, Mailer, Genet — as political theory. One of 1970’s two brick-sized feminist books; Firestone’s was the other. Redstockings Radical feminist group formed in New York in 1969 (Firestone and Ellen Willis among the founders). Speak-outs, including on abortion. The name plays on “bluestocking” and red. Ellen Willis Writer and critic; co-founder of Redstockings. Later a voice in the late-1970s arguments over sexuality and pornography. women’s liberation women's liberation Women’s Liberation WLM The small-group, often radical current of the late 1960s–70s, distinct from NOW’s organizational liberalism though people crossed. In Britain, Women’s Liberation Movement (WLM) is the usual name. Miss America protest Miss America No More Miss America Demonstration at the Miss America pageant, Atlantic City, 7 September 1968, organized by New York Radical Women. Freedom Trash Can on the boardwalk; a “Women’s Liberation” banner inside the hall. About two hundred people. Not a bonfire. Freedom Trash Can The barrel on the Atlantic City boardwalk, 7 September 1968, into which protesters threw bras, girdles, heels, curlers, and women’s magazines. A permit to burn the contents was denied. Robin Morgan Writer and organizer. A principal organizer of the 1968 Miss America protest; the “No More Miss America” leaflet is associated with her. Later editor of Sisterhood Is Powerful (1970). Sisterhood Is Powerful Anthology edited by Robin Morgan, 1970. A thick reader of the new movement, not a single line. Miss Black America A pageant held in Atlantic City the same night as the 1968 Miss America contest, organized as a Black alternative to a white national symbol. A different project from the boardwalk protest, on the same date. Art Buchwald American humor columnist. After the 1968 Miss America protest he helped spread the bra-burning story that the boardwalk itself had not supplied. Gloria Steinem Steinem Journalist and organizer. A public face of liberal feminism in the 1970s; a founding editor of Ms. magazine (1972). Women’s Action Alliance; National Women’s Political Caucus. Cameras could treat her as the movement. The arguments behind her were already about who “woman” included. Ms. Ms. magazine Ms magazine Feminist magazine. A preview ran in New York magazine in December 1971; the first standalone issue is 1972. Gloria Steinem was a founding editor. “Ms.” as a courtesy title was part of the point. Women’s Action Alliance Women's Action Alliance Organization co-founded in 1971 (Steinem among the founders) to supply practical feminist resources. The 12 January 1972 Leffler photograph of Steinem is from one of its news conferences. National Women’s Political Caucus NWPC National Women's Political Caucus Founded 1971 to elect women and feminist-allied candidates. Among the conveners: Bella Abzug, Shirley Chisholm, Betty Friedan, Gloria Steinem. Bella Abzug Abzug New York congresswoman (elected 1970), lawyer, and a convener of the National Women’s Political Caucus. Later a co-chair of the National Women’s Conference in Houston, 1977. Shirley Chisholm Chisholm Brooklyn congresswoman, elected 1968 — the first Black woman in the U.S. House. She sought the Democratic presidential nomination in 1972. A convener of the National Women’s Political Caucus. Unbought and Unbossed (1970) is her campaign book and slogan. Unbought and Unbossed Shirley Chisholm’s 1970 book, and the slogan of her campaigns. The phrase is hers, not a later caption. Women’s Strike for Equality Women's Strike for Equality Strike for Equality Actions on 26 August 1970, the fiftieth anniversary of the Nineteenth Amendment, called by NOW and joined by a wider coalition. A Fifth Avenue march in New York; sister actions in other cities, including Washington, D.C. Friedan had asked for a strike. What the cameras got was mostly a march. Our Bodies, Ourselves Our Bodies Ourselves Women and Their Bodies Women’s health book that began as a 1969 Boston workshop and 1970 newsprint (Women and Their Bodies) from the group later called the Boston Women’s Health Book Collective. New England Free Press, then a 1973 Simon & Schuster edition. The point was that women could know their own anatomy without waiting for a gatekeeper. Boston Women’s Health Book Collective Boston Women's Health Book Collective Boston Women’s Health Course Collective The Boston group that produced Our Bodies, Ourselves. A workshop, then a pamphlet, then a book that outlived the workshop. Title IX Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, signed 23 June 1972. “No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.” Sports became the public face. The text is broader. In 2002 the provision was renamed the Patsy T. Mink Equal Opportunity in Education Act. Education Amendments of 1972 Public Law 92-318, signed by Richard Nixon on 23 June 1972. Title IX is one title inside this law. Nixon’s signing statement did not dwell on the sex-discrimination provision. Patsy Mink Patsy T. Mink Mink Hawaii congresswoman. A principal House advocate of the sex-discrimination provision that became Title IX. The 2002 renaming of Title IX is after her. Birch Bayh Bayh Indiana senator. He introduced the Senate language that became Title IX, 28 February 1972. Richard Nixon Nixon U.S. president who signed the Education Amendments of 1972. The signing statement talked about higher education and busing. It did not sell Title IX as a women’s-sports law. Roe v. Wade Roe Roe v Wade U.S. Supreme Court decision, 410 U.S. 113, announced 22 January 1973. Majority opinion by Harry Blackmun, 7–2. It held that the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause protected a right of privacy broad enough to include a woman’s decision to terminate a pregnancy, structured in trimesters, and struck down Texas’s criminal abortion statute. It was a constitutional holding, not a statute that “legalized abortion.” Overturned in 2022 by Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization. Doe v. Bolton Companion case to Roe, decided the same day (410 U.S. 179). It struck down Georgia’s more elaborate abortion restrictions. Read with Roe, not instead of it. Harry Blackmun Blackmun Supreme Court justice; author of the majority opinion in Roe v. Wade (1973). Equal Rights Amendment ERA Proposed U.S. constitutional amendment: equality of rights shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or any state on account of sex. Alice Paul introduced an ERA in 1923. Congress sent this version to the states on 22 March 1972. Original deadline 1979; extended to 30 June 1982. It fell three states short of 38. Alice Paul Suffrage organizer; author of the original Equal Rights Amendment introduced in 1923. The 1972 ERA is her text’s descendant. She belongs to the earlier capsule; the amendment did not. Phyllis Schlafly Schlafly Conservative organizer (1924–2016). STOP ERA, from 1972, argued the amendment would strip protections from housewives, send women into the draft, and attack the family. The campaign is a fact of the 1970s, not a later invention. STOP ERA Schlafly’s organization against ratification of the Equal Rights Amendment, from 1972. The stop-sign graphic is the image. The argument was that equality on paper would cost women the legal privileges of marriage and motherhood. Lavender Menace Phrase Betty Friedan used around 1969 for the fear that lesbians would discredit the movement. Reclaimed on 1 May 1970, when Radicalesbians disrupted the Second Congress to Unite Women in New York. The insult became a name. Radicalesbians Lesbian feminist group. They wrote “The Woman-Identified Woman” (1970) and staged the Lavender Menace action at the Second Congress to Unite Women, 1 May 1970. The Woman-Identified Woman Radicalesbians manifesto, 1970. It argued that lesbianism was a political position inside feminism, not a public-relations problem for NOW. lesbian feminism A current, not a single organization: the claim that intimate life with women, and a politics built from that fact, was central — not a side issue to be hidden for respectability. Combahee River Collective Combahee Black feminist lesbian socialist collective in Boston, 1974–1980. Named for the June 1863 Combahee River Raid, in which Harriet Tubman helped lead a Union expedition that freed hundreds of enslaved people. Their April 1977 statement is the text this capsule slows down for. Combahee River Collective Statement Combahee statement the 1977 statement Dated April 1977. It argues that racial, sexual, heterosexual, and class oppression are interlocking, and that Black women’s politics have to start from that fact. It uses the phrase “identity politics” for a coalition that does not require anyone to stand aside. Later printings include a 1979 anthology edited by Zillah Eisenstein. Primary authors later named: Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, Demita Frazier. Barbara Smith Writer and organizer; co-founder of the Combahee River Collective; later of Kitchen Table: Women of Color Press. One of the three who later discussed authorship of the 1977 statement. Beverly Smith Organizer and writer; Barbara Smith’s sister; one of the three later named as primary authors of the Combahee River Collective Statement. Demita Frazier Frazier Organizer; one of the three later named as primary authors of the Combahee River Collective Statement. identity politics In the Combahee statement, a name for politics that begin from one’s own structural position — Black, woman, lesbian, working-class — without treating those as separate queues. The later pejorative use of the phrase is not the 1977 use. Black feminism A current inside the era, not a later correction pasted on. National Black Feminist Organization (1973); Combahee (1974–80); writers including the Smiths, Frazier, and, late in the window, bell hooks. The who-counts problem returning in public. National Black Feminist Organization NBFO Founded in New York in 1973 to address Black women’s position in both the women’s movement and Black politics. Combahee began among Boston women who had been in its orbit and wanted a more radical, socialist, lesbian-inclusive politics. Harriet Tubman Tubman Abolitionist. The Combahee River Collective took its name from the 1863 Combahee River Raid she helped lead. The name is a claim of descent, not a 1970s photograph of her. Combahee River Raid June 1863 Union raid on the Combahee River in South Carolina, with Harriet Tubman as a scout and leader, freeing hundreds of enslaved people. The 1970s collective borrowed the name on purpose. bell hooks hooks Gloria Jean Watkins Writer (Gloria Jean Watkins, 1952–2021). Ain’t I a Woman: Black Women and Feminism (South End Press, 1981). Late in this capsule’s window: she is arguing with a movement that has already named itself, not founding NOW. She kept the name lowercase. Ain’t I a Woman Ain't I a Woman Ain’t I a Woman: Black Women and Feminism bell hooks’s 1981 book. The title reaches back to Sojourner Truth’s 1851 Akron speech — and to the later refrain attached to it. In this archive that refrain’s history is in the First Wave capsule. The 1981 book is about Black women and the feminism that had trouble counting them. National Women’s Conference National Women's Conference Houston conference Houston 1977 Federally funded conference in Houston, 18–21 November 1977, following International Women’s Year. Delegates adopted a National Plan of Action (ERA, abortion, lesbian rights, minority women, and more). Three First Ladies appeared. A conservative Pro-Family rally met in Houston the same weekend. International Women’s Year International Women's Year IWY United Nations designation for 1975. It produced a Mexico City conference and, in the U.S., a commission and the 1977 Houston meeting. National Plan of Action The 26-plank document adopted at Houston in 1977, recommendations to the President and Congress. A federal-conference text. Combahee’s statement, months earlier, is a different kind of “we.” Rosalynn Carter U.S. First Lady in 1977. She appeared at the National Women’s Conference in Houston with Betty Ford and Lady Bird Johnson. Betty Ford Former U.S. First Lady; ERA supporter. On the Houston stage, November 1977. Lady Bird Johnson Ladybird Johnson Former U.S. First Lady. On the Houston stage, November 1977, with Rosalynn Carter and Betty Ford. Pro-Family rally Pro-Family Conservative gathering in Houston during the 1977 National Women’s Conference, associated with Schlafly and opponents of the ERA, abortion rights, and lesbian planks. Same city, same weekend, a different “family.” Women Against Pornography WAP Organization founded in New York in 1979. Part of the late-1970s turn toward pornography as a feminist target. The louder “sex wars” continue past this capsule’s 1982 line. MLF Mouvement de libération des femmes Mouvement de liberation des femmes Mouvement de libération des femmes. French women’s-liberation current, named in the press around a 26 August 1970 demonstration at the Arc de Triomphe. Not a branch office of NOW. Manifesto of the 343 343 Manifeste des 343 Statement published in Le Nouvel Observateur, 5 April 1971, in which 343 women declared they had had abortions, then illegal in France. Simone de Beauvoir was among the signers. Simone de Beauvoir Beauvoir de Beauvoir French philosopher. The Second Sex (1949) is earlier than this capsule. She signed the Manifesto of the 343 in 1971. A predecessor and a contemporary, depending on which book you open. The Second Sex Simone de Beauvoir’s 1949 book (Le Deuxième Sexe). A philosophical inventory of “woman” as Other. It is not a second-wave text; second-wave readers treated it as one anyway. Ruskin College Ruskin Trade-union college in Oxford. Site of the first British National Women’s Liberation Conference, 27 February–1 March 1970. Four opening demands: equal pay, equal education and opportunity, 24-hour nurseries, free contraception and abortion on demand. ūman ribu uman ribu ウーマン・リブ ribu Japanese women’s liberation of the early 1970s, from the English “women’s lib.” Tanaka Mitsu’s 1970 pamphlet Liberation from the Toilet is a founding text. Ribu Shinjuku Center (1972–77) was a shelter, clinic, and meeting place. A critique of the family system and of New Left sexism, not a translation of Friedan. Tanaka Mitsu 田中美津 Japanese ribu organizer and writer. Liberation from the Toilet (便所からの解放), 1970. A founder of the Ribu Shinjuku Center. Liberation from the Toilet 便所からの解放 Benjo kara no kaihō Tanaka Mitsu’s 1970 ribu pamphlet. It attacked the treatment of women — including by men on the left — as a receptacle. The title is hers; it is not a metaphor invented for this capsule. Ribu Shinjuku Center リブ新宿センター Ribu Sentā Women’s center and shelter in Shinjuku, Tokyo, 1972–1977. A ribu institution: housing, abortion and legal advice, a paper, a place to go. New Feminism 新女性主義 xin nüxing zhuyi Lü Hsiu-lien’s name for the feminism she promoted in 1970s Taiwan: a 8 March 1972 lecture at National Taiwan University’s law college, then the 1974 book 新女性主義. Slogans included “first a person, then a man or a woman.” This was under martial law, not under the U.S. numbering. Lü Hsiu-lien 呂秀蓮 Annette Lu Lu Hsiu-lien Taiwanese lawyer and writer (b. 1944). She introduced New Feminism in Taipei in the early 1970s after graduate study in the United States. Later vice president of the Republic of China (2000–2008). The later office is not this capsule; the 1974 book is. Stonewall Uprising at the Stonewall Inn, New York, June 1969. Gay liberation is a contemporaneous movement, not a subplot of NOW. Lesbian feminism sits in the overlap. backlash A word later attached, especially by Susan Faludi’s 1991 book Backlash, to the 1980s counter-movement: Reagan–Thatcher conservatism, anti-ERA organizing, a media story that feminism had gone too far. The word is 1991. The conservative turn is already in this lesson’s last years. Susan Faludi Faludi Journalist. Backlash: The Undeclared War Against American Women (1991). A later name for the 1980s, written after this capsule’s dates. Backlash Backlash: The Undeclared War Against American Women Susan Faludi’s 1991 book. Useful as a later diagnosis. It is not a 1977 source. Ronald Reagan Reagan U.S. president from 20 January 1981. His first term is the American half of the conservative turn this capsule ends in. Margaret Thatcher Thatcher British prime minister from 4 May 1979. The other English-speaking conservative date in the after. third wave Third Wave third-wave A later name. Rebecca Walker’s “Becoming the Third Wave” appeared in Ms. in January 1992. This lesson stops before the name. The problems the name tried to hold — race, sexuality, culture, who “we” is — were already on the table. Rebecca Walker Writer. Her 1992 Ms. essay “Becoming the Third Wave” is a usual starting citation for the phrase. It is after this capsule. Becoming the Third Wave Rebecca Walker’s essay in Ms., January 1992. A later christening, not a 1982 event. intersectionality Legal-theoretical name coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989 for the way race and sex (and other structures) compound. Combahee had already stated interlocking oppressions in 1977. The word is later. The problem is not. Kimberlé Crenshaw Crenshaw Legal scholar. “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989) is the usual origin of the word intersectionality. After this capsule; in conversation with it. Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex Kimberlé Crenshaw’s 1989 article in the University of Chicago Legal Forum. The named origin of “intersectionality.” Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization Dobbs Dobbs v. Jackson U.S. Supreme Court decision, 2022, that overruled Roe v. Wade. Not part of the 1963–82 span. Named here only as the later fate of a 1973 holding. Levittown Postwar planned suburbs (Pennsylvania, New York, and others) associated with mass-produced houses and a racial boundary at the door. The 1958 photograph in this lesson is a house in Levittown, New York, made for House Beautiful. Architecture as a clue, not a biography of a resident. House Beautiful American shelter magazine. The Gottscho-Schleisner Levittown negatives used here were shot for it in August 1958. Nineteenth Amendment 19th Amendment U.S. constitutional amendment, ratified 1920, barring denial of the vote on account of sex. The 1970 strike chose its fiftieth anniversary. What the amendment did not undo is in the First Wave capsule. First Wave Later label for the suffrage-era public fights already treated in this archive’s Monday lesson of 16 August 2026. The who-counts problem did not end when the vote arrived. John F. Kennedy Kennedy U.S. president who created the Presidential Commission on the Status of Women in 1961. The commissions, not the Oval Office, are the useful fact here. Students for a Democratic Society SDS Major New Left student organization of the 1960s. A training ground and, for many women, a lesson in being asked to type. Chicago Women’s Liberation Union Chicago Women's Liberation Union Socialist-feminist organization founded in Chicago in 1969. Named here as one of the cities that was not New York. Second Congress to Unite Women Feminist conference in New York, 1 May 1970, where Radicalesbians staged the Lavender Menace action. Seneca Falls Village in New York State; 1848 convention site. In 1977 a torch was walked from there to Houston for the National Women’s Conference — a piece of first-wave ceremony reused as second-wave ceremony. Fourteenth Amendment 14th Amendment Ratified 1868. Roe’s majority located a right of privacy in its Due Process Clause. That reading is the 1973 holding; Dobbs rejected it in 2022. Le Nouvel Observateur French weekly. It published the Manifesto of the 343 on 5 April 1971. W. W. Norton Norton New York publisher of The Feminine Mystique in 1963. National Taiwan University NTU Taipei university. Lü Hsiu-lien lectured on New Feminism at its law college on 8 March 1972. George Washington University GWU GWU Women’s Liberation GWU Women's Liberation University in Washington, D.C. Its Women’s Liberation banner is readable in the 26 August 1970 photograph used as this capsule’s hero. LBJ Library LBJ Presidential Library Lyndon B. Johnson Presidential Library in Austin. The 9 November 1975 Steinem photograph was taken at a women’s conference there. Black Power Late-1960s current in Black politics emphasizing self-determination. Contemporaneous with women’s liberation; not background decoration. Fred Palumbo Palumbo New York World-Telegram & Sun staff photographer. He made the 1960 Friedan portrait in this capsule. Warren K. Leffler Leffler WKL U.S. News & World Report staff photographer. The 1970 Washington march and the 1977 Schlafly STOP ERA pictures in this capsule are his. Thomas J. O’Halloran Thomas J. O'Halloran O’Halloran O'Halloran TOH U.S. News & World Report staff photographer. The 25 January 1972 Chisholm portrait in this capsule is his. Frank Wolfe White House / LBJ Library photographer. The 9 November 1975 Steinem picture is credited to him. Gottscho-Schleisner Gottscho-Schleisner Collection Gottscho New York architectural photography firm. Their 1958 Levittown negatives, made for House Beautiful, are in the Library of Congress with no known copyright restrictions. Mrs. Robert Berman Robert Berman How the 1958 Gottscho catalog names the Levittown house in this lesson: a wife attached to a husband’s mailbox. The catalog entry is the evidence. U.S. News & World Report U.S. News & World Report collection American magazine. Staff photographs by Leffler, O’Halloran, and others, donated to the Library of Congress, are in the public domain under the deed of gift. New York World-Telegram & Sun World Telegram & Sun World-Telegram & Sun New York newspaper. Staff photographs donated to the Library of Congress, including Palumbo’s Friedan portrait, have no known restrictions. Before After suffrage, a quieter movement and a suburban ideal The First Wave (c. 1848–1920) ended, in the United States, with a constitutional sentence about the vote. What followed, in the usual textbook summary, is the doldrums: the suffrage coalition thinned, the Equal Rights Amendment that Alice Paul had already written sat in Congress, and a middle-class public story put women back in the house as if the house were a prize. The word “doldrums” is a later forecast. It describes one organized current going quiet. It does not mean the questions ended, and it does not mean every woman had been in that current. Suburban domesticity had an architecture. Mass-produced houses, a car in the drive, a lawn that looked like a job. Magazines sold the picture. So did advertisers and a certain kind of expert. Friedan would call the picture the feminine mystique — a destiny with appliances. The picture was never a map of the country. Black women, working-class women, and anyone who had not been offered the delicate house were already in the workplace, already in other people’s kitchens, already counted as labor. The gap the First Wave left — who counted as the “woman” the movement was picturing — did not close in 1920. It went indoors and called itself normal. Levittown, New York, 28 August 1958: the Mrs. Robert Berman house on Regent Lane, photographed for House Beautiful. The catalog files the resident as a wife of a mailbox. This is the architecture The Feminine Mystique would write against — and it was only ever one class of house. A two-story suburban house in Levittown, New York, with a car in the drive and young trees along a new lawn, 28 August 1958. There was already law at the start of the 1960s. Kennedy’s Presidential Commission on the Status of Women (1961) produced reports and a string of state commissions. The Equal Pay Act arrived in 1963. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 named sex in employment. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission then had to decide whether that word was a mandate or a joke. The school many organizers came out of was not a commission. It was civil rights and the New Left: SNCC, the antiwar movement, Students for a Democratic Society. Casey Hayden and Mary King’s 1965 memo “Sex and Caste,” circulated in SNCC, is one document of what women learned there — how to run a meeting, and who was expected to take notes in it. The era A bestseller, consciousness-raising, and laws that reached the workplace and the clinic Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique, published by W. W. Norton in 1963, is the public spark American memory keeps. It is not the cause. Friedan wrote about college-educated housewives and “the problem that has no name.” The book sold because a class of readers recognized themselves. Women who had never been offered that house did not need Friedan to tell them they were tired. Treat the book as a public starting point that magazines could review. Do not treat it as the whole movement. Betty Friedan, 1960 — three years before the book. Fred Palumbo’s World Telegram & Sun portrait is the face later attached to 1963. The useful date in the print is 1960: she is already a public person. The mystique had not yet been a bestseller. Betty Friedan in a 1960 studio portrait, three years before The Feminine Mystique. On 30 June 1966, at the Third National Conference of Commissions on the Status of Women in Washington, twenty-eight people founded the National Organization for Women. Friedan became president. Pauli Murray, who had already named “Jane Crow,” helped write the Statement of Purpose: women into the mainstream of American society now. NOW was built like a civil-rights organization — complaints to the EEOC, lawsuits, lobbying. It was one current. Women’s liberation small groups were another: New York Radical Women (1967), Redstockings (1969), Chicago Women’s Liberation Union, and dozens of unnamed living-room meetings. Consciousness-raising was the method. Kathie Sarachild put it on paper in 1968. You spoke from your own life until housework, sex, pay, and shame stopped looking like a private failure. Carol Hanisch wrote a memo in February 1969 defending those meetings against the charge that they were therapy. When Shulamith Firestone and Anne Koedt printed it in Notes from the Second Year (1970), they titled it “The Personal Is Political.” Hanisch has said the title is theirs. The claim is the era’s: the home was already a political economy. So were abortion, heterosexuality, and the unpaid second shift. How it showed: NOW, and the 26 August 1970 Women’s Strike for Equality on the Nineteenth Amendment’s fiftieth anniversary. Women’s liberation groups that would not be NOW. The Miss America protest of 7 September 1968 in Atlantic City — New York Radical Women, a Freedom Trash Can, a banner inside the hall, men kept off the action, no fire on a wooden boardwalk. The same night, a Miss Black America pageant ran in the same city as a different answer to a white national symbol. Our Bodies, Ourselves began as a 1969 Boston workshop and 1970 newsprint from the group later called the Boston Women’s Health Book Collective. Kate Millett’s Sexual Politics and Firestone’s The Dialectic of Sex both arrived in 1970. Ms. magazine’s first standalone issue is 1972; Gloria Steinem was a founding editor. Legislation, in the United States: Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, signed 23 June — a sex-discrimination rule for federally funded education, with Patsy Mink in the House and Birch Bayh in the Senate; sports became the picture people could see. Roe v. Wade, 22 January 1973: a 7–2 Supreme Court, Harry Blackmun writing, held that the Fourteenth Amendment’s due-process privacy covered a woman’s decision to end a pregnancy, with a trimester framework, and struck down Texas’s criminal statute. It was a constitutional holding. It was not a law that “legalized abortion” in a sentence. Doe v. Bolton came down the same day. Gloria Steinem at the LBJ Library, 9 November 1975. The glasses and the microphone are how a movement got reduced to one person. By 1975 the arguments behind the podium — class, race, lesbianism, who “Ms.” was for — were already the story. Gloria Steinem at a lectern, long hair and aviator glasses, speaking at a women’s conference at the LBJ Library, 9 November 1975. Black feminism is inside this span, not a footnote written later. The National Black Feminist Organization formed in 1973. The Combahee River Collective, in Boston from 1974, put a statement in April 1977. Lesbian feminism had already refused to wait: Radicalesbians’ “The Woman-Identified Woman,” and the Lavender Menace action at the Second Congress to Unite Women on 1 May 1970, answering Friedan’s slur by wearing it. By the late 1970s the arguments were also about pornography and about difference — Women Against Pornography dates to 1979 — and those fights run past the 1982 line this lesson uses as a date, not as a conclusion. Shirley Chisholm announcing a run for the Democratic presidential nomination, 25 January 1972. She had been in the House since 1969. A convener of the National Women’s Political Caucus, with Steinem, Friedan, and Bella Abzug. Electoral feminism is one street. It is not the only one. Shirley Chisholm in patterned blouse and cat-eye glasses, photographed 25 January 1972 as she announced her presidential candidacy. The field A crowded field, then three things to look at closely A gallery of three portraits is the wrong picture. Name them, then stop treating the names as the era. Friedan, Steinem, Firestone, Millett. Pauli Murray at NOW’s founding. Shirley Chisholm in Congress and on a 1972 ballot. Bella Abzug. Patsy Mink and Birch Bayh on Title IX. Carol Hanisch and Kathie Sarachild on method. Robin Morgan on the boardwalk in 1968. Phyllis Schlafly on the other side of the ERA. Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, Demita Frazier on a 1977 statement. bell hooks in 1981, late, already arguing with a “women” that had been too small. Tanaka Mitsu in Tokyo. Lü Hsiu-lien in Taipei. The Miss America action as an event that does not belong to one face. Slow down for three, as examples inside the field, not as the field. The Feminine Mystique as a public starting point. Consciousness-raising as a method. Combahee as the who-counts problem returning in public — the same problem the First Wave lesson left unfinished, under a different name. A story Friedan’s book, consciousness-raising groups, and the Combahee statement The book: Friedan gave a class of readers a plot in which their unhappiness was not a personal defect. Magazines could review that plot. Television could book it. NOW could walk through it into the EEOC’s office. The limitation is the same fact as the success. A feminism that begins with a white suburban kitchen will treat everyone else as a later chapter. Working women, Black women, lesbians — they were not later. They were already there, and the usual story did not count them well. The groups: consciousness-raising made a technique out of that omission. You did not begin with a program. You began with what had been called trivia — who does the dishes, who gets believed, who is afraid on the street — and you waited until the trivia had a structure. Hanisch’s memo is the defense of that wait. The New Left had said: those are personal problems; the revolution will fix them; type this stencil in the meantime. CR said the stencil was the revolution’s unfinished business. It could become its own trap: a room of people who already resembled each other, mistaking recognition for a census. The method does not excuse the room. It explains why the room felt like politics. The statement: the Combahee River Collective Statement, April 1977, is not an appendix to Steinem. A Black feminist lesbian socialist collective in Boston, named for Harriet Tubman’s 1863 raid, wrote that racial, sexual, heterosexual, and class oppression lock together, and that they would not be asked to choose which liberation to stand in line for. “Identity politics,” in their usage, is the opposite of a veto. It is a starting position from which coalition might be possible because no one is required to disappear. Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, and Demita Frazier are the three who later talked about writing it. The statement is the collective’s. Four years later, bell hooks’s Ain’t I a Woman (1981) is late in this window on purpose: a book arguing with a movement that had already decided what “woman” sounded like. The title borrows a nineteenth-century question this archive has already complicated. The 1981 argument is new only if you were not listening. Elsewhere Feminism in France, Britain, Japan, and Taiwan in the same years In France the press named a Mouvement de libération des femmes around a 26 August 1970 demonstration at the Arc de Triomphe. On 5 April 1971, Le Nouvel Observateur printed the Manifesto of the 343: women stating they had had abortions, Simone de Beauvoir among them. The Second Sex was already twenty years old. In Britain, the first National Women’s Liberation Conference met at Ruskin College, Oxford, 27 February–1 March 1970, and listed four demands: equal pay; equal education and opportunity; 24-hour nurseries; free contraception and abortion on demand. In Japan, ūman ribu was not a translation of a New York leaflet. Tanaka Mitsu’s Liberation from the Toilet (1970) went at the family system and at men on the left; the Ribu Shinjuku Center (1972–77) was a shelter and a clinic. In Taiwan, under martial law, Lü Hsiu-lien lectured on New Feminism at National Taiwan University on 8 March 1972 and published 新女性主義 in 1974: first a person, then a man or a woman. That is a 1970s feminism. It is not an Asian guest at an American table. The same years, in the same cities, were also civil rights, Black Power, the antiwar movement, student revolt, and, after Stonewall in 1969, gay liberation. Women’s liberation came out of those rooms and fought in them. A lesson that treated those movements as background would be repeating the error it is trying to describe. After The ERA failed in 1982, and later writers named a third wave National Women’s Conference, Houston, 19 November 1977. A White House photograph: Rosalynn Carter with Betty Ford and Lady Bird Johnson. The banner says WOMAN as if the noun were settled. A conservative Pro-Family rally met in the same city that weekend. Combahee’s statement was already six months old. Stage at the National Women’s Conference in Houston, 19 November 1977, with a WOMAN banner, a torch, and a podium marked National Women’s Conference 1977. Houston in November 1977 is one picture of a peak: a federally funded conference, a National Plan of Action, three First Ladies, a torch walked from Seneca Falls. It is also a picture of a split. The Plan included the ERA, abortion, lesbian rights, minority women. Opponents held their own rally. Phyllis Schlafly’s STOP ERA had been at work since 1972. On 4 February 1977 her people were already at the White House fence with stop-sign stickers. Congress had sent the Equal Rights Amendment to the states in 1972. The deadline, extended, expired on 30 June 1982, three states short of thirty-eight. Phyllis Schlafly, STOP ERA, in front of the White House, 4 February 1977. The smile is part of the politics: a claim that housewives had a movement too. The ERA’s clock was already running. Phyllis Schlafly smiling, a STOP ERA badge on her coat, with other demonstrators and a White House fence behind her, 4 February 1977. Margaret Thatcher took office in May 1979. Ronald Reagan in January 1981. Susan Faludi would call the 1980s a backlash in a 1991 book of that name. The word is later. The conservative turn is in these last years: an official mood that feminism had been tried, or had gone too far, or had been a coastal taste. Roe stood until Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization in 2022. That sentence is outside the era. It belongs here as a fate, not as a twist. The turn into what gets called the third wave is a later naming. Rebecca Walker’s “Becoming the Third Wave” is 1992, in Ms. Intersectionality, as a word, is Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989. Combahee did not need the word to state interlocking oppressions. The numbered sequence — first the vote, then the rest, then a third period — is the after. It is useful until it hides the people who were never in that sequence. A question A question to keep asking When a movement says the personal is political, whose personal is allowed to count as politics? Roe v. Wade — oral argument (Oyez) Audio of the Supreme Court argument (1971) and reargument (1972), with the 22 January 1973 opinion. This is the case, not a documentary about it. Carol Hanisch — “The Personal Is Political” (1970), with the author’s 2006 note The essay as printed in Notes from the Second Year. Hanisch’s introduction is the useful correction: she did not title it; Shulamith Firestone and Anne Koedt did. Combahee River Collective Statement (April 1977) The 1977 text. BlackPast hosts it; the statement itself is the source. Primary authors later named: Barbara Smith, Beverly Smith, Demita Frazier. National Organization for Women — Statement of Purpose (1966) NOW’s own posting of the founding statement, co-authored in part by Pauli Murray. Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 — U.S. Department of Justice The statutory text. It is a sex-discrimination rule for federally funded education, not a sports law that later grew a statute. Education Amendments of 1972, Public Law 92-318 (86 Stat. 235) — GovInfo The enrolled law Nixon signed on 23 June 1972. Title IX is in this PDF (86 Stat. 373), not a separate act. Roe v. Wade, 410 U.S. 113 (1973) — Legal Information Institute The U.S. Reports text of the decision. Open transcription of the bound volume; not a summary article. Betty Friedan — The Feminine Mystique (W. W. Norton, 1963) Library of Congress catalog record. The book is still in copyright; this is the record, not a full text. Our Bodies Ourselves — the collective’s own history of the book How a 1969 Boston workshop became 1970 newsprint (Women and Their Bodies) and then the book. Institutional memory, not a scan of the first edition.

subject: psych
title: The bystander effect: a mechanism, then a newspaper story that was not the night
dek: What diffusion of responsibility claims, then Kitty Genovese, the Times story that launched the teaching example, and the later proof that the story was not what happened on Austin Street.
text: The bystander effect: a mechanism, then a newspaper story that was not the night What diffusion of responsibility claims, then Kitty Genovese, the Times story that launched the teaching example, and the later proof that the story was not what happened on Austin Street. 1964 (and the after of the story) This lesson starts with the concept, not the crime. Catherine “Kitty” Genovese was murdered in Kew Gardens in the early hours of 13 March 1964. The text does not describe wounds or sexual violence. It does not use a police portrait of her or of the killer. The Times story of 27 March 1964 is a primary source that later reporting — including the Times itself in 2016 — found flawed. The psychology that followed is real experimental work. The 38 silent witnesses are not. Psych / soc psych 13 Mar 1964 Kew Gardens About 3:15 a.m.: Genovese is attacked near her apartment off Austin Street. She dies on the way to hospital. 14 Mar 1964 A brief The Times runs a short item. The later front-page story has not been written yet. 27 Mar 1964 “37 Who Saw” Martin Gansberg’s front-page Times story. The headline says 37; the text says 38. None, it claims, called the police. 1968 The lab Darley and Latané, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology: group size can inhibit helping. They named the mechanism diffusion of responsibility. 2007 The correction Manning, Levine, and Collins in American Psychologist: no evidence for 38 witnesses, or that they watched, or that they all did nothing. 2016 The paper of record The Times calls its 1964 account flawed and “grossly exaggerated.” An editor’s note is later appended to the online 1964 story. Thirty-seven, or thirty-eight The Times headline of 27 March 1964 counted 37. The story under it counted 38. Reprints have used both. The slip is small and perfect: the number that organized a research program was already unstable on the morning it was printed. What was stable was the moral — a city that would not pick up the phone. bystander effect Genovese syndrome The finding, from laboratory and field studies after 1964, that people are often less likely to help when others are present. Darley and Latané (1968) are the usual first citation. The effect does not require the Times’s 38 witnesses to be true. diffusion of responsibility Darley and Latané’s term: in a group, each person feels less personally responsible for acting. The more people who could help, the easier it is to assume someone else will. A mechanism tested in labs. Not a transcript of Austin Street. pluralistic ignorance A second mechanism in the helping literature: each person looks at the others, sees no one moving, and concludes the event is not an emergency. Silence reads as information. Kitty Genovese Catherine Genovese Catherine Susan Genovese Born 7 July 1935 in Brooklyn; killed 13 March 1964 in Kew Gardens, Queens, at 28. She managed Ev’s Eleventh Hour, a bar in Hollis, and lived on Austin Street with Mary Ann Zielonko. The person is older than the newspaper story. Kew Gardens A residential neighborhood in central Queens, around the Long Island Rail Road station and Austin Street. The murder is a Queens story that the Times turned into a story about the city. Austin Street The Kew Gardens street of the apartment and the first attack. Geography, not a set for a play. 38 witnesses thirty-eight witnesses 37 Who Saw The number the 27 March 1964 Times story made famous. The headline said 37; the body said 38. Manning, Levine, and Collins (2007) found no evidence that 38 people witnessed the murder. 37 Who Saw Murder Didn’t Call the Police 37 Who Saw Murder Didn't Call the Police Martin Gansberg’s New York Times front-page story, 27 March 1964. The article that made the teaching example. The Times later judged it flawed. A. M. Rosenthal Abe Rosenthal Times metropolitan editor in 1964. He later wrote that Police Commissioner Michael J. Murphy, over lunch, called the Queens killing “one for the books.” Rosenthal assigned the investigation and, the same year, published Thirty-Eight Witnesses. Martin Gansberg Times reporter whose 27 March 1964 piece carried the 37/38-witness claim and the neighbor’s line “I didn’t want to get involved.” Michael J. Murphy New York City police commissioner in 1964. In Rosenthal’s later telling, the lunch remark that started the second-day story. Thirty-Eight Witnesses Rosenthal’s 1964 book on the case. The number, bound as a title. John Darley Social psychologist. With Bibb Latané, “Bystander Intervention in Emergencies: Diffusion of Responsibility” (1968) and The Unresponsive Bystander (1970). Bibb Latané Latane Social psychologist. With John Darley, the 1968 paper and the 1970 book that built the experimental tradition textbooks still teach. Darley and Latané Darley and Latane The usual joint citation for the first bystander experiments. Bystander Intervention in Emergencies: Diffusion of Responsibility Darley and Latané, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1968. Group size can inhibit helping. The Unresponsive Bystander Darley and Latané, 1970. The book that named a field. The Genovese story is in the preface; the data are from the lab. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology The APA journal that published the 1968 Darley and Latané paper. Sophia Farrar A neighbor and friend who, after the second attack, went to Genovese, held her, and waited for the ambulance. The newspaper story needed her not to exist. Mary Ann Zielonko Genovese’s partner; they shared the Austin Street apartment. Part of the life the newspaper story flattened into a lesson about strangers. Winston Moseley The man convicted of the murder. This capsule names him once as a fact of the case and does not make him the subject. Robert Mozer A neighbor who shouted during the first attack; Moseley left and later returned. One of the actions the silent-38 story had to erase. Manning, Levine, and Collins Rachel Manning, Mark Levine, and Alan Collins. American Psychologist, 2007: the 38-witness story is not supported by the archive. Rachel Manning Lead author of the 2007 American Psychologist paper that named the 38-witness story a parable. Mark Levine Co-author of the 2007 American Psychologist paper. Alan Collins Co-author of the 2007 American Psychologist paper. The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping Manning, Levine, and Collins, American Psychologist, 2007. Keep the experiments; retire the 38-witness story as history. American Psychologist APA journal. The 2007 Manning, Levine, and Collins paper appeared here. Kevin Cook Author of a 2014 history of the case; interviewed on NPR’s All Things Considered, 3 March 2014, about the police number and the interviews underneath it. Robert D. McFadden Times reporter; wrote the 4 April 2016 Winston Moseley obituary in which the paper called the 1964 account “grossly exaggerated.” Jim Rasenberger Author of “Kitty, 40 Years Later” (The New York Times, 8 February 2004), an early Times reconsideration. Kitty, 40 Years Later Rasenberger, The New York Times, 8 February 2004. Frances Cherry Psychologist who, with others, later argued that neighbors who heard a man and a woman at 3 a.m. often classified it as a private quarrel — a gendered reading the first parable did not pause for. James Solomon Director of the documentary The Witness, which records later reporters’ doubts about Gansberg’s count. The Witness James Solomon’s documentary on the Genovese case and its afterlife. A film, not a primary police file. 9-1-1 911 The U.S. centralized emergency number. In March 1964 New Yorkers reached the police by a precinct number or by dialing the operator. AT&T and the FCC announced a national 911 plan in 1968. urban apathy 1960s press name for the idea that city life makes strangers indifferent. The Genovese story was fitted to it. Ev’s Eleventh Hour The Hollis bar Genovese managed. A job, not a symbol. World’s Fair World's Fair The 1964–65 New York World’s Fair at Flushing Meadows, a few stops from Kew Gardens. Same borough, same spring, a different headline. Civil Rights Act Federal law passed in July 1964. Named here only as a same-year headline, not as a cause of the murder. The New York Times the Times The paper of the 14 March brief, the 27 March story, the 2004 reconsideration, and the 2016 judgment that the 1964 account was flawed. The concept What the bystander effect claims The bystander effect is a claim about groups, not about one Queens street. In its ordinary textbook form it says: a person is less likely to help in an emergency when other people are present. The more potential helpers, the less help. The name that stuck to the mechanism is diffusion of responsibility. Each person feels less personally on the hook. Someone else will call. Someone else is closer. Someone else already knows what this is. That is a statement about psychology. It can be true, false, or true only sometimes. It does not, by itself, require a famous murder, a number of windows, or a city that had forgotten how to be a neighbor. Those arrived later, as a story to hang the claim on. A second, related claim in the same literature is pluralistic ignorance: people treat other people’s inaction as information. If no one moves, the smoke is not a fire. If no one calls, the noise is not a crime. Silence becomes evidence. Diffusion of responsibility is about who must act. Pluralistic ignorance is about whether anything is happening. Textbooks often braid them. They are not the same sentence. The mechanism How Darley and Latané tested helping in a group John Darley and Bibb Latané designed emergencies you could run twice. A subject hears a seizure over an intercom, or sees smoke under a door, alone or with other people present — sometimes other subjects, sometimes confederates who have been told not to move. In 1968, in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, they reported “Bystander Intervention in Emergencies: Diffusion of Responsibility”: group size inhibited intervention. The 1970 book is The Unresponsive Bystander. The Genovese name is in the preface of a field. The data are from rooms where the experimenters could count. Why did they think it worked that way? Because responsibility, in their account, is not a fixed moral stock. It divides. A person alone owns the next move. A person in a group can wait, look, and assume the waiting is shared. Add the fear of doing the wrong thing in public — of being the one who overreacts — and inaction has two supports: I am not the one, and this may not be the thing. That is the theory. It is a theory about laboratories and, later, field studies. It is not yet a theory about Austin Street. Times Square, May or June 1952 — Angelo Rizzuto, Library of Congress. The 1960s press already had a story about cities as crowds. The bystander experiments gave that story a mechanism. The mechanism did not need a particular sidewalk. Pedestrians, a City Omnibus bus, and stacked billboards on a Times Square sidewalk, about 1952. The parable Kew Gardens, the Times, and the correction The teaching example came from a newspaper. Kew Gardens in 1964 was a Queens neighborhood of brick apartments, a Long Island Rail Road station, and Austin Street shops. Catherine Genovese, 28, managed Ev’s Eleventh Hour, a bar in Hollis, and shared an apartment at 82–70 Austin Street with Mary Ann Zielonko. There was no 911. A neighbor who wanted the police dialed a precinct or the operator. The city around them had other headlines: a World’s Fair opening in Flushing Meadows; a Civil Rights Act moving through Congress; a press already fond of the phrase urban apathy. Kew Gardens, west to east, about 1936 — Irving Underhill, Library of Congress. A generation before 1964 the neighborhood was already a grid around the railroad. The crime did not invent the place. The later story made the place stand for a whole city. Wide panoramic photograph of Kew Gardens, Long Island, looking west to east, about 1936. In the early morning of 13 March 1964 Winston Moseley attacked Genovese on the Austin Street side of the building. A neighbor, Robert Mozer, shouted; Moseley left and came back. The second attack was in a rear hallway, out of the street’s sight. Later reconstructions — Kevin Cook, the Times in 2016, the 2007 American Psychologist paper — agree on the shape: two attacks, not three; a layout that made a single continuous audience impossible. She was taken away by ambulance and died on the way to the hospital. Sophia Farrar, a neighbor, had gone to her and held her until help came. The station and the south parking lot from Lefferts Boulevard, 3 May 2019. Genovese parked in the railroad lot, about a hundred feet from the apartment door. The cars and the signage are of this century. The cut in the ground is the same fact. Kew Gardens LIRR station and the parking lot south of the tracks, seen from Lefferts Boulevard in 2019. The Times of 14 March ran a short notice. The story that lasted was assigned two weeks later, after Police Commissioner Michael J. Murphy told metropolitan editor A. M. Rosenthal, over lunch, that the Queens case was “one for the books.” Martin Gansberg’s piece of 27 March 1964 went on page one: “37 Who Saw Murder Didn’t Call the Police.” The text said thirty-eight. It said they had watched. It said none had called. An unidentified neighbor supplied the line the decade needed: “I didn’t want to get involved.” Rosenthal’s book the same year was Thirty-Eight Witnesses. The alley between the station and Lefferts Boulevard, 3 May 2019 — the ground the case is attached to, in daylight, without a body. It is here as geography, not as evidence of what any window saw. A paved alley and stair from the Kew Gardens LIRR station toward Lefferts Boulevard, photographed in 2019, empty of people. Social psychology moved faster than the corrections. Darley and Latané started from the story the papers had already told. Many textbooks gave the experiments those 38 windows anyway. In 2007, in “The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping,” Rachel Manning, Mark Levine, and Alan Collins went back to the archive and wrote that there was “no evidence for the presence of 38 witnesses, or that witnesses observed the murder, or that witnesses remained inactive.” The Times, in Robert D. McFadden’s 2016 obituary of Moseley, called the 1964 account flawed and “grossly exaggerated.” Jim Rasenberger’s “Kitty, 40 Years Later” (2004) had already begun the paper’s own reconsideration. An editor’s note was later appended to the online 1964 story. After What the case still teaches — and what it taught wrongly What it taught wrongly is easy to list. There were not 38 people at 38 windows watching a single continuous crime and choosing, each of them, not to dial. Some neighbors did call. Someone went downstairs. The layout and the two attacks made a single shared audience impossible. Frances Cherry and others later argued that a woman’s voice at 3 a.m. was often classified as a private quarrel — a gendered reading the urban-apathy story did not pause for. James Solomon’s film The Witness records reporters who already doubted Gansberg’s count and did not pick the fight with Rosenthal. The number that organized a research program was already unstable on the morning it was printed: the headline said 37, the story said 38. What the case still teaches is not a shrug. Some neighbors did too little. The emergency number was a maze. A press story can fit a ready moral — urban apathy, a city of strangers — and become harder to unwrite than to run. The bystander literature is larger than one street and has been tested without Gansberg’s count. The teaching problem is the one this lesson is for: a discipline can be right about a mechanism and still be wrong about the story it uses to make students care. Keep the experiments. Label the newspaper story. Do not let the correction become a second simplification — that no one failed anyone that night, or that groups never freeze a person. Diffusion of responsibility does not need 38 silent windows. It never did. A question A question to keep asking If a field’s most famous example turns out to be a newspaper story that was not the night, what should it do with the example — drop it, label it, or keep using it because the experiment still works? Martin Gansberg — “37 Who Saw Murder Didn’t Call the Police” (The New York Times, 27 March 1964) The article that made the teaching example. Read it as a 1964 front page, then read the 2016 correction. The Times paywall may sit in front of the archive. Robert D. McFadden — Winston Moseley obituary (The New York Times, 4 April 2016) The Times’s own later account, including the judgment that the 1964 story “grossly exaggerated the number of witnesses and what they had perceived.” Manning, Levine, and Collins — “The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping” (American Psychologist, 2007) The paper that named the 38-witness story a parable. Abstract and DOI are public; the PDF may sit behind APA’s gate. Jim Rasenberger — “Kitty, 40 Years Later” (The New York Times, 8 February 2004) An early Times reconsideration, forty years on, before the 2007 journal article. NPR / All Things Considered — Kevin Cook, 3 March 2014 Cook, author of a 2014 history of the case, on the police number and the interviews underneath it. WNYC — “An Iconic Murder Helped Create the 911 System” (2014) On the emergency-number afterlife. 911 was a national project; New York’s centralized number arrives later than the murder. The piece is a radio essay, not a statute.

subject: business
title: David and Goliath: how the smaller player wins
dek: Asymmetric competition, judo strategy, disruption, and differentiation — then Honda, Southwest, and Canon as cases, used only for the facts named public sources actually state.
text: David and Goliath: how the smaller player wins Asymmetric competition, judo strategy, disruption, and differentiation — then Honda, Southwest, and Canon as cases, used only for the facts named public sources actually state. frameworks, 1979–2001; cases, 1959– This is a strategy-framework lesson, not a biography of three firms and not a promise that underdogs win. Claims about Honda, Southwest, and Canon are traced to named public pieces: Harvard Business Review essays, an HBS case abstract, and a New York Times anniversary account. Operating statistics that those pages do not state are omitted. “David and Goliath” is a metaphor. It is not a dataset. Business business 1958–59 Small machines Honda Super Cub in Japan; American Honda the next year. Xerox 914: the large copier Xerox would later be slow to leave. 1963 Niceness Honda’s U.S. line: “You meet the nicest people on a Honda.” A different rider than Harley-Davidson’s. 1971 Southwest First Southwest Airlines flights in Texas: point-to-point, not a miniature major. 1979–80 Porter “How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy”; then Competitive Strategy and the generic-strategy triad. 1995–96 HBR Bower and Christensen on disruptive technologies (Xerox/Canon in the list); Porter, “What Is Strategy?” (Southwest vs Continental Lite). 1999–2001 Judo Yoffie and Cusumano in HBR; Yoffie and Kwak’s book. Movement, balance, leverage — use the larger rival’s weight rather than matching it. Continental Lite copied the easy pieces In “What Is Strategy?” Porter’s warning is not that Southwest was mysterious. It is that a major could copy a fare, a smile, or a 737 and still fail, because the advantage was the fit among activities — what the major would have to stop doing. Continental Lite is his named exhibit of a partial imitation. A larger airline can borrow one piece of a smaller rival’s system and still be a larger airline with the old system attached. David and Goliath The biblical mismatch: a smaller fighter against a giant. In strategy writing it is a metaphor for asymmetric competition — not a claim that underdogs usually win. asymmetric competition Competing by a different set of activities, customers, or weapons than the incumbent, instead of matching size with size. judo strategy Judo Strategy David B. Yoffie and Mary Kwak’s name (book 2001; with Michael A. Cusumano in HBR, 1999) for using a stronger rival’s size against it: movement, balance, leverage — not a head-to-head trial of strength. David B. Yoffie Yoffie Harvard Business School professor. With Michael A. Cusumano, “Judo Strategy: The Competitive Dynamics of Internet Time” (HBR, January–February 1999); with Mary Kwak, the 2001 book Judo Strategy. Mary Kwak Co-author, with David B. Yoffie, of Judo Strategy (Harvard Business School Press, 2001). Michael A. Cusumano Cusumano MIT Sloan professor; with Yoffie, the 1999 HBR essay “Judo Strategy: The Competitive Dynamics of Internet Time.” Judo Strategy: The Competitive Dynamics of Internet Time Yoffie and Cusumano, Harvard Business Review, January–February 1999. The public HBR statement of the judo metaphor: fast entrants taking on dominant incumbents without matching them blow for blow. Judo Strategy Yoffie and Kwak, Harvard Business School Press, 2001. Subtitled Turning Your Competitors’ Strength to Your Advantage. Movement, balance, leverage. disruptive innovation disruption disruptive technologies Clayton Christensen’s pattern: a simpler or cheaper offer that incumbents’ best customers do not want yet, which later moves upmarket. The 1995 HBR essay with Joseph L. Bower called these “disruptive technologies.” Clayton Christensen Christensen Harvard Business School professor. With Joseph L. Bower, “Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave” (HBR, January–February 1995); later The Innovator’s Dilemma (1997). Joseph L. Bower Bower Harvard Business School professor; co-author with Christensen of “Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave.” Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave Bower and Christensen, Harvard Business Review, January–February 1995. Why leading firms stay close to current customers and let newcomers take the offers those customers reject — including, in their list, Xerox and the small copier. The Innovator's Dilemma Christensen’s 1997 book. The classroom name that followed the 1995 essay. This capsule uses the essay, which is the public HBR source. differentiation product differentiation In Michael E. Porter’s generic strategies, competing by being different in a way buyers will pay for — not by being the same thing cheaper. In “What Is Strategy?” (HBR, 1996) he tightens this to a unique activity system and the trade-offs that protect it. Michael E. Porter Porter Michael Porter Harvard Business School professor. “How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy” (HBR, 1979); Competitive Strategy (1980); “What Is Strategy?” (HBR, November–December 1996). What Is Strategy? Porter, Harvard Business Review, November–December 1996. Operational effectiveness is not strategy. Strategy is a unique position, trade-offs, and fit among activities. Southwest Airlines is one of his exhibits; Continental Lite is the failed copy. How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy Porter, Harvard Business Review, March–April 1979. The five-forces essay: rivalry, entrants, substitutes, buyers, suppliers. Competitive Strategy Porter’s 1980 book. The three generic strategies — cost leadership, differentiation, focus — live here. The 1996 essay is the later, tighter public statement this capsule leans on. generic strategies Porter’s 1980 triad: cost leadership, differentiation, and focus. A map of positions, not a promise that any one of them wins. Honda Honda Motor American Honda Honda Motor Company. In the U.S. motorcycle market it did not first beat Harley-Davidson at large bikes. It sold small, everyday machines to people who had not been Harley’s customer. Soichiro Honda Co-founder of Honda Motor. The NYT’s 2009 anniversary piece is the public named source this capsule uses for the U.S. entry story. Harley-Davidson Harley The incumbent American motorcycle name: large bikes, a heavyweight identity. The larger rival in the Honda story — strong in a market Honda first declined to contest head-on. Super Cub Honda 50 Honda Super Cub Honda’s small step-through motorcycle (1958 in Japan; sold in the U.S. as a small Honda, sometimes the Honda 50). The machine of a different customer. You meet the nicest people on a Honda Honda’s U.S. advertising line, from 1963. The NYT’s 2009 account calls the approach attacking “with niceness”: a different rider than the existing American motorcycle identity. Honda (A) Harvard Business School case (product 384049, 1983) on Honda’s history and U.S. entry, drawing on an earlier case and the Boston Consulting Group’s motorcycle work. Public abstract on the HBR store page; the full case is paid. Boston Consulting Group BCG Consulting firm. Its 1975 report Strategy Alternatives for the British Motorcycle Industry became the planned-strategy version of Honda’s rise — the version Richard Pascale later argued with. Strategy Alternatives for the British Motorcycle Industry Boston Consulting Group report, 1975, for the British government. The planned, scale-curve telling of Honda that classrooms used before Pascale’s interviews. Richard Pascale Author of “Perspectives on Strategy: The Real Story Behind Honda’s Success” (California Management Review, 1984). The Honda Effect: much of what worked in America was improvised after the large bikes failed. Perspectives on Strategy: The Real Story Behind Honda's Success Pascale, California Management Review, 1984. Interviews with Honda executives that complicate the BCG story of a deliberate small-bike plan. Honda Effect Classroom name for the fight between a planned Honda (BCG) and an emergent Honda (Pascale). A warning against treating a later success as a strategy that was clear on day one. Southwest Airlines Southwest U.S. airline that, from 1971, flew point-to-point on one aircraft type instead of copying the majors’ hub-and-spoke machine. Porter’s 1996 HBR essay uses it as a system of activities; Continental Lite is the copy that did not fit. Herb Kelleher Cofounder and longtime CEO of Southwest Airlines. Bill Taylor’s HBR remembrance (8 January 2019) is the named public source this capsule uses for the person. The Legacy of Herb Kelleher, Cofounder of Southwest Airlines Bill Taylor, Harvard Business Review, 8 January 2019. A remembrance, not a case exhibit — used here for the person, not for invented operating numbers. Bill Taylor Cofounder of Fast Company; author of the 2019 HBR piece on Kelleher. point-to-point Flying city to city without forcing a connection through a hub. Southwest’s network idea; the opposite of the majors’ hub-and-spoke. hub-and-spoke The major-airline network: feed traffic through a few hub cities. Efficient for a large system; slow and expensive to copy if you are small and want the plane back in the air. Boeing 737 The aircraft type Southwest standardized on. One type means one training school, one spare-parts list, one way to turn a plane. Porter’s point is the fit, not the airframe as a fetish. Continental Lite Continental Airlines’ 1990s attempt to copy pieces of Southwest. Porter’s 1996 essay uses it as the exhibit of a failed partial imitation: a few activities, not the system. Xerox The incumbent of large, often leased, office copiers after the Xerox 914 (1959). Bower and Christensen’s 1995 HBR essay: Xerox let Canon create the small-copier market. Xerox 914 Xerox’s 1959 plain-paper copier. The machine that made copying a corporate center, and that made a later small copier look, to Xerox’s best customers, like a toy. Canon Japanese camera and later copier company. In Bower and Christensen’s 1995 list, the firm that created the small-copier market while Xerox stayed with the customers who wanted big machines. incumbent The firm already strong in a market. Strength here is also a constraint: the customers, assets, and habits that make a new offer look small or wrong. For Honda in America, 50 Years of Going Its Own Direction New York Times, 12 July 2009. Named anniversary account of American Honda’s U.S. entry: Pico Boulevard, small motorcycles, Harley and the British bikes as the existing taste, “niceness” as the attack. Rita McGrath Columbia strategy professor. Later commentary has used Southwest as a caution about treating a famous case as a finished recipe. Named here as a limit, not as a source for 1971 facts. Grey Advertising The agency associated with Honda’s U.S. “nicest people” campaign. Named as the usual advertising credit; this capsule does not invent the internal memo. Netscape The 1990s browser company in Yoffie and Cusumano’s 1999 HBR examples of a fast entrant meeting a giant. Microsoft The incumbent in that 1999 HBR pairing. An example from their moment, not a third case in this capsule. Harvard Business Review HBR The journal that published the Porter, Christensen/Bower, and Yoffie/Cusumano essays this capsule cites. A magazine, not a method. California Management Review The journal that published Pascale’s 1984 Honda interviews. The other file in the Honda Effect. The New York Times New York Times NYT Publisher of the 12 July 2009 Honda anniversary account used as a named public source. The problem Why matching a larger rival head-on usually fails A smaller player who attacks an incumbent where the incumbent is already strong is usually volunteering to lose. The larger firm has the customers, the dealers, the plant, the brand, and the lawyers. Matching it blow for blow is a trial of strength. Judo, in the martial-art sense Yoffie and Kwak borrow, is the opposite idea: do not oppose strength to strength. Use the other side’s size against it. That is the problem this lesson is for. Not “how to be inspiring.” Not a tour of three beloved companies. The question is narrower: when the other side is larger, where do you stand so that their size becomes slow? The painting is the metaphor, not the evidence. Strategy frameworks exist because the Bible is not a market study. Caravaggio’s David with the head of Goliath. The framework Three strategy tools, each from a named essay Three named tools, from named essays, because a Saturday business lesson that invents a framework is just a slogan. Judo strategy, as David B. Yoffie and Michael A.
