title: British Invasion (c. 1963–67): Britain sells America its own records back
dek: After rationing, British teenagers learned guitar from American R&B and rock and roll 45s. Skiffle, art schools, and pirate radio turned those records into a local scene. In 1964 American radio named the export a “British Invasion.”
text: British Invasion (c. 1963–67): Britain sells America its own records back After rationing, British teenagers learned guitar from American R&B and rock and roll 45s. Skiffle, art schools, and pirate radio turned those records into a local scene. In 1964 American radio named the export a “British Invasion.” c. 1963–67 “British Invasion” is an American radio and press name for British beat groups hitting the U.S. charts after February 1964. From Britain the same years were also the end of rationing’s long after-effect, a BBC that still limited how many records it could play, pirate radio ships, and a generation that had learned guitar from American R&B and rock and roll records. This lesson looks out from Britain. Motown, the Beach Boys, French yé-yé, and Japanese Group Sounds were running in the same years. They are not decoration, and they are not a required Asia pairing. Music music 1954–56 After rationing Meat rationing ended in 1954. Lonnie Donegan’s “Rock Island Line” (1955–56) made skiffle a cheap way for teenagers to start a group. 1962 Labels / managers Decca passed on the Beatles; Parlophone and George Martin did not. Brian Epstein was already managing them. London R&B clubs were covering Chess and Motown records. 1964 Sullivan / Caroline The Beatles appeared on The Ed Sullivan Show on 9 February. Radio Caroline began broadcasting from a ship in March. The American name “British Invasion” arrived with those months. 1964 London riff The Kinks released “You Really Got Me.” The Rolling Stones kept their Chicago R&B sources louder than variety television preferred. 1965–66 Elsewhere Motown and Stax were hit factories in the United States. The Beach Boys were in the studio. Group Sounds bands were working in Japan. Yé-yé was already on French radio. 1967 The name shrinks Sgt. Pepper, BBC Radio 1, and the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act. Psychedelia made “Invasion” too small a word for what the records were doing. The BBC was limited in how many records it could play Into the mid-1960s the BBC was bound by needle-time: agreements with the Musicians’ Union that limited how many hours of records, as opposed to live studio bands, could be broadcast. Pirate ships were not only a teenage romance. They were a way around a labor and licensing rule. Radio 1, created in 1967, was in part an official answer to that gap. British Invasion American press and radio name, from 1964, for the rush of British beat groups onto the U.S. charts. The people in Liverpool and London did not need the phrase to know they were already playing. skiffle British 1950s homemade jazz-folk-blues: acoustic guitar, washboard, tea-chest bass. Lonnie Donegan’s hit version of “Rock Island Line” (1955–56) put a cheap guitar in a lot of teenage hands. needle-time needle time BBC agreements with the Musicians’ Union that limited how many hours of records (as opposed to live studio bands) could be broadcast. Pirate ships were one way around the rule. R&B rhythm and blues In early-1960s Britain, “R&B” usually meant Black American rhythm and blues and Chicago electric blues — Chess Records, Motown, the records imported or covered in London clubs — not the later pop-chart sense of the letters. rock and roll rock & roll The 1950s American form British teenagers heard on imported 45s and the few U.S. package tours that reached them. Berry, Little Richard, and the rest were a curriculum before they were a nostalgia act. pirate radio Unlicensed stations on ships or forts outside British territorial waters, from 1964. They played the records the BBC’s Light Programme would not schedule in bulk. Radio Caroline The first major British pirate pop station. It began broadcasting in March 1964 from a ship in international waters. Merseybeat The early-1960s Liverpool beat-group sound and scene, named for the River Mersey. The Beatles were the export; they were not the only band in the city. Mod Mods A British youth style of the early-to-mid 1960s: sharp Italian tailoring, scooters, R&B and soul records, later associated with the London look that Carnaby Street sold. A look and a market, not a single band. Carnaby Street Carnaby A short Soho street that became a 1960s boutique strip. The British groups traveled as clothes as well as singles. beat groups beat group The British name for the guitar-bass-drums-vocals groups that filled cellars and ballrooms before “British Invasion” was an American headline. package tours package tour British multi-act road bills: several groups, one night, a shared bus. How most of the country met the records between television appearances. art schools art school British art colleges that a striking number of 1960s musicians passed through. They were cheap, they taught looking, and they left time to form a group. Chess Chess Records Chicago label (Phil and Leonard Chess) that recorded Chuck Berry, Muddy Waters, Howlin’ Wolf. British groups learned the catalog; American radio had often filed it as R&B, not pop. Motown Detroit label founded by Berry Gordy. By 1964 it was a hit factory with its own sound, choreography, and crossover ambition — running in the same years as the Invasion, not waiting to be discovered by it. Stax Memphis label and studio whose house band and singers made Southern soul in the mid-1960s. Another American industry, contemporaneous, not a British invention. Group Sounds グループ・サウンズ Japanese 1960s electric-guitar pop, mid-decade: The Tigers, The Spiders, The Blue Comets. It heard the Beatles and local kayōkyoku at once. Same years, different market. yé-yé French and wider European mid-1960s pop named for the “yeah-yeah” refrain. France Gall, Sylvie Vartan, and others were already on the radio while Britain was invading America. kayōkyoku Japanese popular song of the postwar decades, the domestic tradition Group Sounds bands were hearing alongside imported beat records. Vox AC30 AC30 British 30-watt guitar amplifier, from the late 1950s. The Beatles, the Shadows, and later Invasion groups used it. The chime is a hardware fact, not a metaphor. Ed Sullivan The Ed Sullivan Show Sunday-night U.S. television variety show. The Beatles’ 9 February 1964 appearance is the Invasion’s most repeated American date. It was a broadcast, not the beginning of the music. Parlophone EMI label that signed the Beatles in 1962, with George Martin as producer. Not a small indie — a wing of a large British record company that had room for comedy records and, it turned out, beat groups. Decca British label that, in January 1962, did not sign the Beatles after an audition. It later had the Rolling Stones. A large company can be late and still be in the business. EMI The British record group that owned Parlophone. The Invasion’s “independent” look sat on major-label machinery. BBC Light Programme The British public broadcaster. In the early 1960s its Light Programme carried pop, but needle-time limited how many records it could play. Radio 1, in 1967, was in part an official answer to the pirates. Radio 1 BBC pop network launched in 1967, after the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act squeezed the pirates. An official station for a habit the ships had already trained. Lonnie Donegan Scottish-born skiffle singer. “Rock Island Line” (1955–56) showed a British teenager that an American folk-blues song could be a hit without an orchestra. Lead Belly Leadbelly American folk-blues singer (Huddie Ledbetter). Donegan’s “Rock Island Line” came from his repertoire. Rock Island Line American folk-blues song. Donegan’s London recording became a British hit in 1956 and a starter kit for skiffle groups. Chuck Berry St. Louis guitarist, Chess Records. British groups covered him so often the covers became a curriculum. Johnny B. Goode Chuck Berry’s 1958 Chess single (1691). In Britain it was homework: a riff, a story, two and a half minutes. Little Richard American rock-and-roll singer and pianist. British groups learned his songs and his show; the Invasion did not invent either. Muddy Waters Chicago electric-blues singer, Chess Records. A name London R&B clubs treated as a source, not a novelty. Howlin’ Wolf Chicago electric-blues singer, Chess. Another name on the London club set lists. The Beatles Beatles Liverpool group, then Hamburg, then Parlophone. After late 1963 they were the British act American television used to introduce the rest. This lesson treats them as that introduction, not as the whole scene. John Lennon Liverpool musician; his Quarrymen were a skiffle group before they were the Beatles. Liverpool College of Art is part of the art-school fact, not a romance. Quarrymen the Quarrymen Lennon’s skiffle group, the unglamorous before of the Beatles. Paul McCartney Liverpool musician, Beatles. The relevant fact here is the shared repertoire: Berry, Little Richard, girl-group records, then songs of their own. George Harrison Beatles guitarist. Hamburg and the Cavern before Sullivan. Ringo Starr Beatles drummer from 1962. The American cameras learned four names; the scene behind them had hundreds. Brian Epstein Liverpool record-shop manager who became the Beatles’ manager in 1962. Suits, dates, and a path to EMI were his job. The songs were not. George Martin Parlophone producer who signed and recorded the Beatles. A staff producer at a large company, not a bedroom auteur. I Want to Hold Your Hand Beatles single, British release November 1963; Capitol issued it in the U.S. in late December. The record that made American radio take the group seriously before the Sullivan broadcast. Sgt. Pepper Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band Beatles album, 1967. The useful Invasion story — verse, chorus, suit, scream — no longer described what they were recording by the time it appeared. Revolver Beatles album, 1966. One of the records that made “British Invasion” a poor name for what came next. The Rolling Stones Rolling Stones the Stones London R&B group. They kept the Chess debt in the foreground longer than the variety-show version of the Invasion wanted. Mick Jagger Rolling Stones singer. London School of Economics is sometimes mentioned as if it explained the band. The Chess covers explain more. Keith Richards Rolling Stones guitarist; Sidcup Art College is the art-school line in his case. Andrew Loog Oldham The Rolling Stones’ manager from 1963. He sold a refusal to be variety — a longer haircut, a press image — around a band that had started as a London R&B cover group. The Kinks Kinks North London group. “You Really Got Me” (1964) is a London riff that does not sound like a polite cover. Ray Davies Kinks singer and writer. The later English-village songs are a different chapter. 1964 is the sliced speaker and the riff. Dave Davies Kinks guitarist. The standard account of “You Really Got Me” is that he razor-slashed a speaker cone. Treat the hardware story as the usual one; the record is the fact. You Really Got Me Kinks single, 1964. Distorted riff, London, not Liverpool. A harder sound than the smiling Merseybeat export. The Who London group, Shepherd’s Bush and the Mod circuit. Maximum R&B on the posters; auto-destruction on the stage. Not a Liverpool export. Pete Townshend Who guitarist; Ealing Art College is the art-school line. The Animals Animals Newcastle group with an R&B repertoire, later filed under the Invasion in America. The city is not London; the set list still came from American records. Dave Clark Five the Dave Clark Five DC5 Tottenham group. American television used them as the next British name after the Beatles. A beat group from north London, not Merseybeat. Dusty Springfield British pop and soul singer. She is in the Invasion years and not a beat group: a reminder that the American name flattened more than guitars. Manfred Mann London R&B and pop group (and the keyboardist they were named for). Another name on the 1964–65 bills. The Hollies Hollies Manchester group. The Invasion was not only Liverpool and London. The Yardbirds Yardbirds London R&B group. A club band that made the guitar a problem to be solved, not only a riff to be copied. The Shadows Shadows British instrumental group of the late 1950s–60s. The Vox AC30 was already a local sound before the Invasion name existed. Berry Gordy Founder of Motown. In 1964 his label was not waiting to be invaded. The Temptations Temptations Motown group. “My Girl” is 1964: a parallel American industry, not a footnote to Sullivan. My Girl Temptations / Motown single, 1964. Same year as the Sullivan appearance. The Beach Boys Beach Boys California group. Pet Sounds (1966) is the usual same-years comparison: another studio, another coast, not a British franchise. Pet Sounds Beach Boys album, 1966. Contemporaneous with the later Invasion years; not caused by them. France Gall French yé-yé singer, already a radio name in the mid-1960s. Sylvie Vartan French yé-yé singer. Evidence that “yeah-yeah” was not a British monopoly. The Tigers Japanese Group Sounds band of the mid-1960s. The Spiders Japanese Group Sounds band of the mid-1960s. The Blue Comets Blue Comets Japanese Group Sounds band of the mid-1960s. Cavern Club the Cavern Liverpool cellar club. The Beatles’ lunchtime residency is the tourist fact. The club was one room in a local scene, not the cause of the scene. Crawdaddy Crawdaddy Club Richmond R&B club, early home of the Rolling Stones. London’s version of a cellar, with a different set list. Marine Broadcasting Offences Act 1967 British law that made supplying the pirate ships an offence. The records did not disappear from British life. New Musical Express NME British weekly music paper. One of the teen and trade presses that treated beat groups as a weekly serial. Melody Maker British weekly music paper, older than NME. The other half of the London trade press the Invasion groups had to live in. Before After rationing, cheap guitars, and other people’s records Postwar Britain did not jump from the Blitz to Carnaby Street. Food rationing lasted into the 1950s; meat came off the ration in 1954. What followed was not sudden luxury. It was a narrower fact: a generation that had more pocket money than its parents at the same age, and not enough official culture that sounded as if it belonged to them. The BBC’s Light Programme carried pop. It did not carry enough of it. Needle-time agreements limited recorded music on air. If you wanted more than the official dose, you needed a radio that was not polite, a shop that imported American 45s, or — later — a ship that was not yet in British waters. The records arrived first. Rhythm and blues and rock and roll came as merchant-seamen singles, as classified imports, and as the B-sides of things the Light Programme did not love. Chuck Berry’s “Johnny B. Goode” was a 1958 Chess single from Chicago. Little Richard, Muddy Waters, Howlin’ Wolf, and the Motown 45s were the rest of the homework. In Britain they were not yet a museum. They were what you learned if you wanted a group. Chuck Berry, late-1950s publicity photograph. British beat groups did not invent this stance. They learned it from records and from the few U.S. package tours that reached them. Chuck Berry in a tuxedo, crouched, playing a Gibson electric guitar. Chess 1691, “Johnny B. Goode,” 1958. The object is a Chicago single: two and a half minutes, written by C. Berry. A decade later British groups were still arguing about who owned the riff. Blue Chess Records 45 label for Johnny B. Goode by Chuck Berry, catalog 1691. Skiffle made the homework cheap. Lonnie Donegan’s “Rock Island Line” — a Lead Belly song, recorded in London — became a British hit in 1955–56. A washboard and a tea-chest bass were enough to start. John Lennon’s Quarrymen were a skiffle band. So were many of the people who later grew fringes in Liverpool, London, and Manchester. Art schools did a related job: Liverpool College of Art, Ealing, Sidcup, and the London colleges that Pete Townshend, Keith Richards, and others passed through. They were not conservatories. They were cheap places where looking hard was a skill and a group could be a project. Lonnie Donegan, Cash Box, 23 June 1956. The paper’s joke is that he is “riding” the Rock Island Line. The useful fact is the date: skiffle as a British hit, and a cheap way to start a group, before any American name for what came next. Lonnie Donegan in a 1956 Cash Box publicity photograph, riding the Rock Island Line as a caption joke. By the early 1960s the scenes were local before they were a national story. Liverpool had the Cavern Club and a density of beat groups later tagged Merseybeat. London had the Marquee, the Crawdaddy, and an R&B circuit that treated Chess Records as a source catalog. Manchester had the Hollies. Newcastle had the Animals. Tottenham had the Dave Clark Five. None of this required an American name yet. It required halls, managers, and a BBC that still could not play the records as often as the rooms wanted them. The era How a local scene became an American headline What Americans later called the British Invasion was, from Britain, several overlapping facts. Beat groups filled ballrooms and package tours. Merseybeat and London R&B were not the same accent: Liverpool sold harmony and a smile that television could use; London’s R&B clubs sold Chess covers and longer hair. The look traveled with the singles. Mods, Italian suits, scooters, then Carnaby Street as a boutique strip a tourist could photograph. Teen papers — New Musical Express, Melody Maker, and the American fan magazines that followed — treated the groups as a weekly serial. The industry underneath was not a cottage. Parlophone, Decca, EMI, managers such as Brian Epstein and Andrew Loog Oldham, and producers such as George Martin were large companies and a few intermediaries who had learned that a cellar residency could be a product. A mid-1960s transistor radio. The British groups needed ships and television, but they also needed a private speaker a teenager could hold. The BBC was a household set. This was a pocket. Black portable Orion eight-transistor radio with a gold speaker grille. The American date is easy to point at and easy to overweight. Capitol issued the Beatles’ “I Want to Hold Your Hand” in the United States in late December 1963. On 9 February 1964 they played The Ed Sullivan Show. After that, U.S. charts and variety television filled with British names: the Rolling Stones, the Kinks, the Who, the Animals, the Dave Clark Five, Dusty Springfield, Manfred Mann, the Hollies, the Yardbirds. “British Invasion” is what American radio called those months. From London the same spring, Radio Caroline began broadcasting from a ship. The BBC still had a needle-time problem. The cameras and the pirates were answering the same shortage from different sides of the ocean. MV Caroline, the first Radio Caroline ship. The station began broadcasting in March 1964 from international waters. It was a business and a workaround: records the BBC would not play in bulk, aimed at the same teenagers who were about to watch Sullivan. The ship Caroline at sea, name painted on the bow, masts and a dark funnel against a pale sky. A Vox AC30 Twin, the British amplifier on a lot of Invasion stages. The tag in this photograph guesses at a Shadows connection. Treat the guess as a guess. The hardware is the fact: 30 watts, two speakers, a sound that is not a Fender. A worn Vox AC30 Twin guitar amplifier with diamond grille cloth and a handwritten museum tag. The field Many groups, and three ways they entered the story A gallery of three faces is the wrong picture. The field is crowded on purpose. The Beatles, the Rolling Stones, the Kinks, the Who, the Animals, the Dave Clark Five, Dusty Springfield, Manfred Mann, the Hollies, the Yardbirds — and behind them the American records they learned: Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Motown, Chess. Epstein and Oldham sold the dates. Martin, and the Decca that said no, are the industry’s two hands. Donegan is the cheap starter kit. Sullivan is the American camera. Name them, then slow down for only a few, as examples inside the scene, not as the scene. The Beatles are the group American television used to introduce the rest. Liverpool, Hamburg, the Cavern Club, then Parlophone. This lesson does not need another press shot of four men in suits. The useful facts are the repertoire and the timing. They had already learned Berry, Little Richard, and the girl-group records. “I Want to Hold Your Hand” was a song American radio could not file as a foreign novelty for long. After Sullivan, every other British group on an American bill was using an introduction they had not made. That is not the same as saying the others were copies. It is a fact about cameras and charts. The Rolling Stones are the R&B debt left audible. London clubs, Chess covers, Jagger and Richards, and Oldham’s refusal to package them as variety. They did not invent Muddy Waters. They declined, longer than was polite, to pretend the covers were a phase. When they wrote their own songs, the debt was still the point: a British group selling America a Chicago idea with white faces on the same variety shows that had not booked the Chess roster as pop. The honest version does not scold them for learning. It keeps the Chess label in the shot. The Kinks are a different London hardness. “You Really Got Me,” 1964: Ray Davies and Dave Davies, a riff that does not behave like a cover, and a speaker cone that the usual story says was sliced so the guitar would break up. Treat the hardware story as the usual one; the record is the fact. Liverpool’s export was blend. This was a two-chord shove from Muswell Hill. It is one record, not a theory of the decade. It is enough to stop the Invasion from being told as four smiling men and one television broadcast. Elsewhere The same years, not a ranking of songs In Detroit, Motown under Berry Gordy was already a finished system — writers, a house band, a finishing school for movement. The Temptations’ “My Girl” is 1964. In Memphis, Stax was cutting Southern soul with a biracial house band. In California the Beach Boys were in the studio; Pet Sounds, in 1966, is the comparison the syllabuses never let go. In France, yé-yé — France Gall, Sylvie Vartan — was already a word. In Japan, Group Sounds bands (the Tigers, the Spiders, the Blue Comets) were taking electric guitars into a market that had its own kayōkyoku tradition. Britain was not the only place the 45 rpm single was rewriting a generation. It was the place American television decided to point the camera. That is a fact about power, not a ranking of songs. After By 1967 the chart label no longer described the music By 1966–67 the useful Invasion story — verse, chorus, suit, scream — was already too small. Revolver, then Sgt. Pepper, then a lot of other people’s sitars and tape loops. The turn toward psychedelia was not a British monopoly; San Francisco is in the same late decade. The name “British Invasion” stays useful as a 1964–65 American chart event. It is a poor name for everything that happened next. The Marine Broadcasting Offences Act arrived in 1967. Radio 1 began the same year. The pirates were legislated against. The records did not disappear from British life. A question A question to keep asking If a country sells another country its own music, who counts as the inventor in the room? The Beatles on The Ed Sullivan Show (9 February 1964) Sullivan’s own site on the broadcast. Full performances are licensed; this is the historical record of the date, not a bootleg film. Chuck Berry — Johnny B. Goode (1958) Chess single 1691. The record many British groups learned from. Official/label upload; if it moves, search the title on the label’s channel. The Beatles — I Want to Hold Your Hand (1963) The Capitol single that opened the U.S. market in late 1963 and early 1964. Official Beatles channel. The Kinks — You Really Got Me (1964) Official audio. Distorted riff, London, not Liverpool. The Temptations — My Girl (1964) Motown, same year as the Sullivan appearance. Not a footnote — a parallel industry. Radio Caroline The station still exists. The 1964 ship is history; the site is the living remnant, not a 1964 tape.

subject: feminism
title: First Wave (c. 1848–1920): the fight over whether women counted as political persons
dek: From Seneca Falls to the Nineteenth Amendment, women in the United States and Britain organized for the vote and for legal standing. The movement split over race, tactics, and who was included when organizers said “we.”
text: First Wave (c. 1848–1920): the fight over whether women counted as political persons From Seneca Falls to the Nineteenth Amendment, women in the United States and Britain organized for the vote and for legal standing. The movement split over race, tactics, and who was included when organizers said “we.” c. 1848–1920 “First wave” is a later Anglo-American classroom name. The people in this lesson did not call themselves that. The label is useful because it groups several decades of public campaigns over whether women counted as political persons. It is incomplete as a history, because those campaigns were not only Anglo-American, and because they did not include every woman they claimed to speak for. What follows uses the usual dates, then looks at the same years in China. Feminism feminism 1848 Seneca Falls A two-day convention in Seneca Falls, New York, issued the Declaration of Sentiments. The vote was one demand among many legal and social grievances. 1851 Akron Sojourner Truth spoke at a women’s rights meeting in Akron, Ohio. The famous refrain “Ain’t I a woman?” comes from a later rewrite of that speech. 1870 The split The Fifteenth Amendment barred denying the vote because of race, not sex. Stanton and Anthony opposed ratifying it without women; Stone and Douglass would not block Black men’s suffrage in order to wait. 1907 Anqing Qiu Jin was executed after an uprising in Anqing. She was working in the same decade as British militant suffragettes, under a different government. 1913 Procession / Derby On 3 March, Alice Paul and Lucy Burns organized a suffrage procession in Washington, D.C. In June, Emily Wilding Davison died after stepping onto the course at the Epsom Derby. 1920 Nineteenth Amendment The United States barred denying the vote because of sex. Poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence still blocked many Black women in the South. She copyrighted her own photograph In 1864 Sojourner Truth registered the copyright on her own cartes-de-visite in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan. That was unusual: the photographer usually claimed the image. The cards were printed with her own sentence, “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” She sold them at lectures because lectures did not pay enough. The portrait in this lesson is one of those cards. The “shadow” here is her word for the photograph, not a later flourish. coverture English common-law doctrine that a married woman’s legal identity was “covered” by her husband’s. Property, contracts, and wages were his unless a statute carved out an exception. separate spheres A nineteenth-century middle-class rule: men belonged in public and economic life, and women belonged in the home as moral guardians. It was a class rule as much as a sex rule. Women who earned wages, and enslaved women, were never offered that protected private role. Seneca Falls Village in western New York. On 19–20 July 1848 a convention there issued the Declaration of Sentiments. Later writers used “Seneca Falls” as shorthand for the start of organized U.S. women’s rights. It is a useful date, not the only origin. Declaration of Sentiments Sentiments The 1848 Seneca Falls text, modeled on the Declaration of Independence. It listed grievances including the vote. The vote was not the only demand, and not everyone in the room wanted it named first. Fifteenth Amendment 15th Amendment Ratified 1870. It barred denying the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” It did not mention sex. The omission split the U.S. women’s-rights coalition. WSPU Women’s Social and Political Union Women’s Social and Political Union, founded 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst. The militant wing of British suffrage: window-breaking, hunger strikes, and, in reply, force-feeding. Jim Crow The system of legal racial segregation and disenfranchisement in the U.S. South after Reconstruction — poll taxes, literacy tests, violence. The Nineteenth Amendment did not repeal it. 中國女報 Chinese Women’s Journal Chinese Women’s Journal, edited by Qiu Jin in Shanghai in 1907. Two issues appeared. It argued for women’s education and against bound feet in the same breath as anti-Qing politics. carte-de-visite cartes-de-visite A small albumen photograph mounted on card, cheap to reproduce, sold and collected in the 1860s. Sojourner Truth sold hers with a printed caption and a copyright in her own name. Gage Frances Dana Gage Frances Dana Gage. In 1863 she published a version of Sojourner Truth’s 1851 Akron speech that includes the refrain “Ain’t I a woman?” Contemporary 1851 newspaper accounts do not use the refrain that way. Nineteenth Amendment 19th Amendment Ratified 1920. It says the right to vote shall not be denied on account of sex. It did not touch poll taxes, literacy tests, or the violence that still blocked many Black women in the South. force-feeding In British prisons, hunger-striking suffragettes were restrained and fed through a tube. The Liberal government presented it as medical care. Militants presented it as assault. Both descriptions circulated in the press. doldrums A later name for organized U.S. feminism in the 1920s–1950s. After the vote arrived, the suffrage coalition thinned and public campaigning quieted. The word describes one organized current going quiet. It does not mean the underlying questions ended. Alice Paul American suffrage organizer. She trained with British militants, then with Lucy Burns planned the 3 March 1913 Woman Suffrage Procession in Washington. She later led the National Woman’s Party and wrote an Equal Rights Amendment. Married Women’s Property Acts Married Women's Property Acts Married Women’s Property Act State statutes, beginning in the 1840s, that let a married woman keep some property in her own name. New York’s 1848 act is the usual example. The laws were limited and uneven. They did not end coverture. National Woman Suffrage Association NWSA Founded in 1869 by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony after the split over the Fifteenth Amendment. It opposed ratifying the amendment without women and worked for a federal suffrage amendment. American Woman Suffrage Association AWSA Founded in 1869 by Lucy Stone and others who would not block Black men’s suffrage in order to wait for women. It favored a state-by-state strategy. It merged with the NWSA in 1890. National American Woman Suffrage Association NAWSA The 1890 merger of the National Woman Suffrage Association and the American Woman Suffrage Association. The main constitutional-suffrage organization in the United States until the Nineteenth Amendment. Cat and Mouse Act Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health) Act Prisoners Temporary Discharge for Ill Health Act British 1913 statute that released hunger-striking suffragettes when they were too weak to feed, then rearrested them when they recovered. The nickname compared the government to a cat playing with a mouse. Xu Xilin 徐錫麟 Hsü Hsi-lin Anti-Qing revolutionary. His 1907 uprising in Anqing failed. Qiu Jin, who had been working with the same network, was arrested and executed afterward. Before Married women had no separate legal self, and abolition trained the organizers Under English common law, a married woman’s legal identity was absorbed into her husband’s. The doctrine is called coverture. Her property, her contracts, and her wages belonged to him unless a statute carved out an exception. An unmarried woman had more legal room. Marriage closed it. In the United States, states began to pass Married Women’s Property Acts in the 1840s — New York’s 1848 statute is the usual example — but those laws were limited, uneven, and did not make a wife a full legal person. Industrial work had already left the house. What remained, for middle-class white women, was a public story about respectability: the home as a moral refuge, the woman as domestic, delicate, and good. Historians call this “separate spheres.” It was a rule of class as much as of sex. Enslaved women, and women who worked for wages, were never offered that protected private role. They were already in public as labor, as property, or as exceptions the ideology did not have to explain. Abolition was the training ground for many United States feminists. In anti-slavery societies they learned to petition legislatures, lecture to mixed audiences, edit newspapers, and run a meeting. Those skills transferred to women’s rights. The alliance later cracked, after the Civil War, when the question became which emancipation would be allowed to go first: Black men’s suffrage, or women’s. The era Seneca Falls, the Fifteenth Amendment split, and the 1913 parade On 19–20 July 1848, at Seneca Falls, New York, a convention issued a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the Declaration of Independence. Elizabeth Cady Stanton was the principal author; Lucretia Mott was among the organizers. The vote was one grievance among others — property, divorce, education, and public speech. Not everyone in the room wanted the vote named first. The document still did something new in American public life: it treated women as people who could claim the same political rights the United States had already claimed for men. A 1908 souvenir card titled “Our Roll of Honor,” printed sixty years after Seneca Falls, listing the women who signed the 1848 Declaration of Sentiments. Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton head the first column. This is a commemorative card, not the 1848 manuscript. Printed souvenir card titled Our Roll of Honor, listing women who signed the 1848 Declaration of Sentiments. In 1851 Sojourner Truth spoke at a women’s rights meeting in Akron, Ohio. The famous refrain “Ain’t I a woman?” comes from Frances Dana Gage’s 1863 rewrite of that speech. Contemporary 1851 newspaper accounts do not use the refrain that way. The later version is the one that traveled in print. The historical point does not depend on the catchphrase. A feminism built on white middle-class delicacy treated enslaved women and working women as exceptions — people whose bodies had already been asked to do too much to count as the “woman” the movement was picturing. After the Civil War the coalition split over the Fifteenth Amendment, ratified in 1870, which barred denying the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” It did not mention sex. In 1869 Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony founded the National Woman Suffrage Association and opposed ratifying the amendment without women. Lucy Stone and others founded the American Woman Suffrage Association and would not block Black men’s suffrage in order to wait. Frederick Douglass, who had supported women’s rights at Seneca Falls, took Stone’s side on sequence. The argument was about order, and about who was being asked to stand aside. The two organizations did not merge into the National American Woman Suffrage Association until 1890. In Britain the movement divided by method. Constitutional suffragists collected signatures and lobbied Parliament. The militant Women’s Social and Political Union, founded in 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst, broke windows, disrupted meetings, and, in prison, went on hunger strike. The Liberal government answered with force-feeding, then with the 1913 Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health) Act — the “Cat and Mouse Act” — which released weakened prisoners and rearrested them when they recovered. In June 1913 Emily Wilding Davison died after stepping onto the course at the Epsom Derby in front of the king’s horse. Emmeline Pankhurst in 1913, the year Emily Wilding Davison died at Epsom and the Women’s Social and Political Union’s militancy was impossible to ignore. Constitutional suffragists were still collecting signatures. Pankhurst’s organization was collecting prison sentences. Formal seated portrait of Emmeline Pankhurst, 1913. On 3 March 1913, the day before Wilson’s inauguration, Alice Paul and Lucy Burns organized the Woman Suffrage Procession in Washington, D.C. Inez Milholland rode in white on a white horse at the head of the line. Black women were told to march in a rear contingent. Ida B. Wells refused. She waited until the Illinois delegation passed, then stepped into that line and marched with her state. The crowd on Pennsylvania Avenue, 3 March 1913. Men climbed poles and wagons to see. Alice Paul timed the procession for the eve of Woodrow Wilson’s inauguration so it could not be missed. Being unmissable was not the same as being welcomed: spectators repeatedly stepped into the street and broke the line of march. A dense crowd lining Pennsylvania Avenue to watch the 1913 woman suffrage procession in Washington, D.C. The official program for the same day. The horse, the banner, and the Capitol show who the procession wanted to look like. Ida B. Wells’s decision to leave the “rear contingent” and walk with the Illinois delegation is the part the program does not print. Color official program cover for the Woman Suffrage Procession, Washington, D.C., 3 March 1913, showing a woman on horseback before the Capitol. The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920. It says the right to vote shall not be denied on account of sex. It did not repeal Jim Crow. Many Black women in the South were still blocked by poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence. The amendment changed the federal text. The local machinery that decided who could actually cast a ballot did not change with it. The same years, in a different country: Qiu Jin 秋瑾 (1875–1907). She unbound her feet, left an arranged marriage, studied in Japan from 1904, and in 1907 edited 中國女報 (the Chinese Women’s Journal) in Shanghai. The journal argued for women’s education and against bound feet in the same pages as anti-Qing politics. After Xu Xilin’s uprising in Anqing failed, she was arrested and executed. Her public life does not sit on a line from Seneca Falls to 1920. It belongs in the same decades anyway: a woman deciding she would count in public, under a different state, and paying for it with her life. People Four people the usual story has to include Sojourner Truth c. 1797–1883 Born enslaved in New York. She sold cartes-de-visite captioned “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” The card was a living: lectures did not pay enough, and she needed the sales. It was also a legal claim. She copyrighted the image in her own name, which was unusual for a sitter, and still more unusual for a woman who had been treated as property. Carte-de-visite, 1864, printed with her own line: “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” Ida B. Wells 1862–1931 Anti-lynching journalist; Southern Horrors appeared in 1892. She treated suffrage and racial terror as one fight, which is why a segregated parade order in 1913 was not a small slight. She refused the rear contingent and walked into the Illinois line as it passed. Ida B. Wells-Barnett, photographed by Mary Garrity around 1893. Inez Milholland 1886–1916 Lawyer, and the image the 1913 procession needed at its head. She died in 1916 on a western suffrage tour, at thirty. The photograph of her on the white horse outlived the campaign she was riding for. Milholland on Pennsylvania Avenue, 3 March 1913: white cape, white horse, a planned public image. Qiu Jin 秋瑾 1875–1907 Unbound feet, study in Japan, editor of 中國女報, executed after the 1907 Anqing uprising. If the phrase “first wave” cannot hold her, the phrase is too narrow. Her life is not the problem. Qiu Jin, photographed between 1900 and 1907, in the last years of the Qing dynasty. A story “I sell the shadow to support the substance” Sojourner Truth, 1864. She sold the card because lectures did not pay enough. She also put her own copyright on it. Sojourner Truth’s 1864 carte-de-visite, with the printed line I sell the shadow to support the substance under her portrait. Truth sold her image because lectures did not pay enough. On the card, the “shadow” is the photograph — a thing that can be reproduced, captioned, and passed from hand to hand. The “substance” is the work, and the body that had been treated as property. She put the sentence on the card in English, under her own name, and made the sale part of the argument: I will be paid for the copy of me that you can hold. Keep the card in mind when a movement talks about “women” as if the category were already settled. Someone is always deciding which body is the subject of the campaign, and which body is only used to illustrate it. After After 1920 the coalition thinned, and a later generation named a second wave In the United States the 1920s through the 1950s are often called the “doldrums”: the vote arrived, and the suffrage coalition thinned. The word is a later summary, not a name people used at the time. It describes a particular organized feminism going quiet. It does not mean the questions ended, and it does not mean every woman had been in that coalition. What later writers called the second wave — the 1960s and 1970s — turned to the workplace, to sexuality, and to housework. “The personal is political” became a slogan for that turn. The who-counts problem returned in public, including in the Combahee River Collective statement of 1977, which refused to treat race, sex, and class as separate queues. The wave metaphor itself is a later teaching device. It offers a tidy sequence: first the vote, then the rest. It hides the people who were never in that sequence — and the fights that did not wait for the next numbered period. A question A question to keep asking When a movement says “we,” who is being asked to wait? Time to Remember — Time of the Suffragettes (1911–1913) British Pathé compilation of British suffragette newsreel, 1911–1913. This is not film of the 1913 Washington procession. The Derby — 1912 & 1913 British Pathé racing newsreel. It includes the 1913 Epsom Derby, when Emily Wilding Davison stepped onto the course. Again: Britain, not Pennsylvania Avenue.
